**69,19,3d** And when they said, ‘Yes’, he said to them, ‘My cup you shall drink; but to sit on my right and on my left is not for me to give, but it is theirs for whom it has been made ready by the Father.’”

**69,19,4a** Then again the apostle declares, “God raised him from the dead”, as if he had need of the one who raised him.

**69,19,4b** And, he says, “an angel of the Lord appeared strengthening him, because he was in agony, and sweated, and his sweat became for him like clots of blood”, in the Gospel according to Luke, when he went away and prayed as he was about to be betrayed.

**69,19,5a** And again on the cross, he says, he was saying, “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani”, which is, “My God, my God, to what end have you forsaken me?”

**69,19,5b** And do you see, he says, how he stands in need of help?

**69,19,6a** But as to his saying, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me”, and that “we two are one, so that they too may be one”.

**69,19,6b** So then he speaks of being one not by nature at all, but by concord.

**69,19,7a** And not only this, but they also deny that he took a human soul, preparing this very point in advance.

**69,19,7b** For they confess that he had true flesh from Mary, and everything that is in man, except a soul; so that when you hear of hunger or thirst, or weariness, or journeying, or sweat, or sleep, or deep indignation, and say that it was because of his becoming man that he was subject to these, they will tell you afterwards that flesh by itself does not do these things unless it has the soul.

**69,19,8a** And in fact it is indeed so.

**69,19,8b** “What else is it, then,” he says, “but that his Godhead was in need?” – so that, when they say that his Godhead was in need, they may declare him foreign and alien to the essence and true nature of the Father.

**69,19,9a** And I think that, for one who possesses understanding, when one or two testimonies, or five, of those wrongly devised by them have been refuted and overturned, and the whole truth has been proclaimed and clearly confirmed in the faith of orthodoxy, they will stand refuted before those already mentioned, who possess a godly mind, even if after these solutions they bring forward ten thousand other passages of their devising.

**69,19,9b** For from the few the greater number will be resolved, since they carry the same force.

**69,20,1** And I shall begin first by speaking of the place from which they undertook wickedly to plant the root of their bitterness: the saying spoken by Solomon, “The Lord created me as a beginning of his ways towards his works”.

**69,20,2a** And nowhere at all has Scripture confirmed it, nor has any of the apostles made mention of this passage so as to bring it to bear on the name of Christ.

**69,20,2b** So then it is not of the Son of God at all that he speaks, though he does say, “I, Wisdom, have made counsel and knowledge my dwelling, and I have called upon understanding”.

**69,20,3a** For how many wisdoms of God are there, so called in a loose sense?

**69,20,3b** But the Only-begotten is one, so called not in a loose sense but in truth.

**69,20,3c** For all things are wisdom of God.

**69,20,3d** And whatever is from God is wisdom.

**69,20,4a** But there is another, a peculiar one, which is above all things, that is, the Only-begotten, who is wisdom not in a loose sense but in truth, who is ever with the Father, who is the power of God and wisdom, according to what is written, “But for us Christ is God’s power and God’s wisdom”.

**69,20,4b** And there is “the wisdom of the poor man, despised.

**69,20,4c** And since the world, in the wisdom of God, did not know God, it pleased him to save those who believe through the foolishness of the gospel.

**69,20,4d** And God turned the wisdom of this world into folly; and God bestowed on Solomon a heart like the outpouring of the sea, and he became wise above the sons of Anak.

**69,20,4e** And God gave wisdom to Bezalel, and God filled Uri with wisdom.”

**69,20,5a** And there is much to say about wisdom.

**69,20,5b** And “what is the place of understanding, and where was wisdom found?”

**69,20,5c** So even if this celebrated Wisdom says, “I, Wisdom, have made counsel and knowledge my dwelling; I have called upon understanding.

**69,20,5d** Through me kings reign, and through me great men are magnified, and rulers write righteousness, and princes hold sway over the earth.

**69,20,6a** I love those who love me, and those who seek me shall find me.

**69,20,6b** Riches and glory are mine, and possession of many things, and righteousness; in the path of righteousness I walk, and amid the paths of justice I go about, so that I may share out substance to those who love me and fill their treasuries with good things.

**69,20,7a** If I tell you the things that happen day by day, I shall be mindful to number the things from of old.

**69,20,7b** The Lord created me as a beginning of his ways towards his works; he founded me before the age, in the beginning, before the making of the earth and before the making of the abysses, before the fountains of the waters went forth, and before the mountains were firmly fixed, and before all the hills, he begets me”, and what follows.

**69,20,8a** It is clear that, when some wish to speak against the passage, those on the opposing side make use of a counter-objection, because of the name of Wisdom and the sequence of the text which says, “The Lord created me”.

**69,20,8b** And because of its saying, “I, Wisdom, have made counsel my dwelling”.

**69,20,8c** Namely, that, see, Wisdom, having named herself at the outset and proceeding in order, refers to herself when she says, “The Lord created me”.

**69,20,9a** For see, above she says, “I, Wisdom”.

**69,20,9b** And further down she says, “If I declare to you the things that happen day by day, I shall be mindful to number the things from of old”.

**69,20,9c** And what is it that she says: “The Lord created me as a beginning of his ways”?

**69,21,1a** Now we have said that there are a good many wisdoms, so called in a loose sense, given by God from time to time, because God accomplishes all things in wisdom.

**69,21,1b** But there is one Wisdom of the Father that truly is, the subsistent God the Word.

**69,21,1c** For the text itself in no way obliges me to say that it concerns the Son of God; for it did not declare it, and no apostle made mention of it, nor indeed did the gospel.

**69,21,2a** But if, after all, this were understood as concerning the Son of God, the saying is not the same as it sounds, nor is it set down for straightforward judgement.

**69,21,2b** For the whole book is proverbs.

**69,21,2c** And everything spoken in proverb is not the same in its meaning, but it narrates in one form of words and is allegorized in another meaning.

**69,21,3** If, then, it says this, and some dare to apply this to the Son of God – far be it! – this saying is not applied to his Godhead.

**69,21,4a** But if it can be fulfilled in his coming in the flesh.

**69,21,4b** For since Wisdom herself built herself the house; and if indeed it were said piously from the person of his becoming man, as his coming in the flesh speaks concerning his Godhead, “The Lord created me” – that is, built me in the womb of Mary – “as a beginning of his ways towards his works”.

**69,21,5a** For the body taken from Mary was the beginning of the ways of Christ’s coming down into the world, in his work of righteousness and salvation.

**69,21,5b** But surely he whose heart is damaged, and who has been struck with this dreadful blow, holding in his mind his enmity concerning the Son of God, would leap forward:

**69,21,6a** “Because,” he says, “she said, ‘If I tell you the things that happen day by day, I shall be mindful [also] to number the things from of old.’”

**69,21,6b** And you see that it says “from of old”; but the coming of God in the flesh took place after sixty-two generations, according to Matthew; how then can the things from the beginning of the age be said of this?

**69,22,1** And those who have strayed from the whole way of the truth do not know that the divine Scripture, in all that it wishes to teach, always begins its narration not by setting out at once upon what is most ancient and, so to speak, upon the chief point, but begins from the things nearest at hand, so that it may indicate last what was before.

**69,22,2a** For this is why it also said, “If I tell you the things that happen day by day”, and from these I call to mind “also the things from of old”.

**69,22,2b** So too God showed Moses first the burning fire, and at the outset the vision took place in the fire of a bush.

**69,22,2c** An angel spoke to him at once, and afterwards the Lord from the bush.

**69,22,3a** And straightway, in speaking to him, he does not seek the things that are seen, but asks about the things from the beginning.

**69,22,3b** “Come,” he says, “let me send you to the children of Israel, and you shall say to them, ‘The God of our fathers has sent me, Abraham’s God and Isaac’s God and Jacob’s God’”, naming Abraham and those with him, five or six generations before Moses.

**69,22,3c** And since he said “God of the fathers”, he declared what was ancient.

**69,22,4a** But Moses, graced by God with understanding, asked not about these things but about what was higher still: “If I go away to them, and they put it to me, ‘What is his name?’

**69,22,4b** what shall I say to them?”

**69,22,5a** And he then reveals, “I am he who is.”

**69,22,5b** And at first he began from the things nearest at hand, but at the last he made known what is highest.

**69,22,5c** But Luke too begins from the things below and nearest at hand: “Jesus himself, when he began, was about thirty years old, being the son, as was supposed, of Joseph, of Heli, of Matthan, of Nathan, of David, of Judah, of Jacob, of Abraham, of Nahor, of Noah, of Lamech, of Enoch, of Seth, of Adam, of God.”

**69,22,5d** And you see how he showed first the coming in the flesh, and then what is last.

**69,22,6** That is why Matthew too, in the genealogy according to the flesh, wishing to bring Christ’s coming down to the understanding of men, did not say at once, “The origin of Jesus Christ, son of Abraham”, but first “son of David”, and then “son of Abraham”, so that, pointing out what had lately been done and what was most nearly joined together, and what was higher still, he might indicate what is still above all creation and cannot be taken away.

**69,23,1** That is why the blessed John, when he came, found people occupied with Christ’s coming here below; the Ebionites had gone astray because of Christ’s genealogy according to the flesh, traced down from Abraham and carried back by Luke as far as Adam; and he found the Cerinthians and Merinthians claiming that he was simply a man, conceived by intercourse, and the Nazoraeans, and many other sects;

**69,23,2a** and so, coming last, for he is the fourth to write the gospel, he begins, so to speak, to call back those who had gone astray and were occupied with Christ’s coming here below, and to say to them, like one who comes behind and sees some turned aside onto rough roads, having left the straight and true one: “Where are you being carried?

**69,23,2b** Where are you walking?

**69,23,2c** You who walk the rough road that causes stumbling and leads to a chasm, turn back.

**69,23,3a** It is not so: God the Word, begotten from the Father on high, is not from Mary only; he is not from the times of Joseph her betrothed, nor from the times of Salathiel and Zerubbabel and David and Abraham and Jacob and Noah and Adam; but in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

**69,23,3b** This “was” and “was” and “was” does not admit that he ever was not.

**69,23,4a** And you see how he at once indicates first the things nearest at hand.

**69,23,4b** How Matthew showed the way through the genealogy, and even he did not set it out in exact detail, though he did carry the genealogy down from above.

**69,23,4c** How Mark wrote of the things done in the world and of “a voice crying in the wilderness,” concerning the Lord foretold by the prophets and the law.

**69,23,4d** How Luke, coming later, led upward from the things below to the things above.

**69,23,4e** John, the fourth, made known last the crown and the pure essence of the order on high and of the Godhead that always is,

**69,23,5a** as Solomon too says in a proverb, “the beginning of the ways,” supposing that some should wish to speak devoutly of the incarnate dispensation, as though the text said of Christ’s Godhead that the Godhead itself built the house, that the Godhead itself wrought the flesh and the becoming man, a beginning of his ways toward his works of the salvation and goodness of mankind.

**69,23,5b** Then immediately afterward, as the matter advances, it says, “He established me in the beginning.”

**69,23,6a** Was the Son of God, then, created according to his Godhead and afterward established?

**69,23,6b** Let the engineers tell us, those surveyors of the things above, by what craft wisdom was created, by what tool it was established.

**69,23,6c** But if one must reason at all, let one flee from so great a depth of blasphemy and not lay a hand on the Godhead of the only-begotten, which always exists with the Father and is begotten from him.

**69,23,7a** For the Word was ever with the Father, ever Wisdom, ever Lord, God from God.

**69,23,7b** Ever true Light and not counterfeit, ever having his being from him, being Truth and existing as Life.

**69,24,1a** And why should I say a great deal about this?

**69,24,1b** Then it says, “He established me in the beginning.”

**69,24,2a** So it is possible to see a devout sense: that here it indicates the human soul.

**69,24,2b** For “The Lord created me” is spoken by the incarnate becoming man, if indeed it is to be understood in this way.

**69,24,2c** And “he established” means that he was established in the soul.

**69,24,2d** And “before all the hills he begets me” is said to show the begetting from above.

**69,24,2e** And we have said this not as laying it down as altogether so, but rather as having devoutly understood it of the coming in the flesh.

**69,24,3a** Even if one ought to speak in this way, still no one could compel us to say that this saying is by all means about Christ.

**69,24,3b** But if it is to be said of Christ, it has its own force too, spoken not by way of divination but according to the devoutness of reasoning, so as not to reckon anything of deficiency against God by supposing that he has a Godhead lower than the essence of the Father.

**69,24,4a** For indeed some of our fathers, orthodox men, assigned this to the coming in the flesh, having so understood it, if indeed one should speak thus, the passage about “The Lord created me, and established me.”

**69,24,4b** And this is the devout reasoning, as great fathers have explained it.

**69,24,5a** And if any of the orthodox should not wish to accept it, he will not be compelled.

**69,24,5b** And with regard to those who are strangers and aliens to the faith, the harm comes to nothing.

**69,24,5c** For this will not bring down on us anything of deficiency, since the Godhead is free and is ever with the Father.

**69,24,6a** And whatever Christ suffered, he suffered; but he was not changed in his nature, and his Godhead remained in its own impassibility.

**69,24,6b** Therefore, having willed to suffer by his own good pleasure for the human race, since the Godhead could not suffer, being in itself impassible, he, being Wisdom, took our passible body, so that in it he might consent to suffer and take upon himself our sufferings, the Godhead being present together in the flesh.

**69,24,6c** For indeed the Godhead does not suffer.

**69,24,7a** For how will he who says, “I am the life,” be able to die?

**69,24,7b** No, God remains impassible.

**69,24,7c** But he suffers together with the flesh, so that the suffering may be reckoned to the Godhead, the Godhead suffering, to the end that our salvation may be in God.

**69,24,7d** But the suffering is in the flesh, so that we may not have a passible God but an impassible one, who reckons the suffering to himself by choice and not by necessity.

**69,25,1** Yet these people too, without having either handled or understood the Hebrew words, or how their meaning stands, have rashly and headlong sprung up as dreadful enemies, seeking a pretext by which to maim the faith, or rather themselves, for it is not the truth they maim; and since they came upon “The Lord created me”, they recklessly fall to dreaming, like men seeing visions, bringing into life things of no use and throwing the world into confusion.

**69,25,2a** But the Hebrew does not read so; hence Aquila says, “The Lord acquired me.”

**69,25,2b** And those who beget children always say, “I have acquired a son.”

**69,25,2c** Yet not even Aquila rendered the meaning.

**69,25,2d** For indeed “I have acquired a son” is said as of something recent.

**69,25,2e** But in God there is nothing recent.

**69,25,3a** And should anyone acknowledge that the Son has been begotten from the Father, then he is not created.

**69,25,3b** And he has been begotten timelessly and without beginning.

**69,25,4a** For there is no time between Son and Father, lest some time should come to exceed the Son.

**69,25,4b** For if all things are through him, then the times are too.

**69,25,5a** But if there exists a time that is before all things, how will this be?

**69,25,5b** Unless, then, another son is to be sought, through whom time came into being before the Son.

**69,25,5c** And there are many matters which the notions of men who busy themselves with curiosities and do nothing good lead into endless perplexity.

**69,25,6a** But the Hebrew has adonai, which is rendered “Lord”, and kanani, which can mean both “brought me forth as his young” and “acquired me”.

**69,25,6b** But the most exact rendering is “brought me forth as his young”.

**69,25,6c** And what young one is not born of the nature of the one who begot it?

**69,25,6d** And here, among bodily formed creatures, the young that are brought forth come about through the pairing of male and female, from man to beast and birds and the rest.

**69,25,7** Therefore the only-begotten, being in all things the Wisdom of the Father, and wishing to do all things for correction, so that no one might reckon to him what is not so and fall away from the truth, when he came to dwell among the race of men, and was born by nature of a woman, and lay in a virgin’s womb for the time of pregnancy, was not conceived of the seed of a man, so that pairing and intertwining might not take place in the birth in the flesh as well; but he took the flesh from a mother alone, and fulfilled in himself his own becoming man as complete, not deficient but true.

**69,25,8** And it is not that, because he was not from the seed of a man, he had anything lacking; for he had all things completely, having everything, flesh and sinews and veins and all the other things there are, and a soul truly and not in appearance, and a mind and all that belongs to the becoming man, without sin, as it is written, “tempted in all things as a man,

**69,25,9** without sin,” so that by being born here completely and not deficiently from a mother alone according to the flesh, he might show those who wish to see the truth and not to blind their own minds that above too he has been begotten completely from the Father, timelessly and without beginning, and below he has been born from a mother only, without stain and without defilement.

**69,26,1a** Let us also interpret the expression adonai kanani, which is “The Lord brought me forth as his young.”

**69,26,1b** For everything that begets will beget something like itself.

**69,26,1c** Man begets man, and God begets God; and man begets according to the flesh, but God according to the spirit.

**69,26,2a** And as the man who begets is, such too is the one begotten by him.

**69,26,2b** The man who has begotten his own son did so held within passions; and the impassible God begot the Son begotten by him impassibly, truly and not in appearance, from himself and not from outside himself, being impassible Spirit and begetting Spirit impassibly, being impassible God and having begotten true God impassibly.

**69,26,3** For if he himself created all things, and you confess, Arius, that God has created all things, he himself also begot the Son.

**69,26,4a** And should you say, “If he begot, then in begetting he suffered,” we in turn shall say to you, “If he suffered in begetting, he grew weary in creating.”

**69,26,4b** But all that he wills is at once; he has all things in himself in perfection; and neither will passion fall upon the Son in his creating, nor will the divine be thought to be held by passion because of the undefiled begetting of the Son.

**69,26,4c** For the Father is unchangeable, the Son unchangeable, the Holy Spirit unchangeable: one essence, one Godhead.

**69,26,5a** But you will surely say to me, “Did he beget willing it, or not willing it?”

**69,26,5b** And I am not like you, contentious man, so as to conceive any such thing of God.

**69,26,5c** For if he begot without willing it, he begot unwillingly.

**69,26,5d** And if he begot willing it, then the will was before the Son, and even a moment of time will intervene between him and the Son because of the will.

**69,26,6a** But in God there is no time for counsel, no willing for deliberation.

**69,26,6b** So he begot neither willing nor not willing, but in the nature that is above will.

**69,26,6c** For his is a nature of Godhead, neither needing will nor doing anything without will, but having all things at once from itself and lacking nothing of the things that are.

**69,27,1a** Yet again the same Arius hunts for words, ever roaming over everything and contriving wicked things for himself, not as the divine writing has it, but as one himself sick over questions and disputes about words; and to no useful end, but to the ruin of himself and of those led astray by him, he seizes upon the saying in which the Lord, blessing the disciples, spoke the words, “Father, give them to have life within themselves.

**69,27,1b** And this is eternal life, that they may know you, who alone are true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ.”

**69,27,2** But I have already treated all these matters in the great discourse on the faith, in which, once again, constrained according to our modest ability and weakness by the urging exhortation of the brethren, we wrote on the faith, a discourse to which we gave the name Ancoratus.

**69,27,3** For indeed, as far as our poor mind was able by the help of God, gathering from all Scripture the true things of God’s teaching, we plainly set forth, like an anchor for those who wish it, the holy faith of the fathers, apostolic and prophetic, proclaimed from the beginning until now in the holy church of God, so that the understanding may be held fast and made secure, and not be tossed about by the devices of the devil nor harmed by the surge of the sects that has been stirred up in the world in so many gushing streams.

**69,27,4** For so too the Lord taught his own disciples, saying, “If what you heard from the beginning abides in you, [and if what you heard from the beginning abides in you,] you will remain in me, and I in you; I also am in the Father, and you are in me.”

**69,27,5** So then the true things of the faith heard from the beginning from the Lord abide in the holy church of God;

**69,27,6** and for this reason the holy church of God and the orthodox faith remain in the Lord, and the only-begotten Lord remains within the Father, and the Father within the Son, and we abide in him through the Holy Spirit, if we become temples that have room for his Holy Spirit;

**69,27,7a** as the holy apostle of God said, “You are God’s temple, and God’s Spirit dwells in you.”

**69,27,7b** So then the Spirit is God from God, the Holy Spirit through whom we are called temples, if we make his Spirit dwell in us.

**69,27,7c** For it is the Spirit of Christ, a Spirit proceeding from the Father and receiving from the Son, as the Only-begotten himself acknowledges.

**69,28,1a** All these things, then, we have explained in the discourse on the faith mentioned before, the one which, as I said, was written to the regions of Pamphylia and Pisidia.

**69,28,1b** But here, since we have come to the words that are next in question, we have been eager of necessity to recall the same things again, so to speak, because of the heresiarch Arius now before us and the Arians who follow him, so that we may undo their wickedness, which turns sweet into bitter, and good into evil, and light into darkness.

**69,28,2a** For upon such people the woe is laid down in full by the Lord through the holy Isaiah, upon those who turn good things into evil.

**69,28,2b** And God is nowhere the cause of such things; but each of these, whether through vainglory, or through prejudice, or through self-chosen wisdom, or through demonic conceit, fell away from the truth and brought affliction into the world, their own wickedness.

**69,28,3** Come then, let us examine this passage, so that we may know the things spoken by the Lord, as the holy apostle says, “We too possess God’s Spirit, so that we may know the things graciously given us by God, which things we also speak,” and so on.

**69,28,4a** The Lord, then, says, “Give them to have life within themselves.

**69,28,4b** And this is eternal life, that they may know you, who alone are true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ.”

**69,29,1a** But this Arius and those who follow him leap up, stirring up confusion, and say, of the fact that he prayed to God at all and said, “Father, give them to have life within themselves”: “He is not equal to the one who provides life.

**69,29,1b** For if he were of the essence of the Father, he would himself bestow life, and would not ask the Father to give, through petitions, to those who receive the things given by him.”

**69,29,2** And those who have perverted their understanding against themselves do not know that the only-begotten came in all things to become for you a pattern and salvation, standing in the midst of the world as in a theatre, like an athlete who undoes all that has risen up against the truth from the unbelief and slander and error of the devil, here through idolatry, there through Jewish conceit, there through unbelief, and there through the exaltation of men’s opinion, so that he might teach men to be humble-minded, so that no one, being a man, should think himself to be anything, but should refer the whole to the Father of all.

**69,29,3** And for this reason, though he is life, as his words “I am the life” declare, and has power to provide life, he does not wish to disturb what is right, but came to gather into one principle, into one Godhead, into one truth, into one concord, into one doxology, both the salvation and the understanding of men; and in the presence of the disciples he asks the Father.

**69,29,4a** For what son does not ask of his father?

**69,29,4b** And what father does not give to his son?

**69,29,4c** And what son turns out to be of another kind than his father’s nature?

**69,29,4d** And for this reason the only-begotten Son from the Father, full of grace and truth, was not in need of the fullness, not lacking in the truth, but full of grace and truth.

**69,29,5a** And being full, he both gives and has the power to give.

**69,29,5b** But he wishes to refer everything back to the Father.

**69,29,5c** For the Son glorifies the Father; the Father glorifies the Only-begotten.

**69,29,5d** “For I glorified you on earth,” the Son said to the Father.

**69,29,5e** And to the Son the Father said, “I have glorified you, and will glorify again.”

**69,29,6a** For there is no separation, there is no envy, in the Godhead.

**69,29,6b** “Give them, then, to have life within themselves.”

**69,29,6c** He who is life wishes to receive life from the Father and to give it to the disciples, though he himself is life, so that he may not divide the unity, so that he may not become a stumbling-block to the Jews, so that the Jews may hear him asking of the Father and giving to their disciples.

**69,30,1a** How then does the Son ask the Father?

**69,30,1b** As one who does not have, and so asks?

**69,30,1c** No; but he is indicating the unity of the Trinity, which completely provides worthy gifts to the one who receives.

**69,30,1d** And to indicate that the Godhead is one, in another place again he gives no longer by asking, but by his own authority, what is his own: as a spring from a spring, and God from God, he breathed into their face and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit”; and at another time, raising his hands, he said, “Receive the Holy Spirit.”

**69,30,2a** And he has life in himself, so that he may give it to whom he wishes to give.

**69,30,2b** “For as the Father has life in himself, so the Son too has life in himself.”

**69,30,3** And you see that, for honour’s sake towards the Father, and for the sake of a single unity and a single doxology, and so that the disciples should not think that the Only-begotten had come to lead the minds of believers away from the God of the Law and of the prophets – for this reason, being God and knowing beforehand the malice of men, he addresses his word as though to the Father, and grants the Father a glory that cannot be taken from him, so that the Manichaean may be shamed for denying the Father, so that the disciples may learn that the Godhead in the Old and in the New Testament is the same, so that the Jews may be abashed because the Only-begotten came not to teach of another God but to disclose his own Godhead and that of his heavenly Father.

**69,30,5a** “Give them, then, to have life within themselves,” though he himself was preaching this life.

**69,30,5b** How then did he request of the Father that he give them that which he himself was teaching and bestowing?

**69,30,5c** For afterwards he made plain what the life is, saying, “This,” he says, “is the life, that they may know you, the only true God.”

**69,31,1a** Then Arius and those who follow him leap up because of the phrase, as though they had found something against the truth: “He said,” he says, “‘the only true God’.

**69,31,1b** You see, then, that the Father alone is the true one.”

**69,31,2a** But we too ask you: what then do you say?

**69,31,2b** “The Father alone is the true one.”

**69,31,2c** Then what will the Son be?

**69,31,2d** Is the Son not true?

**69,31,2e** If the Son is not true, our faith is vain, the preaching among us is vain;

**69,31,3** you will be found, blaspheming against yourselves, to be likening the Son to the nameless and lawless idols, of which the prophets spoke in the person of those who had been deceived, as each of the prophets made mention of this word, saying also, “Your fathers made false gods for themselves, and the hills proved false.”

**69,31,4a** So then the only-begotten too is judged in this way among you, and so shamefully do you think about him who redeemed you, if indeed he did redeem you.

**69,31,4b** But you are no longer of his fold, since you deny your Saviour and the one who bought you; for if God is not true, neither is he to be worshipped, and if he is a created being, he is not God.

**69,31,4c** And if he is not to be worshipped, how then is he spoken of as God?

**69,31,5a** Cease, you who again practise the Babylonian nature, who have set up the image and figure of Nebuchadnezzar, who sound this much-talked-of trumpet to unite those who wage war, who with musical instruments and cymbals and psaltery bring the peoples to a fall through your erring words, making them ready to be slaves to an image rather than to God and to truth.

**69,31,5b** And who else is true as the Son of God is?

**69,31,6a** “For who among the sons of God shall be made equal to the Lord?” says the Scripture.

**69,31,6b** And: “Another shall not be reckoned beside him.”

**69,31,6c** And what does it say?

**69,31,6d** So that you may see that it speaks of the Son, it says, narrating in order, “He found out every way of knowledge, and gave it.”

**69,31,7a** “And after these things he was seen upon earth and lived among men.”

**69,31,7b** How then have these things not been said truly of him?

**69,31,7c** He it is who also says, “I am the truth.”

**69,32,1a** But you will say to me, “How did the only-begotten, the true God, say, ‘That they may know you, the only true God’?”

**69,32,1b** So that it might not be thought polytheism, so that there might be no division of the life-giving knowledge.

**69,32,1c** For if the Father alone is true God, the Son from the Father is true, truly begotten.

**69,32,2a** For in honouring the Father and revealing him as the only true God, he showed himself to have been begotten true from the Father.

**69,32,2b** For this reason the Father is true, and the only-begotten Son is the true God.

**69,32,3a** And from where is this to be shown?

**69,32,3b** Well, look at the words here, how here he calls the Father the only true God.

**69,32,3c** In the Gospel according to John, however, it says, “There was the true light.”

**69,32,3d** And what true light is there but the only-begotten?

**69,32,3e** Again, the Scriptures declare concerning God that “God is light”, and it did not say, “God is true light.”

**69,32,3f** But of the only-begotten Son of God it says that the only-begotten is true light.

**69,32,4a** And of the Father, “true God”, and it did not say, “God is true light.”

**69,32,4b** And of the Son, that he is God; and in “The Son is God” it did not add “true”.

**69,32,4c** And where it says “God is light”, it did not add “true light”.

**69,32,4d** What then do we say about the Father?

**69,32,4e** That God is indeed true light; and so we shall not make the divine deficient.

**69,32,5a** And since “the true light” is not written of him in addition, we would be sinning if we said that he is not true light.

**69,32,5b** And since it is written of the Son that he is God, and that God was with the Father who is; for indeed “the Word was God.”

**69,32,5c** And it did not say, “The Word became God,” but “was God.”

**69,32,5d** And from the two the equal balance will be shown: from “The Father is true God” and “The Son is true light”, the equal weight of their dignity will appear; and from “The Son is God” and “God is light”, the equal balance of the doxology will be found.

**69,32,6** And there will be no difference, nor could anyone gainsay the truth; but true God is the Father, and true Son is the Only-begotten.

**69,33,1a** Further, I am compelled to speak here about the Holy Spirit too, so that I may not, by passing over something, give the enemies who wish it the means of having their pretexts.

**69,33,1b** For so too it is with the Holy Spirit, as the Lord in person bears witness in his words: “the Spirit of the truth”, “the Spirit of the Father”.

**69,33,1c** And the apostle calls him “the Spirit of Christ”.

**69,33,2a** So then the Spirit of truth is Spirit of truth and Spirit of God, as true God, as true light, as Spirit of the Father, as Spirit of the Son.

**69,33,2b** For the Trinity is one, the doxology one, the Godhead one, the lordship one.

**69,33,3** Father is Father, Son is Son, Holy Spirit is Holy Spirit; the Trinity is not a blending, not standing apart from its own unity, not lacking in perfection, not other than its own distinctness, but all perfection, three perfect, one Godhead.

**69,33,4a** And the sword of the adversaries has fallen.

**69,33,4b** For indeed so it is written, “They have become an arrow of infants.”

**69,33,4c** For indeed infants, even if they want to take up arrows, are powerless, unable to do anything with them in their hands.

**69,33,4d** And if the infants are thrown into confusion as well, they rather slay themselves and wrong themselves, unable to turn the attack of the arrow upon others, just as these too have marshalled their error against themselves, but will bring nothing down upon the sons of the truth.

**69,34,1a** But I shall pass on again to other words that they have devised.

**69,34,1b** And first of all, it is a matter for astonishment how they have used dissimulation to deceive those who are simple and guileless by nature: as the serpent deceived Eve, who was guileless, in the same way these too, when they wish to win someone over, proceed first with much flattery and lavishness and attention, together with promises and threats, telling those who do not wish to go along with their faith, “You are opposing the imperial orders and the wrath of the emperor Valens.”

**69,34,2a** And what do they say?

**69,34,2b** “Why, what is it that we say?

**69,34,2c** This is the faith; it is only that you are vainglorious.”

**69,34,2d** Let us see, then, whether it is the same faith.

**69,34,2e** They say, then, “We confess the Son begotten of the Father, and we do not deny it.

**69,34,3a** But we must,” they say, “also confess ‘the creature’ and ‘the thing made’.”

**69,34,3b** But nothing is more foolish.

**69,34,3c** For everything that is created is not like what has been begotten, nor is what is begotten like what is created, especially with regard to that one pure and perfect essence.

**69,34,4a** For everything has been created by God.

**69,34,4b** But the Son of God alone has been begotten, and the Holy Spirit alone came forth from the Father and took from the Son.

**69,34,4c** But all other things are created, and they neither came forth as proceeding from the Father nor as receiving of the Son, but from the fullness of the Son, as it is written, “For by the word of God all things were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power.”

**69,34,5a** “But,” they say, “one must also confess ‘the creature’, since the Scripture said it, ‘the creature’ being said rather figuratively, and ‘the offspring’ being said figuratively.

**69,34,5b** For even if we say ‘offspring’, we shall not say it as of one of the offspring.”

**69,34,5c** So then, while they say ‘the offspring’, and yet not a true offspring, they deceive the more guileless.

**69,34,6a** “And we confess ‘the creature’ too,” they say.

**69,34,6b** “For since Christ has also been called door and way and pillar and cloud and rock and little lamb and lamb and kid and calf and lion and spring and Wisdom and Word and Son and angel and Christ and Saviour and Lord and man and Son of man and corner-stone and sun and prophet and bread and king and builder and husbandman and shepherd and vine and all such things.

**69,34,6c** So,” they say, “we say ‘the creature’ too, by an extended use of the word.

**69,34,6d** For we must confess it.”

**69,35,1a** Alas for such wicked supposition and knavery!

**69,35,1b** May the Lord not grant that any of the sons of the truth be led on by such dissimulation as, through such premises, to be persuaded to admit the name of ‘creature’ too for the Son of God, and so to confess it; for let them give us the use of this term, and an account of their reasonings.

**69,35,2a** For all those names have been spoken by an extended use, none of them bearing upon the Godhead of the Son, nor making him deficient in his own essentiality with respect to the Father.

**69,35,2b** Whether he is called door, since through him we enter, or way, since through him we walk, or pillar, since he is the foundation of the truth, or cloud, since he sheltered the children of Israel, or pillar, on account of the radiance of the fire, which shed light in the wilderness, or manna, since they denied him, the bread from heaven, or bread,

**69,35,3a** since through him we are made strong, or angel, since he is the angel of great counsel; for the name ‘angel’ is used of different things.

**69,35,3b** For Rahab received the angels, and those who had been sent were not angels, but only men who brought word about the place.

**69,35,3c** So too the only-begotten, since he announced the will of the Father to men, is the angel of great counsel, announcing the great counsel in the world.

**69,35,4a** And stone: not a stone without sense, but by an extended use, because he became a stumbling-block to the Jews, but for us a foundation of salvation.

**69,35,4b** And corner-stone, because he bound together the old and the new testament, circumcision and uncircumcision, into one union.

**69,35,5a** And lamb, because of his innocence, and because through him sin has been done away from men, in his being offered to the Father as a sheep to the slaughter.

**69,35,5b** Since he who is impassible came to suffer for us, so that we might be saved.

**69,35,5c** And if there is anything else that by the same uses contributes to the salvation of the sons of men, it is referred to him from the divine Scripture by an extended use.

**69,36,1a** What good, then, would ‘creature’ do?

**69,36,1b** Or what use does it serve for our salvation, and for the glorifying of God the Word incarnate, and for his perfect Godhead?

**69,36,1c** What does it profit us to call him a creature?

**69,36,2a** What does a creature accomplish for created things?

**69,36,2b** What does a creature profit created things?

**69,36,2c** And how did God create God, giving him to be worshipped, when he says, “You shall not make for yourself any likeness, either on earth or in heaven, and you shall not worship it”?

**69,36,2d** How then did he create for himself a Son, and give orders that he be worshipped?

**69,36,2e** All the more since the apostle says, “And they rendered worship to the creature in preference to him who created, and became fools.”

**69,36,2f** For it is folly to speak of a creature as God, and to set aside the first commandment, which says, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve.”

**69,36,3** That is why the holy church of God worships no creature, but a Son who was begotten – the Father within the Son, the Son within the Father, together with the Holy Spirit.

**69,36,4a** “But yes,” he says.

**69,36,4b** “For if I do not say that he is a creature,” he says, “I bring a diminution upon the Father.

**69,36,4c** For what is created does not diminish the one who created it.

**69,36,4d** But what is begotten by nature either produces a contraction, or an expansion, or a lessening, or a cutting, or attaches some such passion to the one who begot it.”

**69,36,5a** But great is the folly of those who reason in this way, as people who liken the divine to themselves and wish to attach to God the passions that belong to them, since God is altogether without passion, in begetting and in creating alike.

**69,36,5b** For just as we suffer in begetting, since we are created, so too we grow weary in creating.

**69,36,5c** And if the Father is subject to passion when he begets, then in creating he grows weary too.

**69,36,6a** But how can one speak of passion in God, and of growing weary, if indeed he grows weary?

**69,36,6b** But he does not grow weary; far from it!

**69,36,6c** “For he will not tire,” says the Scripture.

**69,36,6d** God, then, is Spirit, and he begot the Son as Spirit, without beginning and timelessly, God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not created.

**69,37,1a** But I shall pass on from this saying too, and let us again apply ourselves to others among the things that are said and sung by them with wicked suppositions, and that I have set out above.

**69,37,1b** For again they speak vulgarly, misinterpreting this saying: “Accept your high priest, as one faithful to him who made him.”

**69,37,2a** And first of all they reject this epistle, I mean the one to the Hebrews, removing it outright from the apostle and saying that it is not his.

**69,37,2b** But because of their own sickness they take the saying wrongly to their own hurt, as I said before, bringing in ‘the creature’, supposedly from what is said, “being faithful to him who made him”.

**69,37,3** But anyone possessed of understanding might ask them, and they will be at a loss, having nothing to answer, when our Lord took on the name of high priest to be called by it.

**69,37,4** For nowhere before his coming in the flesh did he have these names: being called stone, being a sheep led to slaughter, being man and Son of man, eagle and lamb, and all the others that are referred to him after the coming in the flesh, as also his being called high priest, by reason of the theme the law proclaimed about him: “The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren.”

**69,37,5** So then the word plainly interprets “the prophet” and “high priest” and “from among them” as belonging to the time after his sojourn here, so that one can see on firm ground how, once again, the invincible power and foreknowledge of God, to stop every mouth raised up against the truth, foretold and secured everything with wonderful illumination.

**69,37,6a** For in the same sequence he says thus: “Every high priest chosen from among men is set in office on behalf of men, to bring both gifts and sacrifices, being able to show forbearance.

**69,37,6b** For he is under necessity for his own sins too.

**69,37,6c** But he who has no sin brought himself as an offering to the Father”; and “from among men” is said because of his sojourn, but “not from men” and “having no need” because of his Godhead.

**69,37,7** And of his Godhead he says, “though he was a Son”, but of his coming in the flesh, “he learned from what he suffered,” he says.

**69,38,1a** And you see that all the things of Christ are smooth, and there is nothing twisted in them.

**69,38,1b** For “a high priest faithful to him who made him” does not here describe even the very forming of the body, nor of his becoming man; it does not speak of creation at all, but of the gift of rank after his sojourn; as also the saying, “He gave him the name that is above every name.”

**69,38,2** And this was not fulfilled formerly in the Godhead, but in the present coming, since his becoming man from Mary received the name that is above every name, to be called Son of God together with God the Word.

**69,38,3** And for this reason, through the apostle himself, it has said here again, “But Jesus, who for a little while was made less than the angels, we see crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death,” so that the master and maker of angels might appear made less than the angels, so that he who is awe-inspiring and fearful to the angels, and who created them from nothing together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, might be spoken of as made less, and so that it might appear plainly that here it speaks not of the Godhead but of his flesh.

**69,38,4a** For the suffering of death is not reckoned to the Word before the flesh, but after the coming in the flesh of one and the same who is both impassible and passible, impassible in the Godhead, suffering in the becoming man, so that both are fulfilled in one: Son of man at once, and Son of God at once.

**69,38,4b** For the Son is called Christ in both together.

**69,39,1a** What, then, did he make him?

**69,39,1b** Let the contentious learn from all that has been said before that nothing in this saying is referred to the Godhead, but to the coming in the flesh.

**69,39,1c** And “he made him” is said not as of a making or of a creature, but as of rank after the coming.

**69,39,2a** For if someone asks a king about his own son, “What is this man to you by birth?”, he will hear from him, “He is my son.”

**69,39,2b** “Is he, then, your true-born son, or a bastard?”

**69,39,2c** And he says, “He is true-born, from me.”

**69,39,2d** “What, then, have you made him?”

**69,39,2e** “I have made him king.”

**69,39,2f** Plainly, this is nothing altered from his father’s rank.

**69,39,3a** And surely, from his having said, “I have made him king,” the king does not on that account say, “I created him.”

**69,39,3b** For in saying “I made” he did not deny the begetting, which he had confessed in saying that he had begotten him; that he declared plainly, while by “I made” he made known his rank.

**69,39,3c** So too the Son is, beyond doubt, believed in and worshipped as Son of the Father by those who desire life.

**69,39,4** And his becoming high priest is because in his body he offered himself to the Father on behalf of mankind, himself priest, himself victim; he offered himself for all creation, acting as high priest, and, having ascended spiritually and in glory, he sat down in that very body at the right hand of the Father, having become high priest for ever, and having passed through the heavens once for all, as the same holy apostle testifies of him in the words that follow.

**69,39,5a** And again their pretext-hunting selection from the divine Scripture has fallen to the ground.

**69,39,5b** Since it is life-giving, and has nothing to make believers stumble, nor anything to diminish the Word by blasphemy.

**69,40,1** Then again he recalls another saying, how John, standing in the wilderness and seeing him coming, was saying, “This is the one about whom I told you, ‘After me comes a man who has come to be before me, for he was before me.’”

**69,40,2a** And first, like men with heavy heads, they alter the very words in their meaning, and say, “How is this fulfilled in the coming in the flesh, since he was not conceived in the womb of Mary ahead of John?

**69,40,2b** Rather,” he says, “as the evangelist has it, ‘Now in the sixth month Gabriel the angel was sent into a town of Galilee, to a virgin pledged to a man whose name was Joseph.

**69,40,2c** And coming in to her he said, “Hail, favoured one, the Lord is with you,”’ and the rest of the passage.

**69,40,3a** So when the virgin was troubled at the greeting, he said to her, ‘Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus.

**69,40,3b** And behold, Elizabeth your kinswoman has conceived a son in her old age; it is now the sixth month with her who is called barren.’

**69,40,3c** And you see,” he says, “that six months before Mary received the good tidings, John already existed.

**69,40,4a** How then will ‘he came to be before me’ be fulfilled in Christ’s coming in the flesh?”

**69,40,4b** And which of the simple, who are not also clearly grounded in understanding, will not be troubled on hearing the saying?

**69,40,5** For it speaks the necessary, pure and life-giving things of the divine Scripture, yet to those who draw wicked things upon themselves they appear rather more harmful, though the sayings are in every way illumined in the Holy Spirit.

**69,40,6a** For what has been left out of the saying that makes for security?

**69,40,6b** For see, he says, “This is he,” indicating what is visible and pointing it out to those who see, “of whom I said to you, ‘After me comes’.”

**69,40,6c** And who comes but a man?

**69,40,6d** But none of those who possess understanding would think our Lord a mere man, but only the sects above that have already been indicated, the followers of Cerinthus and Merinthus and Ebion.

**69,40,7a** But together with “man” there is in any case the “for”, as a safeguard.

**69,40,7b** And the true believers know him as Lord, as John too testifies, “What we have heard from the beginning,” that is to say, the one who existed from the beginning, the unseen God the Word, of whom we heard in the divine Scriptures, proclaimed in the prophets, hymned in heaven.

**69,40,8a** And for this reason, “What we heard in the beginning, and saw with our eyes,” so that by “having heard” he might confess God, from the beginning above, and by “having seen” indicate the man, of whom John the Baptist too said, “After me comes a man.”

**69,40,8b** And “our hands have handled,” so that he might indicate God from above, and point out a visible man born of Mary and risen complete from the dead, not having cast off the holy vessel he had taken, and his complete becoming man, but so that, through having handled the side and the print of the nails, he might confess all three unshakeably.

**69,40,9** So, I ask you, understand here too, “This is he of whom I said to you, ‘After me comes a man’,” to indicate the coming in the flesh; “for he was before me,” to point out the Godhead, that “he came to be before me”; for, says the holy gospel, “he was in the world, and the world came into being through him, and the world did not know him.”

**69,41,1a** And if he was in the world prior to John’s being born and conceived, he had come to be in the world before him, which indicates not creation, not making, but follows the usage that men are accustomed to employ in the same terms.

**69,41,1b** “I came to be in Jerusalem, I came to be in Babylon, I came to be in Ethiopia, I came to be in Alexandria,” indicating here not creation, but arrival and presence.

**69,41,2a** For what “I came to be in Babylon”, or in another place, means is “I came there”.

**69,41,2b** So “he came to be before me” is said to show the Word’s constant coming upon the earth, while “he was before me” is meant to show the Godhead that always is.

**69,41,2c** And “coming after me”, to show the conception after John.

**69,41,2d** And for this reason, “I am the voice of one who cries in the wilderness,” a voice that prepares, a voice for the hearing of men.

**69,41,3** For those who call out are accustomed first to utter an inarticulate, ringing sound, calling from afar those who are to hear something from them; and when they have heard the sound alone, and have given their mind to listening, and have prepared their hearing, then the one who uttered the ringing sound at last articulates the word he wished to say.

**69,41,4a** So too John became a voice preparing the hearing of men.

**69,41,4b** For he was not himself the Word, but after him came the Word, for whose sake the preparing voice came to be.

**69,41,4c** And for this reason it says, “A voice of one who cries in the wilderness: Make ready the ways of the Lord.”

**69,41,5a** For the voice makes ready, while the Lord walks upon the ways that have been made ready.

**69,41,5b** And the voice speaks to the hearing.

**69,41,5c** And when the hearing is at leisure, then the word is laid down in the hearing of those who receive it.

**69,41,5d** Nowhere, then, will Arius and those who follow him get a hold on the truth of God, which ever illumines the hearts of believers so that they are not turned aside from the salvation that is in the Word, the Son of God, in uncreated and unbegotten truth.

**69,42,1a** As we advance again and go on to what follows, we shall leave out none of the points set out above for resolution, but shall take up the sequence once more.

**69,42,1b** For again they put forward another pretext, the words spoken by the holy Peter in the Acts.

**69,42,1c** “Let it be known to you, all the house of Israel, that this Jesus whom you crucified, God has made him both Lord and Christ.”

**69,42,2** And again they say that “made” is written here, and they do not look at the saying (for the saying itself makes itself plain): “this Jesus”, to indicate the Lord’s becoming man; for from “this Jesus whom you crucified” it is plain what is meant, that it was flesh which they crucified.

**69,42,3a** For they crucified flesh; and that is why the Lord declares in the gospel, “Now, however, you are seeking to kill me, a man who has spoken to you the truth which I heard from my Father.”

**69,42,3b** But he says it not as separating the Godhead from the becoming man.

**69,42,4a** For neither was the Godhead outside the becoming man when he was about to suffer, nor in the suffering was the coming in the flesh forsaken by the Word.

**69,42,4b** But neither has the Word, impassible as he was before, suffered, though he was in the flesh that suffered.

**69,42,4c** For the one name is true of both, of the Godhead and of the becoming man.

**69,42,4d** For the becoming man of the Word himself is Christ, and the Lord is Christ in that very coming in the flesh.

**69,42,5a** The suffering, however, is in the flesh, just as Peter said.

**69,42,5b** “Since Christ suffered for us in the flesh,” to show the impassibility of the Godhead.

**69,42,5c** And again, “Put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit.”

**69,42,5d** So “this Jesus whom you crucified” is said so that the holy incarnate dispensation might not be left apart from the impassible and uncreated Word, but be united above with the uncreated Word.

**69,42,6a** For this reason God made both Lord and Christ that which was conceived of Mary, that which was united in Godhead; for Mary is not God by nature.

**69,42,6b** For this reason it adds “made” next, as the angel Gabriel too says when she asked, “How shall this be, since I do not know a man?”

**69,42,6c** He says, “The Spirit of the Lord will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.”

**69,42,6d** “Therefore the holy one that is born will also be called Son of God.”

**69,42,7** And when he says, “and that which is born,” he showed beyond dispute concerning God the Word that he is Son beyond doubt, not created, not made.

**69,42,8a** But concerning the incarnate dispensation from Mary, with an addition, he made that which came to be Christ and Lord, as in the other sayings everything was plainly fulfilled, and they contain nothing to labour over.

**69,42,8b** So too here it has been fulfilled in the coming in the flesh; and there is no turning aside for those who care for their own life.

**69,42,9a** For the Word is living from a living Father, Son of the Father, and not created.

**69,42,9b** And all things have been fulfilled in the coming in the flesh, so that it might not be thought an apparition, nor the flesh of one essence with the Godhead above, but his becoming man united into one impassibility, especially after the resurrection from the dead.

**69,42,9c** For “he dies no more,” it says; “death no longer has dominion over him.”

**69,42,10** For he is one Lord, one Christ, one King, who sits at the Father’s right hand, the bodily and the spiritual, one union, one spiritual Godhead, both radiant and glorious.

**69,42,11** And now I shall pass over the saying, considering it sufficiently interpreted, and may I take up the telling of the other things devised by them for the overthrow of their hearers.

**69,43,1** For they say once more, “If he is from the essence of the Father, how is he ignorant of the hour and the day, and instead acknowledges to the disciples by his own word that he does not know what the Father knows, saying, ‘Concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but the Father alone’?

**69,43,2** If, then,” they say, “the Father knows and he himself does not know, how can the Godhead of Father and Son be the same, when the Son is ignorant of what the Father knows?”

**69,43,3** But all that the only-begotten set forth in his teaching mystically, and in his divine wisdom, for the security of the truest knowledge, these people, not recognising what pertains to his human condition, snatch up, every bit of it, to their own harm, like dreadful reptiles that snatch to their own destruction what has been baited by the crafty hunter, not knowing that falsehood will nowhere stand, while the truth in every way sets its own sons right and refutes the falsehood.

**69,43,4a** For let those who have held the wicked supposition about Christ from the beginning tell us which is greater by nature and as regards knowing: God, the master of all and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, or else the day that is brought on and comes to pass by Father and Son and Holy Spirit, and that hour?

**69,43,4b** And surely, when asked, they will be compelled by the truth itself to call the Father greater, as in fact he is.

**69,43,5a** If, then, the Son declares, saying, “No one knows the Father except the Son, and no one knows the Son except the Father,” how is he who knows the greater, that is, the Father, ignorant of the lesser?

**69,43,5b** But the words are divine, spoken by the Holy Spirit, and unknown to any who have not received the Holy Spirit’s gift and grace.

**69,43,6** For being such, the people mentioned before have an unstable way of thinking too, and a foolish understanding that slides into harmful and lower deviations.

**69,44,1a** For they will be met in advance by what was said by the Lord himself: “Be ready, your loins girded and your lamps in your hands, and you will be like good servants awaiting their own master.

**69,44,1b** For as a robber in the night, so the day comes.”

**69,44,1c** And the holy apostle says, “You are not children of darkness but of the day, so that the day may not overtake you like a thief.”

**69,44,2** If, then, the sons of the day are not covered by darkness but become ready, because their master comes on a day they do not know and at an hour they do not expect, will he then not be distinguished from his own servants and sons of the day by reason of his radiant subsistence and Godhead, being himself the cause of these things for them, or will he, like those ignorant of the day who have not been made ready, be overtaken in ignorance and found in deficiency?

**69,44,3** But what madman would reason thus about the Lord, that he himself will be like the men who are ruled by him and have been made his disciples, or like those who are worse because of their unreadiness and ignorance?

**69,44,4a** And the whole thing is foolish.

**69,44,4b** If, then, these things cannot be fulfilled, and the reasoning, if stretched out, will be found to conflict with the usage, then we must seek what meaning we may find, so that, with both preserved without contradiction, we may not turn aside from the truth.

**69,44,4c** For it is impossible for the Lord to lie, and impossible for him to make his explanations for our life in vain.

**69,44,5a** So the Father knows, the Son knows, the Holy Spirit knows.

**69,44,5b** For there is nothing in the Father that differs from the Son, nor anything in the Son that differs from the Spirit, as we have shown in each of the sects mentioned before, when we were placed in need of it, from true demonstrations: that the Trinity is a single Godhead, having nothing within it that differs, but the whole is perfection, three perfect, one doxology and one lordship.

**69,45,1a** But you will say to me, “On what ground, then, did he say this?”

**69,45,1b** I have already spoken elsewhere about this saying.

**69,45,1c** But nothing will prevent me from adding to the same and saying the same true words; for me it is no trouble, for the readers it will be a safeguard, and for the opponents a refutation; for the matter stands in this way.

**69,45,2a** For he brought in three ranks together in the midst: the Father, himself, and all the angels in heaven.

**69,45,2b** And to the Father he assigned the knowing, pointing out not only awareness and knowledge, but also the things that are ever, beyond doubt, held firm and brought into being and accomplished with the Father and with the Son;

**69,45,3a** and the Father knows the day, has seen it, and has wrought it and done it and has passed judgement, as he stated in the Gospel according to John, that “the Father will judge no one, but has given all judgement to the Son.”

**69,45,3b** For in having given it, he has judged.

**69,45,3c** Having judged, then, he knew.

**69,45,3d** Having known, he knows when it comes.

**69,45,4a** For “he who does not believe in the Son has already been judged,” not because the judgement has passed, but because the things that are then to be are already shown forth, so that in this case too such a thing is fulfilled.

**69,45,4b** For Scripture knows of knowing and knowing, as we too have often not failed, coming down to the point that holds the matter together, to set out the clarity and the explanation of each subject from likenesses and examples of things already treated.

**69,46,1a** Let us, then, take it up afresh from the start, and speak about these matters.

**69,46,1b** What do you say, you people?

**69,46,1c** Did Adam know Eve his wife even before the disobedience and transgression, or did he not know her?

**69,46,1d** And you cannot gainsay the truth.

**69,46,2a** For if you will not walk straight toward such an understanding, you will be refuted.

**69,46,2b** “For they were,” it says, “naked, and were not ashamed.”

**69,46,2c** And they were naked, and not blind.

**69,46,2d** For you cannot deny this either, so as to confess that they did not see.

**69,46,2e** “For Eve saw,” it says, “the tree, that it was good for food and fair to look upon.”

**69,46,2f** So then he knew, and they knew.

**69,46,2g** And knowing and seeing one another, they recognised each other [...] it was after a long time, says the Scripture, “and Adam knew Eve his wife.”

**69,46,3** But the first knowing and seeing it speaks of as a knowing that consists through sight and through thought, while of the second knowledge it reports as a knowing that concerns use;

**69,46,4a** as somewhere also of David when he had grown old, as the divine Scripture says, “And David grew old and was not warmed, and his servants said to him, ‘Let a virgin be sought for the king’; and Abishag the Shunammite was found.”

**69,46,4b** And it says, “She warmed him, and lay with him, and David did not know her.”

**69,46,5** How did he not know her who lay body to body and side by side with him?

**69,46,6a** But here it relates not the knowing through thought but the knowing through use.

**69,46,6b** For so too in the case of Jacob: for he spent seven years shepherding with Rachel and Leah, and he knew them.

**69,46,6c** But when it relates the union of their honourable marriage, it says, “He knew Leah his wife.”

**69,46,6d** For the first knowing was through thought and through sight, but the second knowledge and knowing concerned use and act.

**69,46,7a** So too in the divine Scripture, “The Lord knew those who are his.”

**69,46,7b** Not as though he did not know those who are not his; but it indicates the manifest character of the Lord’s laying hold of them.

**69,46,7c** And: “Depart from me, you workers of lawlessness, I never knew you.”

**69,46,7d** Did he not, then, know them as far as awareness goes?

**69,46,7e** But since they were not worthy of him, he takes away from them the knowing that consists in act.

**69,46,8a** And in another place, “You I have known out of all the nations.”

**69,46,8b** Have all the nations, then, and the number of all mankind been left out of his knowledge, and are not, rather, even the hairs of each man’s head known, both of those who serve him and of those who disobey him?

**69,46,8c** For God also knows the ways on the right.

**69,46,8d** Is he then ignorant of those on the left?

**69,46,8e** And how many such things are there to say about knowing and knowing?

**69,47,1a** So too with the only-begotten Son of God.

**69,47,1b** For since the Father has given the judgement to the Son, he has already assigned to the Father the knowledge of the knowing and of the judgement, “No one knows the day except the Father,” in two ways: that he knows when it comes.

**69,47,1c** For it is under his authority that the day and the hour come.

**69,47,1d** And he knows it; for the judgement, handed over to the only-begotten, has already been done by him; so too in the Son of God, the Only-begotten, being God and in nothing altered from the Father, the knowing is the same.

**69,47,2** For he himself knows it, and he himself brings it on and bears it and accomplishes it and judges, and without him it does not come.

**69,47,3** But he has not yet known it by act, that is, he has not yet judged; for the ungodly still act ungodly, and the unjust and fornicators and adulterers still overreach, and idolaters act lawlessly, and the devil is at work, and sects rise up, and error is at work, until the only-begotten Son of God brings that day itself and renders to each what is just and knows it, that is, accomplishes it in power.

**69,47,4** And in the Father it has been fulfilled in two ways, while in the Son it is there by knowing and is not unknown, but by act it has not yet been accomplished, since he has not yet judged.

**69,47,5a** But from the holy angels it has been withheld in two ways, also in that they have not yet known it by act, that is, accomplished it.

**69,47,5b** For they have not yet been commanded to go out and gather the ungodly like the tares, in bundles, and make them ready to be burned in the fire.

**69,47,6** And you see, beloved and God’s servants, that each of those who through some prejudice draw dreadful things upon themselves has campaigned in vain, each in a different way, against himself, against the Son of God, attempting to blaspheme him with lesser and diminished things.

**69,48,1a** But having given a sufficient explanation of this too, let us again turn our mind to other phrases of theirs, with the power of God.

**69,48,1b** For these fine fellows, daring in everything, confess, it is true, not as the Manichaeans do, nor as many other sects do, but hold at least the truth concerning the flesh, and that too deficiently and not most fully.

**69,48,2a** For they confess that the Saviour truly had flesh.

**69,48,2b** But hearing from the gospel itself that he was weary from the journey, and hungered, and thirsted, and slept, and rose, they gather all these things together and refer them to his Godhead, wishing, as it were from such premises, to estrange his Godhead from the essence of the Father.

**69,48,3** “If he is,” he says, “from the Father, when the Father does not toil, nor thirst, nor hunger,” as the divine Scripture says, “He will not toil, nor hunger, nor thirst, nor sleep, nor is there any searching out of his understanding”;

**69,48,4a** “and since these things were thus fulfilled in the Son, he is then,” they say, “alien to the essence and nature of the Father.”

**69,48,4b** And that these things were not fulfilled in the only-begotten before the coming in the flesh they themselves will confess; but when they confess it under compulsion, and come to the things accomplished in his coming in the flesh, and hear that, because he took a body, he for this reason fittingly performed these things, giving way, like a charioteer to his chariot, to the fitting needs, because he put on flesh in truth and not in appearance, then they declare that these things are not from the flesh alone.

**69,49,1a** For in truth, by itself, it will neither thirst nor grow weary.

**69,49,1b** But those who have abandoned the way and turned off onto the contrary tracks are unaware that the Son of God, on his coming, took not only flesh but also a soul and a mind and everything whatever there is in human beings, without sin — not from a man’s seed but from Mary the holy virgin, through the Holy Spirit.

**69,49,2** But they refuse to admit that he took a soul, because of the refutation of them which this brings, the readiest of all for countering their idle talk.

**69,49,3a** For he himself, the true God, who declares concerning himself, “I am the truth”, confesses that “my soul is troubled” and “my soul is very sorrowful”, and “I have authority to lay my soul down and receive it back”; and this to show that he is God, as the one who has the authority.

**69,49,3b** For this saying is not a man’s.

**69,49,4a** For no one has authority to lay down his soul and to take it up.

**69,49,4b** But when he speaks about a soul, he shows that he truly became man, and not in appearance.

**69,49,5a** And again: “I am the good shepherd, who lays down his soul for the sheep.”

**69,49,5b** And to show that these things were true, on the cross he said to the Father:

**69,49,5c** “Into your hand I commit my spirit.”

**69,49,5d** And when the soldiers came, it says, they found that he had already breathed his last.

**69,49,6a** And again, “and having cried out with a great voice” he said, “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani,” meaning, “My God, my God, for what reason have you forsaken me?”

**69,49,6b** As we have already set out the force of this saying too.

**69,49,6c** “And he breathed his last,” says the gospel.

**69,49,7** But since the truth says “he breathed his last” and “into your hands” and “my soul is troubled”, and everything else besides, what fool would let himself be persuaded by such a workshop of purblind and dreaming men, and abandon the very sayings of truth, so full of reason, spoken by God the Word?

**69,50,1a** But then, hunting out words among the things well and rightly said in each scripture, like pirates who mutilate sound bodies, they make use of a certain testimony which scripture often relates, employing it in a rather figurative sense.

**69,50,1b** And what is said figuratively they are accustomed to take as the truth, while what is true and proclaimed plainly they allegorize into another person.

**69,50,2** For at once they spring up, bringing a text from the holy Isaiah on the claim that it is uttered in the person of the Father: “See, my beloved servant shall understand, he in whom I took delight, whom my soul loved,” as though this expression belonged to the Father.

**69,50,3a** And indeed it is true.

**69,50,3b** How then, he says, has the Father too taken a soul?

**69,50,3c** But if we say, “God forbid,” “What then,” he says, “except that it is said rather figuratively?”

**69,50,3d** Then, they say, what is said by the Son has also been said rather figuratively.

**69,50,4a** And they think that in this they find a pretext for hunting against the truth — which will not be granted them.

**69,50,4b** For the truth, being unadorned, stands by itself, neither defeated nor in need of adornment.

**69,50,5a** For let us see the force of both.

**69,50,5b** For if the Father came into a body, and put on flesh, and spoke this saying, he truly had a soul.

**69,50,5c** But if the Father did not put on flesh, yet said “my soul”, this is sung of God figuratively, so as to make firm what is legitimate and to show his legitimate bond with the Son.

**69,50,5d** But the same things can no longer be said of the Son in this matter.

**69,50,6a** For the Father did not take flesh, but the Son put on flesh.

**69,50,6b** The Father has not become a man, whereas the Son has become a man.

**69,50,7a** For the like must be said in the Father’s case.

**69,50,7b** For as he says here, “My soul has loved him,” in the same way he says, “I found David, Jesse’s son, a man according to my heart.”

**69,50,7c** And “my heart is far from them.”

**69,50,8a** If then we accept what is said about the soul on the ground that “my soul has loved” is said rather figuratively, then surely what is said about the heart has also been said rather figuratively.

**69,50,8b** And it is plain that this would be clear to anyone who possesses understanding.

**69,50,9a** If, then, the Father uses figurative speech about a soul, and about a heart which he never took — for he did not bear flesh — such expressions are referred to the Father rather figuratively.

**69,50,9b** But the same must no longer be held concerning the Son.

**69,50,9c** For the Son took flesh and the whole human constitution.

**69,51,1** For this will stand against anyone who speaks rather figuratively of the Son concerning the becoming man in his own person, even if such a supposition has been made in some part of the argument, because he truly became man.

**69,51,2a** For if what concerns the soul of the Son is allegorized, and must be understood of it rather figuratively, then let such things be said about the heart too.

**69,51,2b** And then we shall grant that everything is appearance, and not truth.

**69,51,3a** It has been said figuratively about the flesh too, according to the reasoning of the contentious Arius.

**69,51,3b** And then the Word, when he came, no longer had a heart, nor a liver, nor flesh, nor entrails, nor bones, nor anything of the kind; but from now on everything is allegorized and spoken rather figuratively — or else he took a body kneaded wholly into one mass, having none of the inward parts.

**69,51,4a** How then did he eat and drink?

**69,51,4b** But away with it!

**69,51,4c** But if the Father speaks of heart and soul, and this can be allegorized in his case and said figuratively, then of the Son too figuratively — this because they deny that he took a soul.

**69,51,5a** But pressed on the matter of the heart, they cannot deny it, because they confess that the Lord took the whole constitution of the body; hence there is heart and heart, the one confessed as real, the other allegorized.

**69,51,5b** So too the statement about the soul is true, and is not allegorized, nor said figuratively.

**69,51,6** And since Christ’s becoming man was made complete in every respect — in body and soul and mind and heart, and in all that a human being is, without sin — and it fell to him to do the human things with good reason and to accomplish them perfectly in Godhead for salvation,

**69,51,7a** his Godhead will no longer be dishonoured beside the Father’s perfection; but because of his becoming man in the flesh, thirsting and hungering, drinking and eating, sleeping and being distressed will be fulfilled, while his Godhead remains impassible.

**69,51,7b** And once again their argument on this point has collapsed, since he came into flesh being God.

**69,52,1a** When they say, “If he was from the Father, how did he come into flesh?”

**69,52,1b** one might say to them, “What do you say about the angels?”

**69,52,1c** It is plain to everyone that they confess that the angels were made by the Son.

**69,52,2** For indeed they blaspheme about the Spirit too, and dare to say that it was created by the Son — the Spirit, which is uncreated, going forth from the Father and taking from the Son.

**69,52,3a** If, then, they have the audacity to say this with regard to the Holy Spirit, how much less will they be able to deny, concerning the angels, that they have their being from the Only-begotten, having been created?

**69,52,3b** If, then, the angels made by him — spiritual beings indeed, yet his creatures, and infinitely far beneath his essence, since they are his work — nevertheless did not take flesh, what shall we say?

**69,52,4a** Are they then greater than the Son, they who were created by him — or is the Holy Spirit as well?

**69,52,4b** Why was it not God’s Holy Spirit, or some one of the angels, that came into flesh, and wore flesh, and became man?

**69,52,5** For it was certainly not because the Son was inferior to the Father that he put on flesh for that reason (since then the angels too would certainly have had to put on flesh, or the Spirit as well); but because, being the Wisdom of the Father, and Power, and Word, he himself fashioned all things with the Father and the Holy Spirit —
