**75,4,4c** And again in another place, to bishops and deacons — so that, he says, the same man is bishop and the same man presbyter.

**75,4,5a** And the man who is ignorant of the sequence of the truth and has not met with the deepest histories does not know that, while the preaching was new, the holy apostle wrote according to the circumstances as they arose.

**75,4,5b** Where bishops had already been appointed, he wrote to bishops and deacons.

**75,4,5c** For the apostles were not able to establish everything at once.

**75,4,6a** For there was need of presbyters and deacons.

**75,4,6b** For through these two the affairs of the church can be fulfilled.

**75,4,6c** Where no one fit for the episcopate was found, the place stayed without a bishop; but where there was need and there were men worthy of the episcopate, bishops were appointed.

**75,4,7a** But where there was no great number, no men were found among them to be appointed presbyters, and they were content with the local bishop alone.

**75,4,7b** But without a deacon it is impossible for a bishop to be.

**75,4,7c** And the holy apostle took care that the bishop should have deacons for the service, so that the church received the full complement of its ordering.

**75,4,8** So the places stood at that time; for no undertaking had everything from the beginning, but as time went on whatever served to complete its needs was put in order.

**75,5,1a** For at first Moses is sent into Egypt, in the old covenant, with a staff alone.

**75,5,1b** But when, sent by God, he was entering Egypt, Aaron his brother is added to him as a help.

**75,5,2a** Then, after his brother had put faith in him, the elders’ council and the people’s leaders of that time were gathered to him.

**75,5,2b** And after this, as the work was strengthened and the sequence of events came together, he crossed the sea.

**75,5,3a** And they were not yet living according to the law, until the Lord calls him up the mountain.

**75,5,3b** And he gives him the tablets and shows him how to construct a tabernacle and to set up leaders: rulers of tens, rulers of fifties, rulers of hundreds, rulers of thousands.

**75,5,4a** And do you see how matters broaden?

**75,5,4b** “See,” he says, “you shall make everything according to the pattern shown to you on Mount Sinai.”

**75,5,5** And you see how there were added to the legislation a seven-branched lampstand, priestly robes reaching to the feet, bells and mantles, ephods and turbans, mitres and settings of stones of different kinds, cups, incense pans, basins, altars, dishes, masmaroth, that is, filters, midikoth, which are called cups, machonoth, which are bases, and all that the law discusses: cherubim and the other things, an ark of the covenant, poles for carrying and rings, a tabernacle, and hangings and skins dyed red, loops and the rest, gatekeepers, and trumpets of beaten metal and curved ones, of gold and of silver, of bronze, of horn, and the rest, all that the law spoke of, various sacrifices, teachings.

**75,5,6** Since these things did not exist from the beginning, did not matters receive them after the order had come into being?

**75,5,7a** So too with what is written in the apostle, until the church was enlarged, until it had advanced to its proper measure, until it had been ordered most justly, from Father and Son and Holy Spirit, in the adornment of its understanding.

**75,5,7b** And the argument of Aerius has fallen.

**75,5,8** And that the two cannot be the same — who is a bishop and who is a presbyter — the divine word of the holy apostle teaches, when he says to Timothy, who was a bishop, “Do not rebuke a presbyter, but exhort him as a father.”

**75,5,9a** What business had a bishop not to rebuke a presbyter, if he did not hold authority above the presbyter?

**75,5,9b** As again he says, “Do not hastily receive an accusation against a presbyter, except before two or three witnesses.”

**75,5,10a** And he did not say to any of the presbyters, “Do not receive an accusation against a bishop,” nor did he write to any of the presbyters not to rebuke a bishop.

**75,5,10b** And do you see that the fall of everyone who is shaken by the devil is no small one?

**75,6,1a** But let us look at his other points too and examine them.

**75,6,1b** And let us speak first about the Passover: since he says, “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed,” let us see whether the very man who said it did not keep it.

**75,6,1c** And it says, “He was hastening to keep Pentecost at Jerusalem.”

**75,6,1d** And what sort of Pentecost was Paul observing, unless he had observed the Passover?

**75,6,2a** And with whom has it not been agreed, in all the regions of the inhabited world, that Wednesday and Friday are a fast appointed in the church?

**75,6,2b** And if the Ordinance of the Apostles must also be cited, how did they there appoint Wednesday and Friday as a fast at all times, except during Pentecost?

**75,6,2c** And concerning the six days of the Passover, it is plain how they direct that nothing whatever be taken except bread and salt and water, and what day is to be kept, and how to end the fast towards the dawn of the Lord’s day.

**75,6,3a** And who knows these things better?

**75,6,3b** This deceived man, who has only now arrived and is still alive in the world, or the witnesses who lived before us, who held the tradition in the church before us — they having received it from their own fathers, and those fathers in turn having learned it from those who lived before them — how the church, having received from its fathers, holds even to this day the true faith and the traditions?

**75,6,3c** So let his notion about the Passover collapse in its turn.

**75,6,4a** Then again, even if the apostles themselves had not spoken in the Ordinance on this same subject of Wednesdays and Fridays, we could have shown it in other ways from every quarter; yet they write about it precisely.

**75,6,4b** The church has received it, and it has been agreed in the whole world, before Aerius and the Aerians who come from him existed.

**75,6,5a** For perhaps in this respect too he has received a most fitting name.

**75,6,5b** For he had an aerial spirit, out of uncleanness, from the aerial spirits of wickedness, which dwelt in him against the church.

**75,7,1a** Next, as to reciting the names of the departed, what could be more profitable than this?

**75,7,1b** What more timely and more admirable than this?

**75,7,1c** That those present should believe that the departed live and are not in non-existence, but exist and live with the Master;

**75,7,2** and that they should set forth the most solemn message, how those who pray on behalf of the brethren have hope, as for men who are away on a journey.

**75,7,3** And the prayer made on their behalf is of benefit too, even if it does not cut away the whole of their faults; but at any rate, since while we are in the world we often stumble, unwillingly and willingly, it is made so that what is more perfect may be signified.

**75,7,4** For we make remembrance both of the righteous and of sinners: for sinners, begging for the mercy of God; and for the righteous and the fathers and patriarchs, prophets and apostles and evangelists and martyrs and confessors, bishops and anchorites and the whole company,

**75,7,5** so that we may set the Lord Jesus Christ apart from the rank of men by the honour paid to him, and render reverence to him, bearing in mind that the Lord is not to be equated with any human being, even if each man should be in righteousness ten thousand times over and beyond.

**75,7,6a** For how could this be possible?

**75,7,6b** For the one is God and the other man; and the one is in heaven, the others on the earth because of their remains on earth — apart from those who rose and went in with him, in the bridal chamber, as the holy gospel tells it: “But many bodies of the saints rose up and entered along with him into the holy city.”

**75,7,7a** But which is this holy city that it speaks of?

**75,7,7b** For the saying is fulfilled in both senses, of the city here and of the city above.

**75,7,7c** That they first entered with him into the Jerusalem here is plain.

**75,7,7d** But before the Saviour went up into heaven, no one had gone up, until they went up with him.

**75,7,7e** “For no one has gone up into heaven except the one who came down out of heaven, the Son of Man.”

**75,7,7f** But when we were at the place that concerns these matters, we pointed out the two expressions.

**75,7,7g** And if anyone says that they did, then, enter into Jerusalem, let him learn that on that day, the doors being shut, Jesus stood where the disciples were gathered and says to them, “Peace to you.”

**75,8,1** Then again I shall take up the thread on this subject: that the church necessarily performs this, having received a tradition from the fathers.

**75,8,2a** And who will be able to annul a mother’s ordinance or a father’s law?

**75,8,2b** As in the words spoken by Solomon, “Hear, my son, the words of your father, and do not thrust away the ordinances of your mother,” showing that the Father — that is, God, the Only-begotten, and the Holy Spirit — gave instruction both in written form and unwritten, while our mother the church had ordinances laid up in her that are indissoluble and cannot be annulled.

**75,8,3** Since, then, the ordinances in the church are established and are good, and all things are done admirably, this deceiver too has again been refuted.

**75,8,4** And passing this one by too, having crushed him like a dung beetle, or a blister beetle, or the creature called the buprestis, with the church’s firm foundation and with the power of God, let us proceed once more to those that follow, calling on God as our helper.

### Sect 76: Anomoeans

Against the Anomoeans, the fifty-sixth, but the seventy-sixth in the series.

**76,1,1a** Again, there are certain people called Anomoeans.

**76,1,1b** These are recent.

**76,1,1c** They had as their founder a certain Aetius, a deacon, promoted on account of his babbling by George of Alexandria, who was bishop of the Arians and the Meletians alike; who in the times of Julian, as I have already shown above, was led in procession round the city on a camel;

**76,1,2** who was first shut up by the pagans and suffered much, was led in procession, as I have said, and struck with cudgels, then dragged through almost the whole city, and so died, and after his death was burned and reduced to ash together with many bones of cattle and other animals, and afterwards was scattered by them to the winds; and so he met his end.

**76,1,3a** Someone might say of the man who died in this way, “Was he not then a martyr, having suffered these things at the hands of the pagans?”

**76,1,3b** And if his contest had been on behalf of the truth, and such things had befallen him at the pagans’ hands through jealousy and on account of his confessing Christ, he would in very truth have been ranked among the martyrs, and not among the lesser ones.

**76,1,4** But the cause was not his confession of Christ, but the great violence which, in what was called, forsooth, his episcopate, he inflicted on the city and the populace, at one time robbing people of the inheritances left them by their parents.

**76,1,5** And — not to slander the man — many are the things he did to the Alexandrians: how he took over all the nitre, and how he contrived to manage the marshes of papyrus and of reed and the salt lakes and to draw their profits to himself;

**76,1,6** so that no shameful means of gain in life, pursued with much contrivance down to the smallest matters, was neglected by him; so that he even contrived to make biers, a fixed number of them, for the bodies of the departing, and without those appointed by him no body of the dead was carried out, and most of all those of strangers — not out of hospitality but, as they said, for worldly profit.

**76,1,7a** For if anyone buried a body by his own means, he faced danger.

**76,1,7b** And in this way from each of those carried out some profit came in to him.

**76,1,7c** And I keep silent about the rest — all that the man carried on in luxuries and other things, and in harshness.

**76,1,8a** For all these reasons, then, the sons of the Alexandrians, holding fast to their wrath against him, and the pagans most of all, dealt him this end.

**76,1,8b** I have had occasion to speak about him — how, on hearing of the death of Constantius, those same Alexandrians at once destroyed him in this way — for no other reason [has my account of him come about] than because of Aetius, the deacon appointed by him.

**76,2,1** This Aetius was uneducated even in worldly learning until his full maturity, as the story goes.

**76,2,2** But having placed himself under an Aristotelian philosopher and sophist in Alexandria and studied with him, and having learned their so-called dialectic, he conceived the plan of doing nothing other than casting into figures the account of the doctrine of God; he set about it at great leisure, rising early and sitting at it continually until evening — I mean at speaking about God and defining him by a kind of geometry and by figures, both teaching and initiating.

**76,2,3** And being an Arian of the deepest dye, holding the frenzied teaching of Arius, he became an uncommon destroyer as he wore himself away on these things, sharpening his tongue every day against the Son of God and against the Holy Spirit.

**76,2,4** He is accused by some, and reported to that same Constantius, and he undergoes exile in the regions of the Taurus; in which place he broadened all the matters of his evil teaching and brought them out into the open, bringing them forward boldly; having wiped his brow clean with excessive shamelessness, he displayed the vomitings of his evil teaching without leaving anything out.

**76,2,5a** For he had the audacity to declare the Son unlike the Father and not identical in Godhead with the Father — not that we, for our part, rest on the likeness.

**76,2,5b** For we know the Son to be beyond likeness in relation to the Father, as the same in Godhead and equal and in no way altered.

**76,2,6** For there are many things made like God, but not the same, as though they were equal to the Godhead — as man too is after the image and after the likeness, but not the same as God so as to be equal.

**76,2,7a** And the kingdom of the heavens is like a mustard seed, but it is not the same as the kingdom, nor does it share at all in the same and like leaven.

**76,2,7b** And it is like ten virgins and a man who is a householder by way of likeness, but not by sameness.

**76,2,8a** But since the Son is like the Father and beyond like, through being identical with the Father and equal to the Father, our earnest endeavour has been to establish not the like only, but the same and the equal — as God from God and Son from Father, and not other in essence, but begotten of him.

**76,2,8b** So too concerning the Holy Spirit.

**76,2,9a** But this noble fellow Aetius did not see fit to allow the Son even likeness to the Father.

**76,2,9b** But we ourselves, resting not on the like alone, confess the framework of the faith, insisting in truth on honouring the Trinity.

**76,2,10** For silver too is likened to tin, and gold to bronze, and lead to iron, and precious stones are made to resemble glass; and the like does not reveal the nature, but the semblance.

**76,3,1a** And here, concerning the scripture that confesses that the Son is image of the God who is invisible, we, having by divine gift learned exactly the force of the divine scripture — the scripture that said to the Pharisees, “You do not know the scriptures, nor God’s power.”

**76,3,1b** We know, then, that this relation is twofold, and we make it plain by taking the usage from man, to illustrate the expression.

**76,3,2a** For an image of a man, too, is spoken of, and not in like fashion.

**76,3,2b** For the one is a likeness made in colours, the other comes through consubstantiality by generation, since the son who is begotten bears the stamp of his kind in relation to his father, and is thus found to be a representation of sameness, of consubstantiality and of impress.

**76,3,3a** And for us the only-begotten Son of God is the same in the Father’s Godhead and dignity, and equal through the true image and through a likeness that is not varied but invariable, as a Son truly and consubstantially begotten of the Father.

**76,3,3b** So too in the case of the Holy Spirit, because he came forth from the Father, even though he has not been begotten, because of the Son’s being only-begotten.

**76,3,4** But this Aetius, wishing to oppose the confession of the truth more than the rest, does not even attempt to acknowledge that the Son is like the Father.

**76,3,5** For the others among the Arians, who took their pretext from Lucian and Origen, had been associated with a certain Asterius, who came from the sophists but lapsed in the persecution that took place under Maximian.

**76,3,6a** For some — as I have shown in the heresies above — each of those already named, defined him, the Son of God, as a creature, and they taught that the Holy Spirit is a creature of a creature.

**76,3,6b** But some said that the Son is like the Father, even though they defined him as a creature.

**76,3,7a** But this man revealed plainly the whole of their dissembling and of his own impiety: the harshness and shamelessness of the doctrine towards the Lord.

**76,3,7b** And, as the truth stands, the precision of the reasoning of this Aetius, called also Anomoean, is aimed most justly at those who bring in the creature.

**76,3,8** For everything created is unlike its creator, even if it should be likened to him by grace; and the creator is unlike what he has created, even if he should try to adorn it with various colours — unless perhaps what is impressed exists as a resemblance and a portrait, by an imitation of appearance only.

**76,3,9** And as against the Arians who suppose that God’s Son and the Holy Spirit are created, his argument would have had force — as indeed later, when he had been put out of communion by the Arians themselves (I mean those around Eudoxius and Menophilus and others), he refuted them before the emperor of that time,

**76,3,10a** saying, “As they hold, so I hold, as do they all; but what in me is true, they conceal; and what I plainly show and confess, these all say the same,” but they hide it from the emperor of that time, who was not opposed to the Arian play-acting, but supposed himself, forsooth, to be pious.

**76,3,10b** For, refusing to acknowledge God’s Son as a creature, he was indignant and consigned him to banishment, as has been shown above.

**76,4,1** From this the heresy had its beginning; and, carried away in his mind from this one premise into a great surge of evils, the man grievously wounded his own soul and the souls of those persuaded by him.

**76,4,2** For later he fancied himself able to say, he and those discipled by him: “I know God,” he says, “so very clearly, and I know and understand him so well, that I do not know myself [more] than I know God.”

**76,4,3** And there are other things, all that we have heard about him — how terribly the devil contrived against him, to destroy the souls of men who had been ensnared.

**76,4,4** For with them there is no concern for dignity of life, none for fastings, none for the commandments of God, none for anything else of the things enjoined by God on men for life,

**76,4,5** but only the argument they have ready to hand, the whole thing in one phrase — as if someone, having thrown overboard from a ship and made a jettison of the whole of the cargo, should keep back one of the things put aboard the vessel, a jar, I mean, or something else, so as to be able by one vessel to swim across the whole sea and procure safety for himself; but when such a man is disappointed, and does not find the outcome he supposed about the vessel in his hands, he afterwards goes under the water and loses the whole enterprise and his safety;

**76,4,6** so too this Aetius and the Anomoeans who come from him bring forward the saying spoken by the Lord in the gospel and set forth its wording, but, not rightly grasping its force, he stumbles and they stumble.

**76,4,7a** For when anyone meets them and reminds them about commandments, they say this, as the saying put it: that there is nothing else that God seeks from us but that we should know him only, as Christ too said, he says, when he said, “Father, give them to have life within themselves.

**76,4,7b** And life is this, that they should know you, the only true God, and the one you sent, Jesus Christ.”

**76,4,8a** For we have also heard some people say that they plainly heard from him, when certain men were accused of having been caught in an outrage involving a woman and were being condemned by them.

**76,4,8b** But he was not even troubled about these things, but even mocked idly, saying that such a thing is nothing.

**76,4,9** For the need and the service are bodily: “For just as,” he says, “we itch in the ear” (and I myself am ashamed to repeat all that that unclean man related), “and taking a feather or a twig,” he says, “we scratch the ear and so are rid of the itching in our hearing, so too this,” he says, “happens according to nature, and if anyone performs it, he does not sin.”

**76,5,1** And relating all such things, the man taught everything loosely and badly, so that from his very works it might be seen what he is, and the Lord’s words might shine clearly upon us,

**76,5,2a** as he said, “Watch out for the false prophets, who come to you dressed as sheep, but within are ravening wolves.

**76,5,2b** From their fruits you will recognise them.

**76,5,2c** Do they gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles?”

**76,5,2d** So too the daring of this man’s folly is refuted in every respect, from this side and from that.

**76,5,3a** How he stretched out his mouth against his Master, with an unbridled tongue, not ashamed to blaspheme his own Lord — so that the wise, testing him also from the fruits of his wantonness and slackness, may not pluck his fruits.

**76,5,3b** For a grape cannot be gathered from thorns, so that from his evil teaching his solemnity, too, might be seen.

**76,5,4** But these things we have heard as having happened and befallen in the man’s case; as for what follows from his words, in the madness of the exaltation he dared against the Lord, they are many, as I said, but I shall set out a few of the many, and against them we ourselves shall say what the Lord gives for their overthrow.

**76,5,5** And this is the wrangling of this Anomoean about the faith, and these are the semblances of his arguments — spoken from the scriptures, but not having this meaning in their sense, rather having their force otherwise, though taken in this way by him.

**76,6,1** He says right at the beginning that the ingenerate cannot be like the begotten, since they differ even in name; for the one is ingenerate,

**76,6,2a** the other — but the whole of it is silly and has turned the man to madness.

**76,6,2b** For if we look for a begetter for the ingenerate, so as not to lose the true doctrine about Christ, there will no longer be found one Father, nor a father of the Father, but fathers of fathers sought without end; and there is no longer one God, who always is and has had nothing before himself, and always continues and abides, from whom the only-begotten true Son has been begotten and exists, and his Holy Spirit from him; but those sought will be many gods, and in the end everything will be deceit and not truth.

**76,6,3** But one must know, as indeed is the case, a single God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom is the Holy Spirit as well, going forth from the Father and taking from the Son.

**76,6,4** And this is the single Godhead, one God, one Lord: Father and Son and Holy Spirit, the Son not being some blending with the Father, nor the Holy Spirit, but the Father is Father, and the Son Son, and the Holy Spirit Holy Spirit: three perfect, one Godhead, one God, one Lord, as we have often rendered the glorifying of God in this way in all the heresies.

**76,6,5** Therefore, since God is one and it is not possible to conceive of another besides him who is, the Father is wonderfully both ingenerate and uncreated, and the only-begotten Son of God, begotten of him, is in no way at all unlike him, but the same as the Father and equal in every dignity, even though the one has been begotten and the other is ingenerate.

**76,6,6** For if he has begotten the Son from himself at all, it is impossible that he should not be equal and like to the Father; for everything that begets begets what is like itself, and not only like, but equal in sameness.

**76,6,7** For man begets man and God begets God; and man does so through the union of bodies, but God alone has begotten the Only-begotten ineffably, and not by any utterance, nor contraction, nor expansion; but the Father, being spirit, begot the Son from himself without beginning and without time, like himself in all things and equal, even as the holy gospel says that “the Jews were seeking to put him to death, because not only was he breaking the sabbath, but he was also calling himself Son of God, making himself equal to God.”

**76,6,8** For how is he not like the Father and equal in all things, who holds life within himself and says, “Just as the Father raises the dead, so the Son also raises the dead,” and says, “He who has seen me has seen the Father”?

**76,6,9a** He cannot be different who signifies the Father through himself, and who says, “He who knows me knows the Father,” and, “He who has seen me has seen the Father,” since he is no other than the Father — just as the Father and the Son too signify, “Let us make man after our image and after our likeness.”

**76,6,9b** For were the Son not like the Father, how then did man come to be after the image and after the likeness?

**76,6,10** For what the Father said was not, “Let us make man after my image,” or “after your image,” but after our image.

**76,6,11** And by saying “after our” he showed the equality of the Father in the Son, and the likeness — and not only that, but also sameness in all things, without variation.

**76,7,1** And how can he not be equal and not like, as I have already said, who says, “I am within the Father, and the Father within me”?

**76,7,2** For not only does he himself say this in the gospel, but Isaiah too, prophesying by the Holy Spirit, knew the Son in the Father, and not foreign to the Father nor varied from him,

**76,7,3** as the saying has it, which runs in this sequence — from the Hebrew thus: “phthoou saareim, ouiabōtōn sadik, sōmēr emmouneiō, iesrosmōch, thesar salōm salōm, chibak batoou, betoub baldōnai addōth, chibaia adōnai sōdōlemeim.”

**76,7,4** And from Aquila’s version thus: “Open gates; let a just nation go in, keeping faith, a creature made firm, a guarding of peace, because they have trusted in him; trust in the Lord for ever, because in the Lord is the Lord who made the ages firm.”

**76,7,5** And among the Seventy thus: “Open the gates, let him enter who keeps truth and lays hold of truth and keeps peace, because they have hoped in you, Lord, for ever, the great God, the everlasting.”

**76,7,6** Let the reader observe that “Lord” and the words “the great” stand among the Seventy in place of “in the Lord”.

**76,7,7a** And how many things are there to say about this?

**76,7,7b** But I fear that I may drive the treatment of these arguments to a great bulk.

**76,7,7c** For all things are clear in the divine scripture to those who wish to approach the divine word with pious reasoning, and not, having conceived a craving for a devilish working within themselves, to overturn themselves into the pits of death, as this pitiable man and the men persuaded by him have made war against the truth, beyond all the blasphemers against God and his faith who came before them.

**76,7,8a** And as for the Son’s not being able to be unlike the Father — it was not by resting on this point either that we said these things.

**76,7,8b** For he is not merely like but also equal: identical in Godhead, identical in everlastingness and in power.

**76,7,8c** And we do not say “identical in essence”, lest the term, as used by some, be likened to Sabellius.

**76,7,9a** But we call him identical in Godhead and in essence and in power, in all things equal to the Father and to his Holy Spirit.

**76,7,9b** But we say “consubstantial”, as the holy faith has it, so that by the “con-” the perfect ones may be clearly signified: that the Son is from the Father, perfect from perfect, and the Holy Spirit is perfect too.

**76,8,1a** By one, a second and a third testimony these people will be caught out.

**76,8,1b** For if he is confessed at all to have been begotten by him, he will of necessity be confessed to be like the one who begot him.

**76,8,2a** But it is plain that in word he says “offspring”, while he clearly holds and believes “creature”.

**76,8,2b** And that he is called Son by grace — so judged this surveyor of the heavenly things, divider of the indivisible and geometer of our salvation in Christ.

**76,8,3** But the argument of all these who bring him in among the creatures collapses, just as this man’s too will fall.

**76,8,4a** For I shall say to him, most justly: Tell me, you there, what would you say about the Son of God?

**76,8,4b** Is it a creature you declare him to be, or an offspring?

**76,8,4c** For if you say he is a creature, no longer plausibly conceal the ruin by calling him in name the offspring of the Father.

**76,8,5a** For everything created is not begotten, and if begotten, not created.

**76,8,5b** Leave off, then, calling him begotten even in word.

**76,8,5c** For it does not befit you at all to carry the words of truth on your lips even in a single word; but tell the whole of your plot, that we may discover who you are and thus escape from your plot, you hunter of souls and plotter against those who are dear to you.

**76,8,6a** Do you, then, worship the Son of God, or do you not worship him?

**76,8,6b** “Yes,” he says, “I worship him.”

**76,8,6c** Is it a God you worship, or not?

**76,8,6d** “Yes,” he says, “I worship a God.”

**76,8,7a** What sort of God, then, will he be, who is called created by you and is worshipped?

**76,8,7b** For if the God who is to be worshipped created the one and was pleased that he should be worshipped, while all the rest he who created them does not wish to be worshipped, but even blames those who worship the creation, teaching through the law, “You shall not make for yourself any likeness and worship it, neither in heaven nor on the earth nor in the waters.”

**76,8,8** And the apostle says, “They served the creation rather than the Creator, and became fools.”

**76,8,9a** How then does he command, concerning all things, that they are not to be worshipped?

**76,8,9b** Is there then partiality with God?

**76,8,9c** Far from it.

**76,8,9d** For in that the one is worshipped, he showed that the one worshipped is altogether other than the creation, and the creation that is worshipped other than the Lord who is to be worshipped, God’s Son, begotten from the Father.

**76,8,9e** For because he was begotten of him, he is a Son like him and corresponding to him; for this reason he is also worshipped by all.

**76,8,9f** “Through him he made all things, and without him not one thing came into being.”

**76,8,10a** For in him and in his Holy Spirit, who proceeded from him and receives of the Son, he made all things and made them firm.

**76,8,10b** “For by the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the breath of his mouth all his host.”

**76,8,11** For when the Only-begotten says, as I have said above, “that they may know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ,” he set himself apart from the creation, as the apostle too says, “There is one God, from whom everything comes, and we through him; and there is one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom everything comes, and we through him.”

**76,8,12a** And you see how he showed one God, the Father, and one Lord, the one begotten of him; and he did not put it, “There is one God, and one Lord along with all the things that came into being from him,” but “one Lord, through whom everything comes”.

**76,8,12b** But if it is one Lord through whom everything comes, he is not one among all things, but the maker of all things, being the creator of everything that has been created.

**76,9,1** And since the Son has been begotten from the Father and is from the Father, he through whom all things have come into being is unlike all things, being indeed the creator of them all;

**76,9,2** since it is “one” and “one” — God the Father, from whom everything comes, and the Lord Jesus, through whom everything comes — and the expression above is joined together through “one” and “one” and through “from whom” and “through whom”, by the one it has clearly shown that the Son is from the Father, and by the other it has wonderfully declared that the Son is not from the rest, by saying “through whom everything comes”, so as to show that there is a Father, and that the only-begotten Lord is a Son, being from a Father who is.

**76,9,3** The apostle said these things borne along by the Holy Spirit; and so he had no need to make anything plain about the Spirit — not as though the Spirit were not glorified together with Father and Son, nor so as to mark him out as one from among all that was created through the Son.

**76,9,4a** For it was enough that he had been numbered with Father and Son through the sure confession of the Son, when he said, “Go and baptise into the name of Father and Son and Holy Spirit.”

**76,9,4b** So when the apostle spoke — or rather the Holy Spirit speaking in him — he did not make anything plain about himself.

**76,9,4c** For the knowledge about him was plain, not doubted even by the Jews.

**76,9,5a** But he held back, so that the Holy Spirit should not be his own commender; and the apostle was borne along with the Holy Spirit and spoke of Father and Son, so that the Trinity might be shown to be always existing and never ceasing to be.

**76,9,5b** And do not wonder if you hear, “One God, from whom everything comes, and one Lord, through whom everything comes.”

**76,9,6a** For in naming the Son Lord, the apostle did not at all deny that the Lord is also God.

**76,9,6b** And by saying “one God, through whom everything comes”, he did not deny that God is also Lord.

**76,9,6c** For he is at once both Lord and God, and God and Lord, and it will make no difference to the things preached to us in truth, for our salvation, from God through the apostles.

**76,9,7a** But this same Anomoean, and those who have come from him, abandoned the way of the truth and turned aside, having understood the sayings of God wrongly.

**76,9,7b** And then, having diverted their mind into reasonings and into the parsing of expressions, they sprang away from the truth and fell from the heavenly things.

**76,9,8a** For every expression will refute them, if they are willing to give their mind to the enlightenment of the gospel.

**76,9,8b** For nowhere does the Only-begotten say, even though he came in the flesh, “The Father who created me has sent me,” nor did the Father anywhere declare, in the gospel or in the old covenant, “For you I created the Son”; but “The Father sent me,” and “Out of the Father I came forth, and I am here,” and “he who is in the Father’s bosom,” and “the Word was in the presence of God, and the Word was God.”

**76,9,9** And there is much to consider about our salvation, and not to be carried off by the cheating teaching of this devil.

**76,9,10** For the devil, wishing to destroy the race of men, and possessed by envy of man’s glory, devised various contrivances: first through ignorance, second through idolatry, at another time through depravity, and now at the last through the error and deceit of the heresies, so as to overturn man from every side and cast him down from the heavenly things.

**76,10,1a** How much, then, will the mind of our moderate capacity be able to say to you, O Anomoean?

**76,10,1b** For you are rightly an Anomoean, you who have turned your ways and your mind aside from the men who have acquired understanding of God and who possess the faith of the truth.

**76,10,2** For it was not by advancing towards good that you became unlike men; but by turning aside from the way of the truth you became unlike the sons of the church of God, taking as your pretext the Son of God, who is as his Father is, and calling him unlike the Father; you have become unlike, allotted this name, no longer being like those who are saved in God.

**76,10,3** But so that I may not spend time wearing myself out over his inquiries, come, let us refute his case from the very words he set out, writing dialectically to certain people.

**76,10,4** For he saw fit to display a sort of dialectical error in this treatise of his, which has not a single word of the most simple and guileless faith, adorned with a holy and gentle spirit.

**76,10,5a** I have set down first, entire from beginning to end, his would-be little work that has come into our hands, so that from it we may make against him the rest of the refutation of his disputation.

**76,10,5b** And this is the little treatise of Aetius the Anomoean.

**76,11,1** Since, at the time of the persecution brought upon us by the Temporalists, certain of those mentioned before appropriated, along with many other things, a little work on which I had laboured by myself concerning the ingenerate God and the begotten, and published it corrupted with additions and subtractions, having altered its logical order; and since after this it came to us, one of our zealous friends having brought it to us, I have been compelled,

**76,11,2** as a father, to cleanse it once more and send the treatise out to you, all you athletes of piety, men and women, so that you may know that our little discourse has been spoken in accordance with the sense of the holy scriptures, by which, with brief inferences, you will be able to stop the shamelessness of every man who attempts to contradict you concerning the ingenerate God and the begotten, and above all of the aforesaid Temporalists;

**76,11,3** for I have set out, in the manner of verses, objection upon objection and solution upon solution, for the sake of the easy grasp and the clarity of the arguments, making my beginning with the ingenerate God.

**76,12,1a** 1. If the ingenerate God is able to make the begotten ingenerate, if every essence is ingenerate, neither will differ from the other in being subject to no master.

**76,12,1b** How then could anyone say that the one is changed and the other changes it, when they do not allow God to bring into existence from no underlying matter?

**76,12,1c** 2. If the ingenerate God is superior to every cause, he would for this reason be superior to generation too.

**76,12,1d** And if he is superior to every cause, it is plain that he is superior to generation too.

**76,12,1e** For he neither received his being from another nature, nor did he himself give being to himself.

**76,12,1f** 3. But if he did not give being to himself, not through weakness of nature but because he transcends every cause, on what ground could anyone grant that the nature brought into existence has invariability of essence in relation to the nature that brought it into existence, when such a subsistence does not admit generation?

**76,12,1g** 4. If God continues endlessly in an ingenerate nature, and the offspring is endlessly offspring, the false doctrine of the homoousion and of the homoiousion will be brought to ruin.

**76,12,1h** And what is in incomparable essence stands firm, each nature continuing unceasingly in the proper rank of its nature.

**76,12,1i** 5. If God is ingenerate in essence, the begotten was not begotten by a division of essence, but from an essence that brought it into existence.

**76,12,1j** For no pious reasoning permits the same essence to be both begotten and ingenerate.

**76,12,1k** 6. If the ingenerate was begotten, what prevents the begotten from having become ingenerate?

**76,12,1l** For every nature presses on towards what is proper to it rather than towards what is foreign.

**76,12,1m** 7. If God is not wholly ingenerate, nothing prevents his having begotten essentially.

**76,12,1n** But if he is wholly ingenerate, he was not divided essentially into generation, but brought the offspring into existence by his authority.

**76,12,1o** 8. If the ingenerate God is wholly generative, what was begotten was not begotten essentially, since his whole essence has the begetting but not the being begotten.

**76,12,1p** 9. But if the essence of God, having been transformed, is called offspring, his essence is not unchangeable, since the change has brought about the Son’s appropriation.

**76,12,1q** 10. But if the essence of God should be both unchangeable and superior to generation, what concerns the Son will be confessed only so far as a bare appellation.

**76,12,1r** 11. If the offspring existed within the ingenerate God as in a seed, then after its generation, taking on additions from outside, it grew to manhood, as one might say.

**76,12,1s** The Son, then, is perfect, not from the things from which he was begotten, but from the things he took on.

**76,12,1t** For things that take on what is akin to them are by nature apt to receive the name of “perfect” in a different way, as being constituted from those things.

**76,12,1u** 12. If the offspring was perfect in the ingenerate, it is an offspring, and not from the things from which the ingenerate begot it.

**76,12,1v** For a begotten nature cannot exist in an ingenerate essence.

**76,12,1w** For it is for the same thing both to be and not to be.

**76,12,1x** For an offspring is not ingenerate, and being ingenerate it was not an offspring, since the unlike part, in the case of God, carries the stamp of blasphemy and outrage.

**76,12,1y** 13. If God the Almighty, being of ingenerate nature, does not know himself as of begotten nature, while the Son, being of begotten nature, knows himself as this, which he is, how would the homoousion not be a falsehood, when the one knows himself as ingenerate and the other as begotten?

**76,12,1z** 14. If “ingenerate” does not represent the subsistence of God, but the incomparable name belongs to human conception, God is grateful to those who conceived it, because of the conception “ingenerate”, since he does not bear the pre-eminence of the name in his essence.

**76,12,1aa** 15. If “ingenerate” is observed in God from outside, those who observed it are better than the one observed, having procured for him a name superior to his nature.

**76,12,1ab** 16. If the ingenerate nature does not yield to generation, it is what it is said to be; but if it yields to generation, the passions of generation would be better than the subsistence of God.

**76,12,1ac** 17. If the offspring is unalterable in nature because of the one who begot it, the ingenerate is an unalterable essence, not by choice but by the dignity that lies in its essence.

**76,12,1ad** 18. If “ingenerate” is indicative of essence, it is fittingly distinguished over against the essence of the offspring; but if “ingenerate” signifies nothing, much more does “offspring” indicate nothing; and how could nothing be distinguished over against nothing?

**76,12,1ae** 19. But if the utterance “ingenerate” is distinguished over against the utterance “begotten”, then, when silence succeeds the utterance, it follows that the hope of Christians comes into being and passes away, resting on a difference of utterance and not in natures that are such as the meaning of the names intends.

**76,12,1af** 20. If “ingenerate” confers nothing more by way of superiority of essence as against the offspring, the Son, surpassed only in utterance, will recognise as better than himself those who gave the names, not the one so named, his God and Father.

**76,12,1ag** 21. If the ingenerate essence is superior to generation, having its superiority from within itself, it is itself ingenerate essence.

**76,12,1ah** For it is not by willing, because he wills it, that he is superior to generation, but because he is so by nature.

**76,12,1ai** God, then, being himself ingenerate essence, permits no reasoning to conceive of generation in its case, thrusting every inquiry and every reasoning to be directed against the begotten things.

**76,12,1aj** 22. If “ingenerate” in the case of God is indicative of privation, and “ingenerate” is nothing, what reasoning could take away anything from what is not?

**76,12,1ak** But if it signifies what is, who could part from what is that which it itself is?

**76,12,1al** 23. If privations are removals of states, then “ingenerate” in the case of God is either a privation of states or a state of privation.

**76,12,1am** But if it is a privation of a state, how could what does not belong to God be counted along with him?

**76,12,1an** 24. But if “ingenerate” is a state, a begotten essence must be presupposed, so that, having thus taken on a state, it may be named ingenerate.

**76,12,1ao** 25. But if the begotten has partaken of ingenerate essence, having undergone the loss of a state, it has been deprived of ingeneracy.

**76,12,1ap** It would then be a begotten essence, and “ingenerate” a state.

**76,12,1aq** 26. But if “offspring” is indicative of a passing over, it is plain that it is significant of a state, whether it has been remodelled from some essence or is itself this which is called offspring.

**76,12,1ar** 27. If “ingenerate” is a state and “begotten” is a state, the essences come before the states, while the states, though they come second to the essences, are nevertheless held in greater honour.

**76,12,1as** 28. But if “ingenerate” is the cause of the begotten’s being, which is what is signified, the offspring bringing in its cause together with its own essence, then “offspring” is indicative of essence and not of a state; and since the ingenerate nature brings in nothing together with itself, how could the ingenerate nature be a state and not an essence?

**76,12,1at** 29. If every essence is ingenerate, as is that of God the Almighty, how could anyone call the one passible and the other impassible?

**76,12,1au** But if, by the allotment of an ingenerate nature, the one continues superior to quantity and quality and, in a word, to every change, while the other is liable to passions, then, it being granted that it has invariability of essence, one who so wishes may entrust it to chance, according to what has been said before; or at any rate the consequence is to call the one that acts ingenerate, and the one that is changed begotten.

**76,12,1av** 30. If the ingenerate nature is cause of the nature that came into being, and “ingenerate” is nothing, how could nothing be the cause of what has come into being?

**76,12,1aw** 31. If “ingenerate” is a privation, and a privation is the casting off of a state, and what is cast off either perishes entirely or passes over to something else, how is it possible for the essence of God to be designated by the appellation “ingenerate” through a state that passes over?

**76,12,1ax** 32. If “ingenerate” indicates a privation that does not belong to God, how do we say that he is ingenerate and not begotten?

**76,12,1ay** 33. If “ingenerate” is a bare name in the case of God, and the bare utterance exalts the subsistence of God above all begotten things, then the utterance of men is more honourable than the subsistence of the Almighty, since it has adorned God Almighty with an incomparable pre-eminence.

**76,12,1az** 34. If a cause has been allotted to every begotten thing, while the ingenerate nature is without cause, “ingenerate” does not indicate a cause, but signifies a subsistence.

**76,12,1ba** 35. If everything that has come into being has come into being by another, while the ingenerate subsistence came into being neither by itself nor by another, “ingenerate” must indicate essence.

**76,12,1bb** 36. If the ingenerate subsistence is manifested together with the essence of the offspring as its cause, having invariability as against every cause, it is incomparable self-essence, not displaying inaccessibility along with it from outside, but being itself incomparable and inaccessible, since it is also ingenerate.

**76,12,1bc** 37. If the Almighty rises above every nature, it is through the ingenerate that he rises above it, which is the cause of continuance for begotten things.

**76,12,1bd** But if “ingenerate” is not indicative of essence, whence will the nature of begotten things have its preservation?

**76,12,1be** 38. If none of the invisible things pre-exists itself in seed, but each continues in the nature allotted to it, how does the ingenerate God, who is free from allotment, see his own essence now as second in an offspring, now as first in the ingenerate, according to the order of first and second?

**76,12,1bf** 39. If God continues in an ingenerate nature, let his knowing himself in generation and in ingeneracy be taken away.

**76,12,1bg** But if it is granted that he extends his own essence into the ingenerate and the begotten, he himself is ignorant of his own essence, being drawn hither and thither by generation and ingeneracy.

**76,12,1bh** 40. But if the begotten too has received a share in ingenerate participation, yet continues endlessly in a begotten nature, it knows itself in the imperfect nature, being plainly ignorant of the ingenerate participation.

**76,12,1bi** For it is not possible for it to have knowledge about itself as of both ingenerate and begotten essence.

**76,12,1bj** 41. But if “ingenerate” is easily despised on account of an aptitude for change, it is a dignity of nature, an unchangeable essence, since the ingenerate essence has been acknowledged to be superior to every cause.

**76,12,1bk** 42. If the ingenerate is exempt from every cause, and there should be many ingenerates, they will have an invariable nature.

**76,12,1bl** For the one would not make and the other come into being, unless by the allotment of some nature it had partaken of something common and something proper.

**76,12,1bm** 43. If every essence is ingenerate, neither will differ from the other in being subject to no master.

**76,12,1bn** How then could anyone say that the one is changed and the other changes it, when they do not allow God to bring into existence from no underlying essence?

**76,12,1bo** 44. If every essence is ingenerate, every essence is invariable.

**76,12,1bp** And since the essence has invariability, acting and being acted upon must be ascribed to chance.

**76,12,1bq** 45. And if there are many ingenerate and invariable beings, they will differ from one another beyond number.

**76,12,1br** For things that stand apart, whether wholly or in some respect, would not be countable, since every separation displays some allotment by a cause, whereas the ingenerate nature has been set apart from cause.

**76,12,1bs** 46. If “ingenerate” and “God” indicate the same thing in parallel, the ingenerate begot an ingenerate.

**76,12,1bt** But if “ingenerate” indicates one thing and “God” another, it is not absurd for God to have begotten God, each having received existence from ingenerate essence.

**76,12,1bu** 47. But if there is nothing before God, as indeed there is not, “God” and “ingenerate” indicate the same thing, since the offspring does not admit “ingenerate”.

**76,12,1bv** Therefore it does not even allow itself to be named together with its God and Father.

**76,12,37a** May the God who is self-begotten, who also was called the only true God by the one who was sent, Jesus Christ — who truly subsisted before the ages and is truly of begotten subsistence — keep you, men and women, in good health and safe from impiety, in Christ Jesus our Lord, through whom be all glory to the Father, both now and always and to the ages of ages.

**76,12,37b** Amen.

**76,12,37c** Here ends the treatise of Aetius.

**76,13,1a** And this, as I have said, is the opening — which we are refuting — of his destructive expressions that have reached us in part.

**76,13,1b** For they say that he composed three hundred chapters in all, of the same kind as these, full of every blasphemy.

**76,13,2** But here, as when the body of a serpent has perished and rotted, and some diligent person who came upon it has gathered the bones from the serpent’s remains, the little treatise contains, for the ruin of certain people, the plot he boasts of having made, writing to certain persons, forsooth, as if out of love of what is fine; and its beginning runs thus.

**76,13,3a** For this reason let us too, gathering by the working of God the healing words of the divine scripture, prepare from beginning to end a refuting antidote for those who wish to be healed of his venom, setting the refutations directly against each expression of these syllogistic chapters of his, as follows.

**76,13,3b** The words of Aetius the Anomoean.

**76,14,1** Since, at the time of the persecution brought upon us by the Temporalists, certain of those mentioned before appropriated, along with many other things, a little work on which I had laboured by myself concerning the ingenerate God and the begotten, and published it corrupted with additions and subtractions, having altered its logical order; and since after this it came to us, one of our zealous friends having brought it to us,

**76,14,2** I have been compelled, as a father, to cleanse it once more and send the treatise out to you, all you athletes of piety, men and women, so that you may know that our little discourse has been spoken in accordance with the sense of the holy scriptures, by which, with brief retorts, you will be able to stop the shamelessness of every man who attempts to contradict you concerning the ingenerate God and the begotten, and still more of the aforesaid Temporalists;

**76,14,3** for I have set out, in the manner of verses, objection upon objection and solution upon solution, for the sake of the easy grasp and the clarity of the arguments, making my beginning with the ingenerate God.

**76,15,1a** Refutation.

**76,15,1b** Word for word I shall make the refutation of your dialectical bragging and your syllogistic labour in vain, neither passing over nor setting in second place the untold mass of your expressions, whether they seem to you weighty or slight.

**76,15,2** And first, since above, writing to the men and women athletes of your company, you said that certain Temporalists had appropriated what you had in hand of your little work, the expression you used, when examined, would convict you rather, and those discipled by you — not to say led astray — of possessing this name.

**76,15,3a** For the holy faith of God, being from the beginning and ever ancient and never growing old, exists always, and its foundation has been made firm, and it has its Master, who is timeless.

**76,15,3b** Therefore it is not itself temporal either, but it always lives as a citizen with the angels and adorns saints from generation to generation.

**76,15,4a** But you rather are temporal, beguiled by error and puffed up in mind, and having carelessly entangled the beasts of your herd in a thorny pasture.

**76,15,4b** For none of the ancients thought as you do, Aetius — you who write against temporal men while being temporal yourself, and not ancient.

**76,15,5** And right from your first attempt, by saying, as you put it, that you had written a little work concerning the ingenerate God and the begotten, you astounded the world with so brilliant an attempt at argument — so that in this way I may make laughable the reasoning of your disputation, of your so great newly invented coinage of names.

**76,16,1** For which of the Christian children who possess the saving preaching of God would abandon it at your urging, through your fabulous error, and, letting go of God, who always is, and his Holy Spirit, who always is, come and hear from you about a begotten God, so as himself also to be counted among fools, being taught to worship the creation rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever, amen?

**76,16,2** For we do not have a created God, nor a made one, but one uncreated and ingenerate, begotten of the Father without beginning and without time.

**76,16,3a** For even if you play the sophist with “begotten”, wishing to call him begotten in an equivocal sense, I will not receive your term, even though you may not mean it so, as something lessened in comparison with being begotten of the Father; for they do not gather grapes from thorns, nor figs from thistles, nor could a right word be left over from a man gone astray; for the Lord too muzzled the demons when they confessed him as Christ.

**76,16,3b** And you claim that your little discourse accords with the sense of the divine scriptures.

**76,16,4a** Tell me, which divine scripture taught that a made God is to be worshipped?

**76,16,4b** And that God is ingenerate would be clear to anyone.

**76,16,5a** But not even this is set down by name in the divine scripture.

**76,16,5b** But from right and pious reasoning, and from understanding itself, it stands firm to think and to say this piously about God.

**76,16,6** And you say that the chapters were composed by you in brief and easily grasped language after the manner of verses, so that those whom you call athletes, men and women — but who are rather led astray — may know how to answer each person.

**76,16,7a** Therefore, against these very words of yours that seem strong and sophistical, which you have practised for disputing against greater men — or rather, so that you may lift up your mouth against the truth — we, the humble and unlearned, not greater but lesser than many in the holy church of God, shall make, as I said before, the refutation of this incoherent and utterly paltry babble.

**76,16,7b** And let the reply of our littleness to your preface go thus far.

**76,17,1** And now, having set down in order the beginning of your chapters, I shall set directly against each expression and chapter the counter-arguments from the divine scriptures and from right reasoning, and the refutations of your logical inquiries, so that the servants of God and true athletes, on reading and perceiving all your absurdity, may laugh you to scorn, saying, “The pride of your heart has done these things to you.

**76,17,2a** For you said these things in your mind:

**76,17,2b** ‘I will go up into heaven, and above the stars of heaven I will set my throne; I will sit on a lofty mountain.

**76,17,2c** Upon the lofty mountains towards the north I will go up above the clouds, and I will be like the Most High.’

**76,17,2d** But now you will go down into Hades, into the earth’s foundations,” and what follows.

**76,18,1a** And this is the beginning of the chapters of Aetius.

**76,18,1b** 1. If the ingenerate God is able to make the begotten ingenerate.

**76,18,1c** Refutation. In the first place, to reckon anything impossible for God was impious.

**76,18,1d** Only what is unbefitting his Godhead — and this not because he is unable to do it, but because baseness is unbefitting God, to whom nothing is impossible; rather, because what is base is impossible for his divine and mighty goodness, since he himself is good.

**76,18,2** And in another way. If the begotten’s being ingenerate were reckoned by God a good thing to bring about, but he is unable to accomplish well what is done for good, this would be a defeat for the Mighty One, since he would wish to achieve what is preferable and not be able to.

**76,18,3** But if the ingenerate is good, and the begotten has come into being well in its own order — the order of the begotten being good, from a good God, and so reckoned by him — he would not make what is well begotten ingenerate, since its being so has been well reckoned by him to be good.

**76,18,4a** Since, then, the order of what is good is left unchanged not because of impossibility, but because it is well as it is, the ingenerate God is therefore good, and good are the things that have come from him in their own order, not having received the name of the ingenerate.

**76,18,4b** For he did not make created gods, so that the one, stretched out alongside the other, should by the shared title obliterate the namelessness of the greater as against the lesser.

**76,18,5** For if the one is ingenerate God and the other begotten God, their natures having nothing in common, it is impossible for them to share by nature in the dignity of the name, except perhaps by some grace loosely applied, and that by participation, the rich one bestowing it on the lesser.

**76,18,6a** But the lesser would never call himself by the name of the greater, knowing that he is altogether a stranger to the dignity and the name that belong by nature.

**76,18,6b** Someone might say to you, Aetius, “The Word was God, and the Word did not become God.”

**76,18,6c** How will he possess the name of noble birth that is his by nature, or how will he be put on an equal footing, if anything at all has come into being in the dignity of Christ?

**76,18,6d** Or how will the “was God” be cut away, since the “was” does not admit of time making a division even in the slightest degree?

**76,18,7** But you shall know that God without beginning and God ingenerate begot from himself God like himself — and not only like, but equal in all things.

**76,18,8a** And he did not create him, lest the one created, becoming unlike, should obliterate the name “God” through the distance of the difference.

**76,18,8b** For it is impossible for the begetter to beget what is unlike and unequal to himself, and for the begotten to be unlike the one who begot him.

**76,18,9** Therefore here one will grasp what belongs by nature to the sameness, from the testimony of the gospel, “All that is the Father’s is mine” — that is: the Father is God, and I am God; the Father is life, and I am life; and so on, all that befits Father and Son and Holy Spirit in one Godhead, the Trinity having nothing varied —

**76,18,10** since it has been made clearly secure to us in perfect knowledge that the subsistent Word of the Father, and the subsistent Holy Spirit, from the Father and from what is the Son’s, are without beginning and without time.

**76,19,1a** 2. If the ingenerate God is superior to every cause, he would for this reason be superior to generation too.

**76,19,1b** And if he is superior to every cause, it is plain that he is superior to generation too.

**76,19,1c** For he neither received his being from another nature, nor did he himself give being to himself.

**76,19,2** Refutation. If the ingenerate God is superior to every cause, and the one begotten from him has been begotten unworthily of him and not in equality, and yet stands in the Father’s preferred name, the offspring brings dishonour on the one who begot it, since it has the dignity of a name other than that of the creatures that have come into being, and does not, as the things made do, procure honour for its maker.

**76,19,3** For the things outside him procure glory for their creator, not being equal to their maker, nor called by their maker’s name, but having become servants for the glory of their maker, so that from the glorious things — from what lies above the glorious things that have come into being — the preferable, which is beyond them, may be contemplated by analogy.

**76,19,4** But he who is no longer called by their naming, but has his dignity through consubstantiality with the preferable, from being ranked in union with it — if he differs from the preferable by variation, he will also procure a lesser dignity for the preferable, since the offspring’s communion with the preferable is made different.

**76,19,5** Therefore the shoot, like from like and equal from equal, has been grasped by us in faith, not from a bodily notion, but as God from God, light from light, and the Father’s Word, subsistent, while the unchangeable glory of the preferable is preserved, in that the preferable is not its own cause, but begets from itself the equal in an undefiled and incomprehensible essence — consubstantially, the essential and subsistent divine offspring, of which it is the image, not a lifeless one, but one that bears the stamp of the Father’s kind, as the divine scripture says, setting the offspring in equality with the begetter, saying, “the image of the invisible God.”

**76,19,6** And so that no one should think that the image is something different from sameness, the Father himself, providing for the restoration of our life, said before this saying, “Let us make man after our image and after our likeness,” not distinguishing himself from the Son, but using a word that is dual and shared in name, “Let us make man,” so as to signify two, himself and the Son — or, I might also say, the Holy Spirit too.

**76,19,7a** And as to the equality of the image, not putting it in through two words, he said one image, but by “our” he declared the duality.

**76,19,7b** And the man who came into being came into being as an image, not by the image of the one, but by the likeness and equality of the two, so that it might be wholly clear that what is to be done in Father and Son and Holy Spirit abides in sameness and is not altered.

**76,19,8** For neither the Father nor the Son nor the Holy Spirit received from another nature, or gave to another nature a share in his own nature and dignity; nor did the Only-begotten’s being from him come about by some cutting or effluence, nor did the Holy Spirit work an alteration of the nature; but just as from the beginning there always was a preferable nature, ingenerate and uncreated, so he has clearly proclaimed to us a preferable offspring and Holy Spirit always from him, and not in an altered way.

**76,20,1** 3. But if he did not give being to himself, not through weakness of nature but because he transcends every cause, on what ground could anyone grant that the nature brought into existence has invariability of essence in relation to the nature that brought it into existence, when such a subsistence does not admit generation?

**76,20,2** Refutation. You ought, Aetius, attending to what is above and considering your own pitiable state, to restrain the excess of impiety of your daring mind, so that we too, not raving along with such fearlessness, may not be supposed to have been worsted, but rather to be counselling both you and ourselves towards piety.

**76,20,3** For while you suppose that, out of much error, you have come forth with a kind of pious composition, making God unlike and unequal to the one begotten from him in the necessary matters and in what befits God, you rather proclaim God, in the most unbefitting terms, to be like things that do not befit his Godhead.

**76,20,4** And in the first place, to conceive so great a depth of folly about God is the fruit of impiety and, still more, of a frenzied mind.

**76,20,5a** For by saying “cause of himself”, or “he gave himself being”, you have pierced yourself through with two evil suppositions, groping about and inquiring how God existed — whether always, or giving being to himself, or existing of his own accord.

**76,20,5b** And I fear and shudder as I stretch myself alongside your evil reasoning.

**76,20,6a** Stop, then, and we shall stop, holding it sufficient and holy always to think of God and to believe that God always was.

**76,20,6b** For in this too, speaking and reasoning foolishly, you said, as though you had greatly honoured God, that he did not give himself being — nor, then, by your reckoning, if the salvation of the faith rests on expressions and syllogisms, since it holds the likeness of the argument even in inferior or pitiable bodies.

**76,20,7** For none of the creatures is its own cause, or gave being to itself, from vermin up to man and from men up to angels.

**76,20,8a** For none of the things that have come into being gave itself being, but each received the beginning of its being from him who alone is.

**76,20,8b** Since, then, you have here been caught in a syllogism by the very means by which you thought to syllogise, do not force yourself, against nature, to stretch yourself out alongside the greater.

**76,20,8c** For you will be undone in every respect, since the Only-begotten is equal and like to the Father, even though he has from the Father the dignity of having been brought forth, that is, begotten.

**76,20,9** For in this respect he will differ in nothing from equality with the Father, just as he does not differ from the likeness either, in that things which have come into being cannot give themselves being; as the preferable one too, perfect in all things, did not have his beginning from anyone above; for he did not even begin to be.

**76,20,10** For he always was and always is, even though he remains in sameness and did not give himself being — it is not expressions of the same name that are being sought, but contemplation, in its purity, directed towards piety.

**76,20,11** And in another way. Since you said, “But if he did not give himself being, it is not owing to weakness of nature but because he has transcended every cause,” learn yourself too that it is not owing to weakness in the Son that the name will be his, but owing to what befits the one who begot him that he has the distinction of consubstantiality.

**76,20,12** For indeed, as transcending every cause is most fitting for the Father, so also the same one Godhead befits the only one from the only Father together with the only Spirit — a Godhead unable even to admit a cause, not through weakness but because it has transcended every number of the things that come from what is not, the Godhead being one, a Trinity numbered in one name and proclaimed to those who are being enlightened in one seal of the names of Father and Son and Holy Spirit, and having nothing in itself that varies, through the words in truth that fill out an equality of naming, of Father and Son and Holy Spirit.

**76,20,13** And again you said, “How could anyone grant that the nature which has been brought into existence has no variation in essence from the nature which brought it into existence, when such an existence does not admit of generation?” — and you neither perceive now nor have ever perceived that you have made yourself a stranger to the true knowledge of God, not being taught the things of the truth by the Holy Spirit, but trying to intrude into the things above by a worldly wisdom that has been made foolish.

**76,20,14a** For in consequence you too will hear that you have become futile.

**76,20,14b** “For God knows the reasonings of the wise, that they are futile.”

**76,20,15** For he who begets the Word that has real subsistence begot him as his own equal, in no way varying from his own Godhead — not on account of any variation in the offspring, but because it was wholly unfitting that we should imagine the very one who begot to have begotten an offspring unworthy of himself, unequal, and inferior to its begetter.

**76,20,16** That is why he said that all things came into being through the Son and subsistent Word: so that he might number him not among the things that have come into being, but as being in the Father, like and equal, because he is what befits the naming of the Father, ever existing in essence in very truth, not a stranger but true-born, as a consubstantial Son begotten from him.

**76,21,1a** 4. If God remains endlessly in ingenerate nature, and the offspring is endlessly offspring, the false doctrine of the ‘consubstantial’ and of the ‘unlike in essence’ will vanish.

**76,21,1b** “But that which is in incomparable essence stands firm, each nature remaining unceasingly in the proper dignity of its nature.”

**76,21,2** Refutation. If God remains endlessly and unceasingly, as you said, in ingenerate nature, and God’s nature is eternal, possessing its dignity endlessly, not on account of anything else but because it is God in itself and eternal in itself, then surely the offspring too will be consubstantial, if with you it has received the name of ‘endless’, as you have plausibly theorised in your shifting way so as to grant it to the Son.

**76,21,3a** For you will grant it, being forced also to confess the name of ‘endless’, which in all things is immeasurable and uncontainable.

**76,21,3b** How then will it not be consubstantial?

**76,21,3c** Since you saw fit to scoff, trying to outrage the truth through a name of false doctrine, you are refuted by the very words you spoke.

**76,21,4** For either you will assign an end to those whom you blaspheme as varied in essence, or, having defined him as endless, you will be compelled to bring him in as in all things unchangeable and unvarying from the dignity of the endless, since the truth does not admit that the Son has an end — “for of his kingdom”, says the Scripture, “there shall be no end” — because he reigns for ever with the Father and with his Holy Spirit; since all that has had a beginning shall likewise come to an end, should he who furnished being to what received its beginning so will; which is admissible in the case of all things, but in the case of the Son is inadmissible.

**76,21,5a** For he is ever from him who is, and ever with him who is, never ceasing to be.

**76,21,5b** Therefore he was and is and will be consubstantial, only from only, and varied in nothing in essence; but in accordance with the dignity of the names the Godhead remains in its sameness, neither having fusion nor providing itself with a beginning of being nor admitting that the unlike exists in it — the Godhead which ever is and never ceases to be, and which befits itself, existing ever in the dignity of Father toward Son and of Son toward Father and of Holy Spirit with Father and Son, and never failing.

**76,21,5c** For the Trinity is beyond comparison in itself, admitting no division in its dignity.

**76,22,1a** 5. If God is ingenerate in essence, what was generated was not generated by a division of essence, but from an essence that brought it into existence.

**76,22,1b** “For no pious reasoning permits the same essence to be both generate and ingenerate.”

**76,22,2a** Refutation. Many times, sir, you have come out before us bringing forward the ‘ingenerate’ and ‘generate’, vaunting yourself over the name of God — you who have buried your own mind in every lawlessness.

**76,22,2b** But this is what everyone in want longs for — an abundance of what he lacks, for his comfort — and to carry it on his lips, if he has no plenty of such a thing.

**76,22,3** And you, since you happen to be godless, pride yourself at least on uttering his name by means of this name, since you never possessed him by nature in accordance with the fear of him and faith and hope and love toward him.

**76,22,4a** Otherwise it would have sufficed you to say this once, and not to overstep the appointed limit of consistency.

**76,22,4b** For clear is the declarative proof given us by the Saviour, that “by their fruits you will know them”, in that you are clothed in a sheep’s fleece but within are a ravener, comparable to a wolf.

**76,22,5** For if you had been born of the Holy Spirit and schooled by prophets and apostles, you ought to have gone through, from the beginning of the world’s creation as far as the days of Esther, the Old Testament’s twenty-seven books, which are reckoned as twenty-two, and the four holy gospels, and the fourteen epistles of the holy apostle Paul, and those before them, and, together with the Acts of the Apostles of their times, the catholic epistles of James and Peter and John and Jude, and the Revelation of John, and the Wisdoms — of Solomon, I mean, and of the son of Sirach — and, in short, all the divine Scriptures, and to condemn yourself, because you came to us bringing a name which is nowhere set down — not unfitting for God, indeed, but reverent toward God, the name ‘ingenerate’ — yet nowhere spoken in divine Scripture; for no one has ever been so mad as to conceive of a generate God.

**76,22,6** But neither did they have any need to call the Father alone ingenerate God, on account of the one begotten from him, lest anyone should think that this is fulfilled in the Father alone, rather than also in the Son and in the Holy Spirit, since sound thinking and the Holy Spirit instruct all who are sons of truth to hold this of themselves, not as a matter of wonder, but to know it in accordance with what is required, and is present in itself, of reasoning directed to piety concerning God.

**76,22,7a** It is needful, since he is ingenerate — and this is agreed by us, though the term does not have the grounding of its naming from Scripture — to know of ourselves, through our reasonings, this point of piety: that it is so.

**76,22,7b** For why will what was begotten be a division of essence, if in truth it has the name of having been begotten in a natural and ineffable manner befitting God and the one begotten from him, timelessly and without beginning, in truth, and not by some loose supposition?

**76,22,8a** Hence we say that the essence is not created, nor alien as something made, but begotten essentially, and not other than the one who begot it.

**76,22,8b** That is why it remains uncreated and not made, but begotten from the same essence of God, not falling under time.

**76,22,8c** For he who in truth begot did not fall under time, so as to bring into existence a temporal essence.

**76,22,8d** For such as the offspring is, such is the begetter; and such as the begetter is, such also is the one begotten.

**76,23,1a** 6. If the ingenerate was generated, what prevents the generate from having become ingenerate?

**76,23,1b** “For every nature presses toward what is its own rather than toward what is foreign to it.”

**76,23,2** Refutation. If the ingenerate made and did not beget, the naming being ranged under the one sameness, and the one not being extended alongside the other through the correlative naming that is in truth, then the force of the relation stands in discord on the one side, sharing nothing with the other except only in respect of authority, and of the causality of the pre-eminent nature toward everything created by it.

**76,23,3** But since between the making and the made, and the created and what is being created, there is another naming, which draws near to the name ‘ingenerate’ but stands far off from the name ‘created’, it is impossible, Aetius, to confound everything and of your own accord to do away with the communion in the perfect naming, according to true relation, of a Son toward the Father, a Son who ever is and is uncreated.

**76,23,4** It is impossible for the ingenerate and uncreated nature ever to become created, and then, repenting of having been created, to run back again to its own ingenerateness — even if you weave us countless Aristotelian questions, having abandoned the simple and pure teaching from above, the teaching of the Holy Spirit.
