**76,24,1** 7. If God is not wholly ingenerate, nothing prevents his having begotten essentially; but if he is wholly ingenerate, he was not divided essentially for generation, but brought an offspring into existence by authority.

**76,24,2** Refutation. Both God is wholly ingenerate and uncreated, and the one begotten from him is uncreated, and his Holy Spirit — belittled by you, carnal Aetius, natural man examined by the spiritual — has in a form all its own the distinction of being from him, not likened to the many things created from the same, and through him, and by him.

**76,24,3a** Therefore it will neither share with all things, nor could anyone share in its dignity.

**76,24,3b** For everything flies aside, gives way and leaves behind every syllogistic ground before the teaching word from the divine Scripture: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor the Father except the Son, and he to whom he may reveal him.”

**76,24,4a** And it is through the Holy Spirit that he makes the revelation — not to those who reason about him by syllogisms, but to those who have believed in him sincerely and perfectly.

**76,24,4b** For you could neither search out his judgements nor trace out his ways, as it is written, even if you come to us babbling countless things, you pitiable little man, as I see you.

**76,25,1a** 8. If the ingenerate God is wholly generative, what was begotten was not begotten essentially, since his whole essence has begetting, not being begotten.

**76,25,1b** “But if the essence of God, having been transformed, is called offspring, his essence is not unchangeable, since the change brings about the Son’s individuation; but if the essence of God should be both unchangeable and superior to generation, what concerns the Son will be confessed as going no further than a bare appellation.”

**76,25,2a** Refutation. Now it was right to have nothing more to do, after a single warning, not only with you, Aetius, but with every heretic as well, as the holy and wise word directs.

**76,25,2b** For you are self-condemned, drawing destruction upon yourself, and not compelled by another.

**76,25,3a** Who then will have pity on a man who turns out wicked toward himself and good toward nobody?

**76,25,3b** But so that you may not suppose, regarding the evils you have sprouted for the world and hold within yourself, that they are great matters and arguments to the contrary, we too will persist with patience with the two-edged sword, cutting out your thorny roots by the word of Christ, in the sound, perfect and true confession toward God.

**76,25,4** For glory to the Merciful One, who has caught you out for what you are, holding the place of Judas, who was numbered with the disciples but was cut off, not having the mind of Christ, but having received from Satan the denial of God against his Master.

**76,25,5a** For you have confessed that you hold the Son of God in your mind by a bare term.

**76,25,5b** And what need is there of talk with you, when you are altogether a stranger to Christians, and to prophets and apostles and evangelists, and to martyrs and all the saints, who stand ready to convict you on the day of judgement, because they endured to the death, racked, scourged, scraped, thrown to beasts and fire and to slaughter by the sword, so that they might not deny him who is Son of God and truly begotten from him?

**76,25,6** For the Father is begetter of the only Only-begotten, and of no other besides after the one, and the one who pours forth the Holy Spirit, and no other spirit; but he is creator and maker of the things that have come into being and are ever coming into being by him.

**76,25,7a** Therefore there are no further many sons being begotten, nor many spirits proceeding from him, since the same Godhead ever remains and is glorified in the Trinity, and is never added to, neither ceasing nor ever failing as though it were not.

**76,25,7b** That is why the dignity in the case of the offspring does not stop at a bare naming;

**76,25,8** since otherwise he would have had many brothers after him like himself, as in the saying, “Sons I have begotten and raised on high,” and in “he who has given birth to the drops of dew,” and in “from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named,” and in “Is there not one father of you all?” and in “my servant Jacob,” and in “my firstborn Israel.”

**76,25,9a** For all these, having advanced by a bare word in being brought up from non-being into being, stand in the true naming not according to essence, but merely and by grace.

**76,25,9b** Therefore it was through the one who is named neither by grace nor by a bare naming, but in truth, that they were created — from the one, through the one, together with him who proceeds from him and receives of the same.

**76,26,1a** 9. If the offspring existed seminally within the ingenerate God, then after its generation it came to manhood, so to speak, by taking on additions from without.

**76,26,1b** “The Son, then, is perfect not by virtue of the things from which he was begotten, but of those which he took on besides.”

**76,26,1c** “For things that take on additions of a kindred sort, as being constituted from them, are naturally disposed to admit the name of ‘perfect’ in a different way.”

**76,26,2a** Refutation. If the begetter were not confessed to be incorporeal, let everything be staged as a play by you.

**76,26,2b** But by your staging you frighten no one else; rather you muddy your own mind, away from the true confession.

**76,26,3a** For God, being perfect, begot from himself a perfect Son, not other in nature.

**76,26,3b** For he is not unbefitting in relation to the begetter, nor in need of addition from without.

**76,26,3c** For there is nothing greater beyond the essence of God, that it could impart addition to one in need of it, for perfection.

**76,26,4** For he who ever is incorporeal has begotten him who is incorporeal, with him who is, ever by way of begetting — the perfect has truly and ever begotten the perfect — God, who is spirit, having begotten the subsistent Word, who is spirit.

**76,26,5** For the whole thing would be foolish on the part of you, Aetius, who intrude and search out the doctrines concerning God by syllogisms, and of your fondness for reasoning: that to him who made all things out of what is not and was able to work all things perfectly at once, having no need of increase by addition, but who bound these things by an ordinance, you ascribe a Word in need of a maturing essence of additive Godhead, and do not even put him on a level with the things created by him.

**76,26,6** For having made them perfectly from the beginning, he determined by a law of wisdom that what still springs from them should need addition — and these are the things in which are those that have come and are coming into being in order, as, for example, heaven, earth, water, air, sun, moon, stars, and the things brought forth from the waters, up to man himself.

**76,26,7a** He did not make heaven imperfect, nor the earth most imperfect, but the earth perfect and heaven perfect, though invisible and unformed at that time, because of the adornment he was going to make.

**76,26,7b** And water together with the first-created light — having made all things by means of the true Light, which is uncreated and gives life;

**76,26,8** and then the things that grew from the earth; and before this the firmament did not come into being as something half-finished, but all things in perfection: “For let the earth bring forth the herb of grass, sowing seed according to likeness upon the earth, and the fruit-bearing tree, whose seed of them is in it according to likeness upon the earth.”

**76,26,9** And you see that the things that came into being did not at once need any increase by addition, but are found at once full-grown, so to speak, and perfect through the command;

**76,26,10** but the things given to man, which are under him and in him seminally for his dominion, were handed over not perfect, so that man might always know the one who does him good and furnishes being to all, who is over all and furnishes the increases of each thing made for the support of the things that serve him.

**76,26,11** He handed things over to him seminally, setting the earth before him as a base, so to speak, and giving it over to him to serve as a womb, in order that, in the case of the things which he himself sows seminally with understanding upon the earth from the produce of the things made perfect by God — such as a tree, for example, and other produce — he himself, gathering in small portions, like a pebble, from the perfect things, and depositing this in the earth,

**76,26,12** might receive what belongs to the increase given by the perfect God for growth; so that the things seeded by him might be increased from without, lest, failing to recognise the supplier of the increase, he should think himself the creator and fall away from the truth.

**76,26,13a** For even if Noah planted a vine, it is not written that he was a maker of plants, but that he became a man, a husbandman.

**76,26,13b** For one is he who furnishes the originals to the things that are to be, and another is man, who has received being from him and has been entrusted with the cultivation of what is his, so that the one may cultivate the things that need increase for their completion, and the other may furnish perfection through his own increase of the things created by him and growing to perfection.

**76,26,14** So too with the animals and with the birds, so too with the cattle and creeping things and sea creatures: all came into being perfect in the beginning through him who commanded, but by the will of wisdom they now need increase, for the benefit, in understanding, of man who has dominion on earth, so that he may recognise the God who is over all, the supplier of the seeds and of the increase of their growth, who is God and Lord.

**76,26,15a** That is why God left in their perfection the things in heaven, which are not sown by the hands of man, and which neither beget nor are begotten.

**76,26,15b** For they did not fall upon the mind of man to occasion scheming and the conceit of vainglory, as one may say, for instance, of the sun and moon and stars.

**76,26,16** For neither is the moon altered in its manner on account of being born, or waning, or waxing, but on account of being the establishing and supply of the seasons which God appointed for the luminaries.

**76,26,17** How then did God, by his will, at once make perfect the bodily things and the waning and the perishing things, yet beget the one whom he begot from himself, one from one, him who ever is, by way of begetting, with him who is, as one needing increase?

**76,26,18** Stop, then, Aetius, bringing us empty and Aristotelian terms, since we are well enough provided and are not deceived, according to the true teaching of our Lord, the teaching that declares, “From the Father I came forth, and I am here,” the expression not having its force in a loose sense, but signifying the essence of perfection and of the dignity of God.

**76,27,1a** 10. If the offspring was perfect, it is offspring in the ingenerate, and not from the things from which the ingenerate begot it.

**76,27,1b** “For it is not admissible that a generate nature should be in an ingenerate essence.”

**76,27,1c** “For the same thing both is and is not.”

**76,27,1d** “For an offspring is not ingenerate, and, being ingenerate, it was not offspring, since the unlike part holds, in the case of God, the form of blasphemy and outrage.”

**76,27,2a** Refutation. Aetius brings in contradictions, wishing to comprehend God from syllogistic namings of human invention, and as it were by means of words he tries to mutilate the sure hope of the evident faith, clashing unlike against unlike in unlike fashion and inserting word beside word subversively, so as from this to force them to signify the unlikeness of the one who is toward the Father, which is impossible.

**76,27,2b** For by the very syllogisms he taught the world he himself too will be caught in a syllogism.

**76,27,3a** For he says, “If the offspring was perfect, it is in an ingenerate offspring, and not from the things from which the ingenerate begot it.”

**76,27,3b** “For it is not admissible that a generate nature should be in an ingenerate essence; for the same thing both is and is not.”

**76,27,3c** “For an offspring is not ingenerate, and, being ingenerate, it was not offspring, since the unlike part holds, in the case of God, the form of blasphemy and outrage.”

**76,27,3d** So the parts of his counterfeiting of the words are refuted on every side, since it is not admissible for the Son to be unlike the Father, nor unequal to his perfect Godhead.

**76,27,4** For if he speaks at all in a forced way, and turns against himself the texts which he expounds, ever speaking of the generate and the ingenerate, let him learn from this about the created and the uncreated, that it is not admissible for the one to share with the other in respect of the dignity, which is the whole that is worshipped.

**76,27,5** For if the unlike, put on a level with the unlike, is worshipful at all, reason will no longer distinguish the one from all things, since unlikeness cannot be ranked in the order of its own dignity — even if the one, out of all things, which are unlike toward the one, should surpass them in glory, on account of the unlikeness of all things toward the one, which has no share with the one.

**76,27,6** And then sun and moon and stars and earth, and the things still lower than these, will be worshipful, and it will no longer be the One together with the one Spirit, which is one Trinity and one Godhead and one worship.

**76,27,7a** Then if this is to be inferred by syllogism through this, will it indeed be so in truth, since the one Word is not like all words, nor the one Son equal to all who are called so by elevation?

**76,27,7b** For he is not with all, but the one through whom all are.

**76,27,8** At any rate, what Aetius himself laid down from the outset as impossible, and as bearing the form of blasphemy, to outrage, on account of the ‘part’ which he said is in God — which is a part not of difference but of equality, the Godhead not being divided but ever being most perfect, three that are perfect, one Godhead — has rather made the

**76,27,9** ‘unlike’ secure for us for the establishing of the faith that is in truth, so that we should neither think nor be persuaded by those who, contrary to what is fitting, stumble through the prejudice of the Greeks’ rashness and stand condemned for worshipping the whole creation, which is folly in relation to the Father who is worshipped in the Son and the Son worshipped in the Father together with the Holy Spirit, whose is the glory unto the ages.

**76,28,1** 11. If God the Almighty, being of ingenerate nature, does not know himself to be of generate nature, while the Son, being of generate nature, knows himself to be this which he is, how could the ‘consubstantial’ not be a falsehood, since the one knows himself as ingenerate and the other as generate?

**76,28,2** Refutation. Aetius has said — and he declared it, this distinguisher and boundary-setter who pronounces on the nature of God, though he is a man by nature and wishes to know the things beyond nature, and to know them not by following Scripture but from syllogisms of mortal thoughts — that God the Almighty, being of ingenerate nature, does not know himself to be of generate nature.

**76,28,3** And he does so always, constantly and from the beginning of his discourse — no longer after the manner of the old Arians, even if he chooses to call the Only-begotten a Son in a veiled way.

**76,28,4a** But observe in everything, sons of the truth, how he wants him to be altogether alien to the Father, and to have no share at all in the divine essence, from the things he constantly and boldly pronounces.

**76,28,4b** For when he says that he knows himself as ingenerate and does not know himself to be of generative nature, then with him even the calling of the Son ‘Son’, if only by a bare word, is in vain.

**76,28,5a** But his argument will be overturned.

**76,28,5b** For indeed the Father is ingenerate and eternally begot the Only-begotten, being of a nature befitting itself, in that he has begotten one only, the Only-begotten, and has brought forth the Spirit — the only begetter, alone, of an only-begotten — and he coexists with the Son begotten without beginning; being spirit, he has begotten spirit, and is not a body divided in bodily fashion, nor waning and waxing and undergoing severance.

**76,28,6** Therefore with all the others who have begotten and are begotten, need admits of other things in the case of many, but here the dignity of the One toward the One is not like all the things that are.

**76,28,7** Therefore he who was begotten, in a unique manner, from him who begot in a wondrous manner, has been begotten as it were from the ingenerate, befitting the begetter; and he himself does not beget — no longer in respect of essence, I mean — so that, from his no longer begetting according to essence, and from the Father’s not having been begotten, the whole glory of the dignity may be preserved on both sides in the one unity of the dignity of God: perfect Father, perfect Son, and perfect Holy Spirit.

**76,28,8** And for this reason the divine Scripture does not know the ‘consubstantial’ as a falsehood, nor does the pious reasoning which has learnt piously about Father and Son and Holy Spirit, having received from God the grace to glorify and worship.

**76,29,1** 12. If ‘ingenerate’ does not represent the subsistence of God, but the incomparable name belongs to human conception, God owes gratitude to those who conceived it, on account of the conception ‘ingenerate’, since he does not bear the pre-eminence of the name in his essence.

**76,29,2a** Refutation. ‘Ingenerate’ too — as we said, addressing ourselves to Aetius — [and] we do not deny: even if it is not contained in divine Scripture, it has been piously conceived.

**76,29,2b** And calling the Father ingenerate, we also confess him ingenerate, and the Son we do not refuse to call generate — but not created.

**76,29,2c** For if we define the Son as generate, we cannot deny that he has his essence from God the Father; for he begot him by way of generation, and did not create him.

**76,29,3** For as you, thinking crookedly about everything concerning the generate and the ingenerate, wish to turn yourself aside (for it is nothing else), so you too hear, from human syllogisms and syllogistic antithesis and human vain-mindedness, the saying, “The mind of man is diligently bent on evil things from his youth.”

**76,29,4** We too will say that it is much more an unfitness for the uncreated God to create the things created, and for the unmade to make; for it is not admissible that the uncreated should create the things created, and that he who did not come into being should make the things that are to be, if it does not befit the ingenerate to beget, according to Aetius’ argument.

**76,29,5** But since the creatures are seen, and the greater part of essence appears as subsistence, which, as having been created by him, is not befitting to the uncreated God — so that the incomparable, carried over into the change of the things that have come into being, may not be thought by Aetius unfitting rather than fitting — then one will have to seek one God who is the uncreated, and another who was created and is able to create in proportion to himself.

**76,29,6a** And since the one who was created and has the power to create is not self-originated but created, another will also have to be sought who became his cause, and from him yet another will be conceived.

**76,29,6b** And great will be the idle talk of the thoughts of the abyss of error, the mind no longer standing firm but fulfilling the saying, “The servants of God have become fools, and every man has become a fool from knowledge.”

**76,29,7** For no one lives to himself, nor dies to himself, nor will anyone know anything apart from God, who has revealed the true faith to us, himself saying, “This is my beloved Son; listen to him,” and apart from the one begotten from him, who made his Father known to us, saying, “I came out from the Father and I am here.”

**76,29,8** And neither did God have his incomparability from the naming of men, nor will the dignity of the true, subsistent God the Word, begotten from the Father without beginning and consubstantially, be turned aside on account of the incomparability, since neither of the names is indebted to the conceptions of men.

**76,29,9** For the Divine receives nothing in the way of dignity or addition; rather the Divine itself furnishes to all from its own fullness, which ever remains in sameness and is not diminished, but ever bears in its own essence the dignity of name and power and essence.

**76,30,1** 13. If ‘ingenerate’ is contemplated in God from without, those who contemplated it are better than him who was contemplated, having procured for him a name superior to his nature.

**76,30,2a** Refutation. No one is better than God — my word is addressed to Aetius, who has conceived things in this way — as the truth holds.

**76,30,2b** For how could anyone be better than God, when all have received their being from God?

**76,30,3** And since God is the cause of the things created by him, rational and irrational, seen and unseen alike, it is he who is better than them all, even if the rational beings should come to be of a mind upright toward piety, so as to honour the better in part — since not even all things gathered together into one, and countless more conceived beyond them, able to stretch out in the hymning of God, could contain within themselves the perfection of the same glory, the glory of the better ever surpassing the thought of the inferior, even though they stretch out to the hymning of the better according to their power and beyond their power.

**76,30,4a** For he is better not in word, but in power and name and word; yet the glorifying of the better by the inferior will not separate the incomparable from the incomparable.

**76,30,4b** For it knows the better in the Father through the ingenerate, and the better begotten from him.

**76,30,5** Therefore the right understanding granted to men by God confesses the consubstantial, lest, conceiving the ‘unlike in essence’ of the Son toward the Father, it should make a division of the better and pure perfection, through him whom it knows to have been begotten in truth by the one who begot him, who incomparably surpasses all thoughts because of what is better.

**76,31,1** 14. If the ingenerate nature does not yield to generation, it is what it is called; but if it yields to generation, the passions of generation would be superior to the subsistence of God.

**76,31,2a** Refutation. To speak of passions in God at all is most impious.

**76,31,2b** For the Divine is not contained within passions at all.

**76,31,2c** And since it is far above such things as in us fall under divisive notions, Aetius’ argument will be overturned in every way.

**76,31,2d** For everything that happens in us with passion subsists in God without passion.

**76,31,3a** For in us willing is in some part a passion — I do not mean willing to be pious, but willing to do something that is beyond nature, owing to the inability to accomplish what belongs to the will, as, to speak of man, flying, being borne into the air, discerning the veins of the deep, knowing the foundations of the earth, and things like these.

**76,31,3b** And as much as is held in me by passion, so much is present in God without passion.

**76,31,4** For this reason he can do everything he wills, since his nature does not work against his will, while ours works against our wishes in us, in so far as it lies in us to reach out toward the impossible.

**76,31,5a** And not because we said that God does what he wills would anyone at all say that he therefore does what is unfitting — by no means.

**76,31,5b** For he wills those things which he also does, in proportion to his dignity, neither his will working against him so that he is unable, nor his ability being opposed to his willing; it is not through inability, but through not willing.

**76,31,6** And in another way. After such impassibility, which exists in God but in us and in other creatures is passible, if one happens to think in this way, then again another passion must in truth be confessed, and after the second a third too may be conceived.

**76,31,7a** We beget and are begotten with passion, for our own nature, like that of the other things that are begotten and beget, admits severance and is subject to flux, to expansion and contraction, swelling and diminution, and all the other things that are held by passion for such a cause.

**76,31,7b** But in God none of these was present in his having begotten the Son.

**76,31,8** For if any one of such things had been present in God, according to the pretext-seeking supposition aimed at overturning the offspring, then from the other part, on our side, it must be said against them in reply that in us, who beget and are begotten with passion, there is a second passion in creating, and we suffer in begetting and in being begotten.

**76,31,9** But God, conceived by you as creator and not begetter — you who bring forward passion against begetting, to overturn it, so that you may deny the Son’s true sonship, but consign to oblivion the passion involved in creating, which itself too, in God, is no passion, God forbid.

**76,31,10a** For neither do we attach passion to him when we confess that he is the creator of all things, nor again do we conceive of passion as being in him when we confess him to be the begetter of the true Son, in truth, with no beginning and outside time.

**76,31,10b** Therefore we know his nature to be incomprehensible and not held by passion.

**76,31,11a** For this reason we confess him both an impassible begetter and an impassible creator.

**76,31,11b** For it was without undergoing passion that he begot the Only-begotten, and sent forth from himself his Holy Spirit without undergoing severance, and created the things created, and those being created, without toil and without being held by passion; and he does what he wills in a manner befitting his Godhead — not first willing, so that by reflection he may learn whether what is being accomplished ought to come about, nor willing to act and unable to supply his will, so that what is being completed comes about through passion.

**76,31,12** For he has at once the willing, the doing, the having begotten the Only-begotten, the having created all things, since the divine nature and dignity is far above Aetius’ syllogistic notion and all humankind, God being better than every conception, not yielding to passion, but being far above all passions and every supposition.

**76,32,1** 15. If the offspring is unchangeable in nature on account of the one who begot it, the ingenerate is unchangeable essence, not by intention, but by the dignity that is in its essence.

**76,32,2a** Refutation. How long will this man keep coming to us, contriving to say the same thing and to go no further than what lies before him?

**76,32,2b** For whatever he has said from beginning to end, he has set forth the same things about the same matters and nothing else — not showing us mysteries,

**76,32,3** not teaching the God whom he professes, not the faith by which the apostles, working and naming the firm confession of the truth, raised the dead and cleansed lepers, and all the other works of the good harmony, by which they displayed the examples of the true working, but setting forth vain and boastful syllogisms that go no further than the utterance of tautology, those very same things and nothing else; therefore we entreat that none of the readers may blame us if we too are carried against the same things, being compelled to speak in answer to his tautology.

**76,32,4a** For the offspring is unchangeable, as far as befits Godhead, and the begetter is unchangeable, as befits, in proportion, his unchangeable nature.

**76,32,4b** And he who begot remains, ever having the one begotten from him, allowing no supposition to the things created by him that they might know a Father without a Son, or ever know, apart from the Father, the one begotten and his perfect Spirit, the Spirit that issues from the Father and takes from the Son.

**76,32,5** And this befits the dignity of God’s essence: to need no dignity by way of addition, but to have it eternally in its own sameness.

**76,33,1a** 16. If ‘ingenerate’ indicates essence, it is rightly set in contrast to the offspring’s essence; but should ‘ingenerate’ signify nothing, much more does ‘offspring’ indicate nothing.

**76,33,1b** “And if nothing, how could it be set in contrast?”

**76,33,1c** “But if the utterance ‘ingenerate’ is set in contrast with the utterance ‘generate’, then, when silence succeeds the utterance, it follows that the hope of Christians comes to be and ceases to be, lying in a differing utterance, and not in natures that are such as the meaning of the names intends.”

**76,33,2a** Refutation. How is it that those who have learnt to dazzle the minds of the inexperienced are accustomed to forestall the testimonies against themselves?

**76,33,2b** For Aetius, who alone possesses his hope in utterance and not in truth, has himself boldly come forward to attribute this to us, not being ashamed to confess a Son of God and God the Father by a bare word; whereas we most emphatically confess that there is a Father by nature, a Son by nature, and a Holy Spirit by nature.

**76,33,2c** For nothing else will be compared with the Trinity.

**76,33,3** And for this reason the support of our confession is truly the consubstantial, and not by way of an utterance that is abolished through coming to be and not coming to be, as is Aetius’ opinion about Father and Son and Holy Spirit.

**76,33,4** For there is in reality a true Father, and in reality a true Son, and a true Holy Spirit, even if he sows countless vain syllogisms, as the divine word says, speaking of such people: “I will set aside the discernment of the discerning,” and, “The Lord knows the reasonings of men, that they are futile,” and so on.

**76,34,1** 17. If ‘ingenerate’ assigns nothing more toward pre-eminence of essence than ‘generate’, the Son, being surpassed only in utterance, will recognise as better than himself those who gave the appellation, not the one so addressed, his God and Father.

**76,34,2a** Refutation. No pious reasoning would grant — even if Aetius stages countless dramas for us — that the better are those who got their being from him who is.

**76,34,2b** For he himself too confesses that they came into being through him.

**76,34,3** For neither do the Christians, who by his kindness have been counted worthy, know how to call the offspring so by utterance of speech, but as true begotten from true — because they know him in truth, and have been taught through the Father and not by flesh and blood, and for this reason are fittingly called blessed, like him who recognised him as Son of God with the addition ‘of the living’ — even while they spiritually examine the natural man Aetius, who does not receive the things of the Spirit, and even though he who is spirit and only-begotten should say,

**76,34,4** “I go to my Father and your Father, and my God and your God,” since neither of these two namings can be put on a level with names of another kind,

**76,34,5** the truth ever remaining and teaching clearly each needful order in the Son of God in truth.

**76,34,6** For neither is ‘my Father and your Father’ to be fulfilled with reference to them according to the flesh (for how is God the Father of flesh, God who did not put on flesh?), nor is ‘my God and your God’ to be fulfilled according to the Godhead of the Son and according to the adoption of the disciples;

**76,34,7a** but ‘my God and your God’, on account of the incarnation among us — thus he who speaks truth in all things mysteriously made the disciples secure.

**76,34,7b** And ‘my Father and your Father’, on account of what is mine toward him by nature, and of my communion toward you, of which I, having come to dwell among you out of love for mankind, granted you to become partakers, through the text, “He gave them authority to become children of God.”

**76,34,8** That is why he himself, having come among them, took the form of a servant, sharing newly in what is new, while the things of old remain in their sameness and do not pass over into confusion — the sons of men being changed into incorruption through participation, but not united into consubstantiality, and the one who assumed a servant’s form showing, through ‘having taken’, what is new, and, through ‘being in the form of God’, not passing over into change.

**76,34,9** These things being so, and being thus clearly confessed in perfect knowledge by those taught by God, neither ‘my God and your God’ nor ‘my Father and your Father’ will, through the reasonable communion by the shared name, cause a departure from the pure essence, from the pre-eminence of the proper distinctiveness of Father toward Son and of Son toward Father, and of the Holy Spirit likewise.

**76,35,1a** 18. If the ingenerate essence is superior to generation, having its superiority from itself, it is ingenerate as essence itself.

**76,35,1b** “For it is not by willing, because he wills, that he is superior to generation, but because he is so by nature.”

**76,35,1c** “God, then, being himself ingenerate essence, permits no reasoning to conceive generation in its own case, thrusting away every examination and every reasoning, so that they are carried against the things that are generate.”

**76,35,2** Refutation. Aetius has involved us in the same vexations, causing us, as I said, to repeat ourselves many times, because of his tautology about the same things from beginning to end.

**76,35,3** For never has the faith that saves every believer been founded on the syllogistic supposition of men, since the minds of men are unreliable and cannot reach out to the infinity of the essence of God.

**76,35,4** For indeed the whole life-giving mystery of our salvation, the mystery of Christ, is to Jews an offence and to Greeks folly, but to us the called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ is God’s power and God’s wisdom; because what is foolish in God is wiser than men, and what is weak in God is stronger than men.

**76,35,5** How then could one fail to rank Aetius with the Jews, on account of the offence his syllogisms give, and count him a Greek because, from his own self-chosen wisdom, he considers the truth of God foolishness?

**76,35,6a** For indeed the creator and fashioner of all things is one, and superior to all creation and workmanship; yet not on this account, because he is superior to the things begotten by him, does he fail to make and create the things that have come into being through him; for neither does he begrudge his own goodness.

**76,35,6b** For he has from himself goodness itself, which is superior to all things.

**76,35,6c** For he is not contained within passions, or envy, or malice; and he brought to completion the things that are out of what is not.

**76,35,7** For the things created by him, which came into being by him but fall below his incomparable Godhead, were not devised against himself, but for his glory, to show his ungrudging Godhead: being goodness itself and essence itself, it shares with the things created from him out of what is not, he having willed that they should be, and that each of the created things should share in what is his according to the proportion of the gift of each foundation;

**76,35,8** on the luminaries he has bestowed light, on heaven the beauties of its adornment, on earth and the other things he bestowed portions of excellence according to his will, on angels and on other holy powers the gift of incorruption, and on man the dignity of the image and the gift of life and knowledge and the rational endowment.

**76,35,9a** And this belonged to him not from will alone — in a deferring way, as one might say, or with regard to the future, or by deliberative reasoning — but in accordance with goodness itself.

**76,35,9b** For he is by nature goodness itself, having and making and working all things in a manner befitting himself.

**76,35,10** Just as, then, this gained for his goodness not unfitness but glory, and knowledge of the praise of his ungrudgingness among the things that came into being by him, once it had come into their knowledge and perception, so too the glory of his Godhead is not by way of addition.

**76,35,11** For the Divine never stands in want of glory added to it, but is glory itself, virtue itself, wonder itself and hymn itself — that the Father should beget, though he himself has not been begotten, so that from a spring that ever is an eternal spring coexists, being from him, spring from spring, and God from God, and light from light, not having begun to be, not having fallen under time, but at once truly having a Father, and the Father at once truly having a Son, not unbefitting the Father, not doing away with his incomparability.

**76,35,12** For he is not some bodily separation, but a subsistent Word, being God from the Father, spirit from spirit, and God from God, shutting out every syllogistic supposition, being for life to the faithful and to all who have come into being by the Father, through him and from him, who believe and know and do not consider God’s power and God’s wisdom foolishness — the wisdom which surpasses every examination and every reasoning, especially of corruptible men, as Aetius himself too has unwillingly confessed.

**76,36,1a** 19. If ‘ingenerate’, in the case of God, is indicative of privation, and ‘ingenerate’ should be nothing, what reasoning could remove nothing from what is not?

**76,36,1b** “But if it signifies something that is, who could separate from God, who is, what is his very self?”

**76,36,2** Refutation. Aetius brings us the things said by way of privation among the outside dialecticians, treating this as though it served the knowledge of God and our benefit, without first knowing in what cases the privative is taken among the outsiders.

**76,36,3a** For the dialecticians’ arguments do not hold that being spoken of by way of privation is admissible in the case of all things, but in the case of things that possess something by nature.

**76,36,3b** For to these, since they can come to stand in the opposites of what belongs to them by nature, the privative is applied, but no longer to things that cannot.

**76,36,4** For example, no one would say ‘blind’ of a stone; for it is one who by nature can see and afterwards loses the power of sight who is termed blind; if, however, a bird or a man or a beast, being by nature able to see, is deprived of it, it is called blind privatively;

**76,36,5** so too we would not call the stone ‘without anger’, or ‘guileless’, or ‘without envy’, for it is not of such a nature; but in the case of a man or a beast, which is by nature able to be angry, when it is not angry one might speak by way of privation, but no longer in the case of things that cannot.

**76,36,6** So too must it be taken in the case of God, the argument addressing itself to Aetius and examining him by questions: Tell us, Aetius, do you know him as incomparable with all who are not of the same essence, or would you dare to number him too with all things?

**76,36,7** And if you should number him among all things — those which are not of his essence, but have been brought into being out of what is not by him, through the one who is from him according to essence — excepting only him and the Holy Spirit, who comes from the essence and belongs to the incomparable Father and to his only-begotten Son, your confession would be most absurd.

**76,36,8a** For how is he still one of all things, he from whom all things have come into being out of what is not?

**76,36,8b** For that cannot be, and you yourself would not say it either.

**76,36,8c** And since it is not admissible that he should be like or equal to the things that have come into being from him out of what is not, it is inadmissible that he should undergo the same things as those unlike him, whose being is from him out of what is not, and all that is in them, and to whom it happens that the opposite exists by way of privation.

**76,36,9** For some things see, though not by their own power — since they do not possess even their being from themselves — but by the bestowing grace of the giver; and in them the passion occurs by privation of the things that were in them by the giving of the giver — who is impassible, owes his being to none, and is incapable of being deprived — to the things that came to exist out of what is not.

**76,36,10** If then that Son, or the Father, or the Holy Spirit, is not equal to these, but the Son is other than they, not called by an equal naming, but having a distinguished and incomparable name, being goodness itself from goodness itself, what connection could there be with the privative, which involves an opposite?

**76,36,11** For superfluous is the argument of Aetius, who brought in the privative for us, since the ingenerate God and the generate Son have their existing dignity not by way of the privation that belongs to creatures, but by what of itself, and in a manner all its own, befits his own essence and Godhead — as with ‘without anger’, not because of being angry but because of being without anger in himself, and ‘ingenerate’ because of being ingenerate in himself, even though the Son be generate from the ingenerate — the privative expression being idly applied to the one who is incomparable with the others, according to the mind of this man who puts it forward.

**76,36,12** For neither are the other things made equal to the one begotten, nor does the ingenerate impart consubstantiality to the things created — not because the one who is able is charged with inability, but because the things without power do not reach to what is possible, owing to the distinction of the one God and of the only-begotten Son from him, with the Holy Spirit.

**76,37,1a** 20. If privations are removals of the states themselves, then ‘ingenerate’ said of God is either a privation of a state or else the state of a privation.

**76,37,1b** “But if it is a privation of a state, how would what does not belong to God be counted with him as belonging?”

**76,37,1c** “And if ‘ingenerate’ is a state, a generate essence must be presupposed, so that, having thus taken on a state, it may be named ingenerate; but if a generate essence has partaken of ingenerate essence, having undergone the loss of a state, it has been deprived of ingenerateness.”

**76,37,1d** “The essence, then, would be generate, and ‘ingenerate’ a state.”

**76,37,1e** “But if ‘offspring’ is indicative of a passage, it is clear that it is significant of a state, whether it has been remoulded from some essence, or else is this very thing that is called offspring.”

**76,37,2** Refutation. Already, then, Aetius, having fought many battles on the subject of the privative hypothesis as an ally of those estranged from the faith, has himself also armed himself against the faith on an equal footing with them, saying nothing from the faith, and not remembering the text addressed to those who utter empty words of their own and do not hold fast the beginning of the faith, as the word says to them by way of refutation, “I said in my ecstasy, ‘Every man is a liar’”, together also with “I was greatly humbled.”

**76,37,3** But now, wearing himself out again on the same things, and putting forward a load of privation, naming and state, and of syllogisms of unreliable human supposition, and being spiritually examined, he does not have regard enough for himself to check his own impulse, which comes from human cunning, but gives himself leave to say about God whatever he wishes.

**76,37,4a** But he compels us too, though we have discoursed at length about privatives, to dwell again on the same things and to wear ourselves out in the refutations addressed to him.

**76,37,4b** And the refutation before this one was indeed sufficient, being able, because of the equal tendency and identical terms of his syllogistic argument, to be brought against both.

**76,37,5** But since one must neither let a hard-mouthed horse go without a bridle, whether it is rushing toward the pits or has already been checked in its charge, nor yield to a man who repeats the same things against the faith, and leave him without an answer, we will say again that,

**76,37,6** if privations are removals of states, ‘ingenerate’ said of God is either a privation of a state or else the state of a privation; and again, if it is a privation of a state, how would what does not belong to God be counted with him as belonging?

**76,37,7a** And as for your thinking of God in this way or in that, Aetius, and conjecturing states concerning God — your mind will be the thing that suffers privation.

**76,37,7b** For whatever your heart may rise up to lay down concerning God, apart only from believing and marvelling exceedingly and glorifying with the whole mind, you will be shown unable to reason out God by syllogism, or his Son, or his Holy Spirit — lest God convict you and you become a liar, as it is written.

**76,37,8a** For in us both states and wills and thoughts are unreliable, since we are of such a nature and essence.

**76,37,8b** Now ‘nature’ and ‘essence’ are also said of God; yet hearing ‘nature’ and ‘nature’, ‘essence’ and ‘essence’, is no reason for us to compare God, who admits no comparison, with our own nature.

**76,37,9** So too in everything you may say about God, Aetius, the whole of it is without combination, incomparable, perfect in itself, needing nothing; for it is perception itself and will itself.

**76,37,10** Therefore, having incomparably begotten an incomparable only-begotten Son, he has suffered no privation of his own essence, nor has the one begotten been deprived of his own, only from only; and his Holy Spirit, which has no equality with the other things, whether of dignity or of nature or of any other foundation,

**76,37,11** has not deprived itself, either in state or in essence, of his incomparable Godhead; nor has the offspring from him, as I said, been deprived of the Father’s dignity and equality, being incomparable,

**76,37,12** as is his Holy Spirit, with anything whatever; which is a perfect Trinity — Father perfect and Son perfect and Holy Spirit perfect — not being some fusion, nor at variance with itself, nor having in itself anything inferior,

**76,37,13** lest what is distinguished should do away with the incomparable, and what is altered should bring about a privation of being, spoken of only as a state and not in truth, or named by a bare word in passing, and not being, as your mind wholly imagines, trying to make things alien to the word of the faith,

**76,37,14a** that “one who approaches God has to believe that he is, and that he becomes a rewarder to those who seek him out”; which cannot be fulfilled in the Father alone.

**76,37,14b** For he who does not have the Son does not have the Father either, and he who speaks of the Son cannot do so apart from the Holy Spirit.

**76,37,15** For in very truth the Father is true God, as is attested by the Son, who knows the Father; and the Son is true light, known by the Father and attested by him; and the Spirit is the Spirit of truth, not alien, but issuing from the Father and taking from the Son.

**76,37,16a** And these things take away all the syllogistic fable-telling of your arguments, Aetius, and it is not admissible to urge us to become disciples of Aristotle, your master, and to abandon the word of the fishermen enlightened in the Spirit of God, who were unlettered in speech and untrained, but were heralds of the truth in the power of God, of which they had been counted worthy.

**76,37,16b** For it is not in syllogistic talk and boastful talk that the kingdom of heaven consists, but in power and truth.

**76,37,17** For indeed we have had our fill of hearing, ever since your discourse began, about privation of states and of positions, and about a generate essence taking on and not taking on ingenerate essence, and undergoing, together with a state, the loss of a state, and about an essence entangled, generate, and a state ingenerate, and an offspring spoken of in passing, but signified in a state alone, and indicative of a state, as being reshaped out of some essence, even if it is called offspring, as you said.

**76,37,18** For your mind speaks the same things about the same things, bringing nothing to completion, uttering words that are carried along over the same ground.

**76,38,1a** 21. If ‘ingenerate’ is a state and ‘generate’ likewise a state, then the essences come before the states; yet the states, though second to the essences, are nevertheless more honourable.

**76,38,1b** “But if the ingenerate is the cause of the generate, of its being, as is signified, the offspring bringing in its cause together with its own essence, then ‘offspring’ is indicative of an essence and not of a state; and since the ingenerate nature brings in nothing together with itself, how could the ingenerate nature too be not an essence but a state?”

**76,38,2a** Refutation. Aetius is trying again, as you see, friends of the truth, to construct for us an argument distinguishing states in God and in what comes after God.

**76,38,2b** And he posits some things as first and others as second.

**76,38,3a** But in the case of God it is not even lawful to speak of taking things as first or second.

**76,38,3b** For in God all things are present at once, and he needs no addition.

**76,38,3c** Therefore pious reasoning also admits that the offspring is to be conceived not from time.

**76,38,4** For with God — Father and Son and Holy Spirit, that is, the Trinity, which is what God who is is — the Father is called he who is, and the Son he who is, being toward him who is, begotten with no beginning and outside time, as in “With you is the spring of life,” and “In your light we shall behold light,” as well as “he who is in the bosom of the Father,” and “In the beginning the Word was, and the Word was in God’s presence, and the Word was God”; and likewise concerning the Holy Spirit, “My Spirit stands in your midst.”

**76,38,5a** And you see that there is nothing recent in the Trinity.

**76,38,5b** Hence essence does not precede state, nor does state precede essence.

**76,38,6** And a state — not in the manner of the so-called unreliable states, which have change in each of the things that have positive states — if you will compel us, Aetius, to speak of a state in God at all; and there is nothing in God more honourable or later-born, but whatever befits the dignity for glorifying: to the one Godhead both one glorifying and one honour, so that they may honour the Son as they honour the Father;

**76,38,7** and so that they may not blaspheme the Spirit, because of the word of threat, which does not forgive them the sin here or in the age to come; so that it is fitting [it is] to think, or to show reverence, or to glorify in no way differently concerning the Trinity, but in the Father ‘Father’, in the Son ‘Son’, in the Holy Spirit — to speak thus and to glorify thus in truth, which is, fittingly, to render reverence in worship to the one Trinity, the true faith, and to know its dignity.

**76,38,8** And neither does the ingenerate need the generate to be brought in together with itself in essence, so that the offspring, being indicative, should become for it a cause of essence, nor is the essence of the one begotten a state of the ingenerate nature, or said to be so.

**76,38,9a** For the Trinity needs nothing, nor does it take on the addition of anything.

**76,38,9b** For it is not that, because the Trinity itself always was and none of the created things was, the Father on this account devised for himself, for the sake of some allotment, or of some name gained by addition, or of an addition to his dignity, to create heaven and earth through the Son, and all things visible and invisible, and by his Spirit made firm all the power of the very things created by him, so that from the creating of the created things and the fashioning of the things that have come to be an added contribution might accrue to the Creator — to one who hears — and something might be conceived as gained by addition for the Father as Craftsman, for the Son, through whom and from whom the created things have come into being, or for the Holy Spirit, in whom the things made firm have been made firm.

**76,38,10a** For it was not as one turned from one state to another, and altered in nature and in essence, that God made the things he has made, as though by a fresh notion and a change.

**76,38,10b** For he had in himself that which is ever creative, and perfect, and in need of no acquisition of glory.

**76,38,11** And just as, in the case of the creatures, one who reflects about God must not suppose the dignity of God’s essence and glory to be of a state and worth gained by acquisition, so Aetius will be beaten back, who wishes to reason about God by syllogism in terms of ingenerate and generate, according to the argument he brings against us about his state and essence, since it is agreed that all the created things truly exist, and were not devised for the sake of an acquisition of glory for God, who lacks nothing; just as also in the case of the Only-begotten and of his Holy Spirit one cannot say the same as of the creatures; for that is inadmissible to say.

**76,38,12a** But since Aetius comes bringing us syllogisms, talking of lofty matters and boldly stretching himself out toward the things above, while reasoning in counter-syllogisms from the creatures below, and himself being found to be nothing by his syllogistic argument — for both the wisdom of men passes away and the syllogistic diction of men is buried.

**76,38,12b** “For his spirit shall go forth, and he shall return to his dust.”

**76,38,13a** For all the syllogistic devices of men pass away, and men too, together with Aetius’ syllogistic art and his technical practice against the faith.

**76,38,13b** But the faith which he subjects to syllogism abides, and hope and love, according to what is written.

**76,39,1a** 22. If every essence is ingenerate, as that of God Almighty is, how could anyone call one passible and another impassible?

**76,39,1b** But if, by the allotment of an ingenerate nature, the one abides superior to quantity and quality and, in a word, to every change, while the other is liable to passions, though it was conceded to be without variation as to essence, then let whoever likes assign this to chance, as was said before; or at any rate it follows to call the one that acts ingenerate, and the one that is changed generate.

**76,39,2** Refutation. We do not say that every essence is ingenerate, nor that every one is generate from God, because he who begot the one begotten from him, and sent forth from himself his Holy Spirit, a Spirit that partakes of what is the Son’s, did not beget all, but one — therefore Only-begotten — and sent forth one from himself — therefore Holy Spirit; but through the one he created, and in the one he made firm, all things: some that beget and, after creation, are begotten; others created, neither begetting nor begotten.

**76,39,3** But the uncreated essence of the Trinity stands far apart from the things created by the Trinity and not begotten of the Trinity.

**76,39,4a** Therefore the Trinity has impassibility and invariability, while all the things after the Trinity are subject to passion, unless the Impassible should bestow impassibility through incorruption on those to whom he wills to grant it as a gift, without stint.

**76,39,4b** But they do not have incorruption from a bodiless nature, but from the bounty of the good and impassible God.

**76,39,5a** For neither does the suffering of the Only-begotten in the flesh bring passion upon his Godhead, although it is believed by the true faith, from a true confession, that the Word, being impassible God, suffered.

**76,39,5b** But the same remained in impassibility, not turned in his nature nor altered.

**76,39,6** Therefore, being Wisdom and being impassible God, and knowing that through suffering he saves those who are subject to the sufferings of death, he sent no ambassador, no angel, nor was it as with the prophets before him, but the Lord himself came, and, taking the passible into himself, truly suffered, while his Godhead remained impassible.

**76,39,7a** For his coming in the flesh did not blunt the power of his Godhead.

**76,39,7b** For he is found in his Godhead working the works of God, and not shut out by the flesh: rebuking wind and wave and sea, calling Lazarus by his own authority, and doing countless other things beyond these;

**76,39,8** who also permitted to the flesh what was reasonable — that the devil should tempt, that men should strike, and that those who arrested him should seize him — so that in the passible the Impassible might suffer, remaining impassible, being in his own Godhead,

**76,39,9** not a stranger to the impassible God, but doing all things willingly according to his astonishing mystery; just as the Father, God, together with his Only-begotten himself and his Holy Spirit — a Trinity ever perfect and impassible — one Godhead, encompasses all things: one God, one lordship of the same God who encompasses the universe.

**76,39,10a** And it is not because he encompasses all things that he falls under passion, though the things encompassed fall under passion.

**76,39,10b** For God is within all things and outside the whole of all things, unmixed with all things.

**76,39,11** Hence no one will introduce passion into the impassible God on the ground that he is everywhere, or that he is outside all things, or that he encompasses all things, or that all things move in him; just as no one will introduce passion into the Holy Trinity on the ground that he has begotten the Only-begotten, or that the Only-begotten has been begotten, or that his Holy Spirit has been sent forth from him.

**76,39,12** For neither is the Holy Spirit passible, descending in the form of a dove upon the Jordan, nor the Only-begotten, baptised and touched by John, nor the Father, calling aloud from above in a voice that men could hear, “This is my Son; listen to him.”

**76,39,13a** The Son, then, is without variation; and the Father is ingenerate, while the Son is generate, impassible, and the Spirit came forth impassibly, while the other things are created, the perfect Trinity abiding in its number and its uncreated name; neither does the superior change, nor is what was begotten held by passion; for neither was he who begot held by passion.

**76,39,13b** For the offspring is not bodily, but spirit from spirit and Son from Father.

**76,39,14** Likewise the Holy Spirit too, from him, is the Father’s Spirit, Christ’s Spirit — neither created nor begotten, no brother, no forefather, no descendant — of the incomparable essence of Father and Son and Holy Spirit, which surpasses every thought and every mind — not only, I would say, of men, but of angels too.

**76,39,15** For the Only-begotten did not admit change, nor did his Father, nor his Holy Spirit, by the Only-begotten, who is impassible, suffering in the flesh, and by his Holy Spirit being in the form of a dove, and by the Father impassibly sending forth a sound from above for the hearing of men;

**76,39,16** just as the created angels and heavens and earth and all things did not bring change and passion upon him who made them; but the whole is an astonishing mystery, according to the saying, “How deep are God’s riches and wisdom and knowledge!”

**76,40,1** 23. If the nature which has come to be has the ingenerate nature as its cause, while ‘ingenerate’ were nothing, how could nothing be the cause of what has come to be?

**76,40,2a** Refutation. The ingenerate nature does indeed exist in relation to the only-begotten offspring and to the Holy Spirit who is from it, in a different sense and not in the same sense as toward all things; but not as a cause, in the way that what exists is cause in relation to what is not.

**76,40,2b** For he who was begotten is not from things that are not, nor is he who begot non-existent, nor the Holy Spirit who is from him; but of the other things that which is is the cause.

**76,40,3a** Therefore the Holy Trinity is ever united with its own glory, ever existing in correspondence with each name of its dignity.

**76,40,3b** For it is through it, and not apart from it, that the things which have come to be came to be when they were not.

**76,40,3c** Wherefore neither is the Father by himself the cause of the things that have come to be, but Father and Son and Holy Spirit made all things.

**76,40,4a** But if the Son were alien, as one who did not exist and came from a cause, he too, having come forth along with all things, would have become their equal.

**76,40,4b** And God would be the cause of one brought forth no longer by way of begetting but by way of creating, and it would no longer be admissible for the one to be called offspring and the rest creatures, but either all things together with him would be called offspring, or he together with all would likewise be called a creature;

**76,40,5** and there would be nothing distinctive, since the one would be put on a level with all in respect of being from things that are not — not only angels, I would say, being made equal to the Only-begotten, their Maker and Creator, but also men and beasts and whatever falls immeasurably short of his nature and dignity.

**76,40,6** He who is exists together with him who is, having been begotten of him timelessly and truly, not from things that are not, but from him.

**76,40,7** And his Holy Spirit exists, not alien to his essence, nor procured in addition for God as for assistance, as Aetius’ argument has it.

**76,41,1** 24. If ‘ingenerate’ is a privation, and privation is the casting-off of a state, and what is cast off either perishes entirely or passes over to another, how is it possible for the essence of God to be named by the title ‘ingenerate’ after a state that passes over or perishes?

**76,41,2** Refutation. If from your time onward, Aetius, the opinion concerning God has been furnished to God by your syllogisms for his glory, according to the arguments you stated at the very beginning, then I too, addressing myself to you, will, God permitting, say the like to you: that, since none of the ancients — of the holy apostles or prophets in the Old Testament and in the New — held this view, you set yourself up as better and surer than God himself.

**76,41,3** For from your time onward, as by your account, the Godhead has taken on, for faith in it, this syllogistic technical jargon of yours — the talk about privation in ‘ingenerate’ and in ‘generate’, and about the total casting-off of a state, and about change, and about naming in respect of God in the appellation of the essence of God.

**76,41,4** For it is not because God is the Creator of all the things that come after his Only-begotten and his Holy Spirit that, through the constitution of the created things, the privative expression for what does not belong to God was invented, or the affirming expression for what does belong to him was adopted, so that what was created afterwards might bring the better to God, and he might be conceived as pure by means of the privative and unchangeable terms applied from it to these things;

**76,41,5** but because it ever is, being itself wholly glory, and wholly beyond the grasp of all the things created by it, glorified according to the measure of those who stretch forward to its glorification — by angels in the tongue of angels, which is declared by the apostle to be preferable to that of men, and by men in the tongue of men, which is lower in measure, and according to the capacity of those lower still;

**76,41,6a** and not at all because the glorification has been lowered proportionately in each creature, or changed; but it is unchangeable in itself, every creature falling short of reaching out to the infinite in glorification, since the supreme essence ever surpasses every mind, not acquiring, through what all say is permitted to it, either turning, or change, or advance.

**76,41,6b** For the same Godhead is superior, and incomparable, and glorified.

**76,41,6c** 25. If ‘ingenerate’ indicates a privation that does not belong to God, how do we say that he is ingenerate, but that he is not generate?

**76,41,6d** Refutation. He is indeed ingenerate, but it was said nowhere — not by the prophet, not by an apostle, not by an evangelist.

**76,41,6e** For it was no marvel at all to say this about God.

**76,42,4a** For it belonged to pious reasoning by the very law of nature.

**76,42,4b** But you, Aetius, introducing this to us as a novelty, think that by saying it you contribute a marvel to your own credit.

**76,42,4c** But you have jumbled and mixed up with the pious law of nature and with the ordinance of the faith, which was granted by God for the addition of improvement, the notion that a generate one is made equal in dignity to the ingenerate, so that the unlike one whom you worship might be found equal to the one proclaimed, on your view, as unlike.

**76,42,4d** If, then, you worship the Father with a bare name, you have offered your honour in mockery.

**76,42,4e** And if you worship the Son while acknowledging him as unlike the Father, you have produced confusion in your worship, having honoured the unlike equally with the one unlike him.

**76,42,5a** But if, because of your preconceived unbelief, you refuse to worship the Son, you will be convicted by all, for not acknowledging him who is worshipped by all, as is his due, and is equal.

**76,42,5b** For all God’s angels will worship him, and Mary worshipped him when he had gloriously risen in the flesh, and all his disciples.

**76,42,6** For they know that, begotten from the Father, he does not bear the name of a thing that came into being, nor of a creature, and they worship him who is from him who is, and the Holy Spirit who is from him.

**76,42,7a** For they know him to be alien in essence from the things that have come to be.

**76,42,7b** For he is not a thing come into being or a creature, but begotten from the Father.

**76,42,7c** Therefore, Aetius, after toiling over everything, spending many years and bringing in strange arguments, you will worship him.

**76,42,8** For “all must stand before his judgement seat, and every tongue will acknowledge that Jesus Christ is Lord” — he who is not alien to God — but “to God the Father’s glory”, as it stands written and is believed.

**76,43,1** 26. If ‘ingenerate’ is a bare name in the case of God, and the bare utterance exalts the subsistence of God above all generate things, then the utterance of men is more precious than the subsistence of the Almighty, since it has adorned God the Almighty with an incomparable pre-eminence.

**76,43,2a** Refutation. ‘Ingenerate’ is neither a bare name in the case of God, nor one shared with the creatures in respect of essence.

**76,43,2b** Therefore neither are the creatures indicative of a bare name; but when another name is sought between ingenerate and created — namely ‘Son’, and not ‘created’ — to which should the distinction be assigned?

**76,43,3** And if we grant the shared name to the created things, then, since neither of the things spoken of is named by a bare name —

**76,43,4** as in the case of the ingenerate one who creates and of the created things that have come to be a bare name is not admissible, so in the case of the generate one, the Son, which does not admit a bare name — that which is falsely charged in vain will show the confusion in Aetius’ syllogizing, because the created essence, which is in truth and not a bare name, is not put on a level with the name of the Son, since the Son himself too does not admit the name of Son as a bare one.

**76,43,5** And since the only-begotten Son, and the Holy Spirit, is not without subsistence, nor spoken of by a bare name, he is joined to the glory of the Father, and is not confounded with the name of the creatures.

**76,43,6** For the Godhead does not need exalting, as though it did not exist, nor is it in want of height, even if it is not exalted by some who are in ignorance; nor does the essence of the Godhead subsist through anyone’s utterance.

**76,43,7** For the utterance of men or of others will not boast as though it procured glory for a God in need, or adorned God Almighty, God to be worshipped, God its own Overseer and Creator and Craftsman.

**76,43,8a** For it does not consider itself surpassingly glorious and the adorner of its own Craftsman, since then it would consider itself worthy of worship, and not as worshipping the One who is worshipped.

**76,43,8b** And your argument, Aetius, stirs up argument against everyone in vain.

**76,44,1** 27. If a cause has been allotted to everything generate, while the ingenerate nature is without cause, ‘ingenerate’ does not indicate a cause, but signifies subsistence.

**76,44,2a** Refutation. A cause has indeed been allotted to everything generate, and we do not confess this as people who have learned it from you.

**76,44,2b** For the faith of the truth foresees this, and confesses beforehand, and teaches, that God is the one free of every cause, and unmixed, and not liable to any equality.

**76,44,3** For this is why we ourselves do not worship anything that falls below the essence of God himself: because it is fitting to render reverence to him alone who is liable to nothing — to the Father, the ingenerate, and to the Son, who is from him, and to the Holy Spirit, who is from him and through the Only-begotten — since there is nothing in the Trinity that is created and falls under a cause.

**76,44,4a** For nothing in the Trinity is from things that are not, as are the other things that have fallen under a cause and been allotted a cause.

**76,44,4b** Therefore the Trinity, being free of any such cause, has taught without error that it alone is to be worshipped, since it alone is without cause.

**76,44,5** But all other things have fallen under a cause; for they have come to be and been created, whereas the Father is uncreated, having a Son who was begotten from him, yet is no creature, and a Holy Spirit who issues from him and was not fashioned.

**76,44,6** This being so, neither has the Son who is worshipped, nor the Holy Spirit, been allotted the passion of a cause, even if he has the Father as begetter; nor could the remaining creatures, created by Father and Son and Holy Spirit, be without the passion of being allotted a cause;

**76,44,7** but plainly the Only-begotten would be without the passion of being allotted a cause, and his Holy Spirit too, as is the Father also, because the Son is offspring and not creature; and the Son will not be allotted a cause of passion from his having been begotten, nor the Spirit because he proceeds from the Father;

**76,44,8** for neither is the Father, because he begot and brought forth from himself, and created all other things after the Son and the Spirit, found to be under the passion of a cause, although all the others are held by passion in creating or begetting.

**76,44,9** Without cause, then, are the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit; yet of all things the Trinity is cause, creating and fashioning them together, and knowing nothing within itself that is created or fashioned.

**76,45,1** 28. If everything that has come to be has come to be by the agency of another, while the ingenerate subsistence has come to be neither by itself nor by another, ‘ingenerate’ must indicate essence.

**76,45,2** Refutation. Aetius comes bringing us this too once again, as though expounding something new and fresh, so that he may be seen as the discoverer of a dialectical syllogistic, merely declaring superfluously this very thing, which is not even disputed, nor is it against the truth: what is always confessed in the catholic church is contained in it.

**76,45,3a** For everything that has come to be comes to be by the agency of another, while the ingenerate subsistence has come to be neither by itself nor by another, even if ‘ingenerate’ must indicate essence.

**76,45,3b** And what is more necessary than this?

**76,45,4** For the name of ‘essence’, which among the Anomoeans and Arians themselves Aetius has always taken up in shifting fashion, he has plainly confessed, compelled by the truth.

**76,45,5** Since, then, ingeneracy is essence, and has begotten the Only-begotten from itself and not from things that are not, undefiledly and impassibly, timelessly and without beginning, and has brought forth the Holy Spirit from itself and not from things that are not, the Trinity is plainly proclaimed in the holy catholic church, in orthodox fashion, as consubstantial, while none of the created things can be called by this name, since there is nothing that resembles the Only-begotten and the Holy Spirit, either in nature or in the reverence due.

**76,45,6** For those are created from things that are not, and are not to be worshipped, but the Trinity ever is: the Father is perfect Father, and the Son is perfect Son, begotten from the Father; and the Holy Spirit a perfect Spirit, who came forth from the Father and takes from the Son.

**76,45,7** And to us all the things of the divine Scripture and of the holy faith are full of light, and nothing is crooked, or contrary, or tangled.

**76,46,1** 29. If the ingenerate subsistence is manifested along with the essence of the offspring as its cause, holding invariability over against every cause, it is incomparable essence itself, not weaving inaccessibility into itself from outside, but being this itself — incomparable and inaccessible, since it is also ingenerate.

**76,46,2a** Refutation. Aetius often rushes at the same points, as I myself have often said, bringing us only to weariness and nothing more.

**76,46,2b** Therefore in the present case too we have been obliged to add to our weariness and to repeat the same things on the same points, since it so seemed good to him as well.

**76,46,3a** For if the ingenerate one that begot is indeed manifested along with the essence of the offspring, the begetter, in begetting what was begotten, will differ from it in nothing as to dignity.

**76,46,3b** For he begot from himself, essentially, spirit from spirit, and not body from body.

**76,46,3c** Therefore the begetter is manifested together with the begotten, incomparably and in fitting accord, and the begotten with the one who begot.

**76,46,4a** For the Godhead needs no addition, so as to be called Father at one time and not at another; nor will the Son be found, from the bond on high, once not to have been and now to be.

**76,46,4b** Therefore God the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit are essence itself, and not of another essence.

**76,46,5** For he is neither a brother nor begotten afterwards; but the name ‘Father’ fits ineffably together with the Son, who is consubstantial, and there fits together with the Father and the Son that which is from him, through him and of what is his — his Holy Spirit.

**76,46,6** Therefore inaccessibility belongs to Father and Son and Holy Spirit in relation to all the things that are lower and were created by the Trinity itself, but the Trinity is not inaccessible to itself; for it is uncreated and ingenerate and incomparable.

**76,46,7a** Therefore nothing can be made equal to the Father; nothing of the things that came to be from things that are not, and were not begotten, is worshipped together with him.

**76,46,7b** For to none of the things that have come to be did he ever say, “Sit at my right hand.”

**76,46,7c** Nor indeed has the Only-begotten said about anyone, “He who has seen me has seen the Father”, and “I am within the Father, and the Father within me”, and “Nobody knows the Father except the Son, and the Son except the Father, and the one to whom he may reveal him.”

**76,46,8** And he reveals through the Holy Spirit, who knows and teaches and announces in the world the things of the Son, and searches even the depths of God.

**76,46,9a** For this is why he says, “He who does not honour the Son as he honours the Father, the wrath of God abides on him.”

**76,46,9b** And he did not say, “He who does not honour angels as he honours the Father.”

**76,46,9c** Nor again did he say, “He who does not honour the Son too”, but the Son as the Father; and likewise that “it shall not be forgiven him who blasphemes against the Spirit, neither here nor in the age to come”, so as to signify the inaccessibility and incomparability of the Trinity in Father and Son and Holy Spirit.

**76,47,1a** 30. If the Almighty transcends every nature, he transcends it because of being ingenerate, which is the cause of continued existence for generate things.

**76,47,1b** But if ‘ingenerate’ is not indicative of essence, whence will the nature of generate things have its preservation?

**76,47,2** Refutation. It is fitting to say and to confess, and so to hold, that the Almighty surpasses every nature — he from whom the Only-begotten, God the Word, ineffably came forth for us, and his Holy Spirit.

**76,47,3a** And for this reason we securely refrain from declaring a creature to be God, so that we may not become fools.

**76,47,3b** But we glorify the Trinity which transcends all nature — Son together with Father, and his Holy Spirit — because it is ingenerate and uncreated.

**76,47,4** For since neither the Only-begotten nor the Holy Spirit is of another nature, but God from God and Light from Light, the Only-begotten himself too, together with the Almighty Father, has been called Almighty, as the divine Scripture plainly has it.

**76,47,5** For the Only-begotten is not different from the dignity of the Father, but is in fitting accord with the dignity of the Father, as the holy apostle expressly testifies for me, speaking in the Holy Spirit about the sons of Israel: “Whose”, he says, “is the worship and the covenants, and whose are the fathers, from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever, amen.”

**76,47,6** For this is why the Only-begotten is to be worshipped, and the Only-begotten is God, and the Holy Spirit is divine Spirit, and besides the Holy Trinity there is no other God.

**76,47,7** And the Father is Almighty, and his only-begotten Child, Jesus Christ, is in fitting accord with the dignity of the Father, and is called Father of the age to come, and is in fitting accord with his Holy Spirit too, uncreatedly — the Trinity ever being made manifest and known,
