**76,47,8** from which Trinity the cause is present to all things that have come to be, if indeed it is indicative of an essence pure and beyond compare — the Father within the Son, the Son within the Father, together with the Holy Spirit — the Trinity ever having in itself the eternity of continuance, from which Trinity preservation belongs to the things that have come to be.

**76,48,1** 31. If none of the invisible things pre-exists itself seminally, but abides in the nature allotted to it, how does the ingenerate God, being free of allotment, now see his own essence as second in an offspring, and now as first in the ingenerate, according to the order of first and second?

**76,48,2a** Refutation. Aetius ought to have indicated to us beforehand, and put forward his questions clearly — above all this one, an expression open to censure and having no kinship whatever among its comparisons, neither of the things named by him being capable of being put on a level with the other.

**76,48,2b** For he comes bringing us the names of many invisible things.

**76,48,3** For there are invisible living beings too, the spiritual ones — I mean the Seraphim and Cherubim — and also angels, and spirits, and certain others, in whom it is truly fulfilled that nothing exists in them seminally.

**76,48,4a** For no one would call the invisible things bodies.

**76,48,4b** For indeed they neither beget nor are begotten; but they were created, plainly, by the will of the Godhead that ever is, and each of the created things has received as its lot whatever measure of excellence he who is assigned to it in the abundance of his ungrudging love for mankind, and each was allotted what it has been allotted, and abides in it;

**76,48,5** and God is free of every cause, having the whole in himself, not having the Son after periods of time, by delay or by change of mind, or his Holy Spirit; but, as befits his ever having a begotten Son, having a Son, and him only-begotten, who ever has the Father in himself, he has also the Holy Spirit, who is from the Father and takes from the Son, having him always.

**76,48,6a** For indeed the abundance of the Godhead, which ever is, is neither for lack of glory nor for an addition of glory.

**76,48,6b** And since none of the created things ever always existed, when did the Trinity see itself in lesser abundance — and at one time see this, at another see itself in an addition of essence, as one in need, after having created the created things, now seeing itself in a greater addition of glory or of abundance?

**76,48,7a** And from every side none of those who wish to bring forward their syllogistic human suppositions against the truth and set them out in public will strike home, since the worth of God — Father and Son and Holy Spirit — surpasses every mind of angels and beyond; how much more, then, that of human nature?

**76,48,7b** For since the reasonings of men are timid, and their thoughts corruptible, piercing themselves through on syllogisms and disputes —

**76,48,8a** as others, examining matters by their own syllogisms according to some sophistical supposition, ask, some about evil, whence it began, others whence the devil came, or why he came to be, and others about man, who was going to sin, why God created him so.

**76,48,8b** And why does he who made him such afterwards blame him?

**76,48,9** So that, when all have beaten back their own reasonings and learned that they are corruptible, they may render reverence and knowledge to him who is in Father and Son and Holy Spirit — in other words, to the one Trinity;

**76,48,10** and that, asking of him the knowledge of the true faith and obtaining it, they may not try to overstep their own measure, but may learn to keep still from a blinded way of thinking, and not play the sophist with an inflamed tongue and senseless reasonings, but rather be brought to a sound mind by the wise saying of the holy and divine Scripture, which forbids thinking above what one ought to think, and bids one think so as to be of sound mind.

**76,49,1a** 32. If God abides in an ingenerate nature, let the notion that he knows himself in generation and in ingeneracy be removed.

**76,49,1b** But if it is conceded that he extends his own essence into ingenerate and generate, he himself is ignorant of his own essence, being led about by generation and ingeneracy.

**76,49,1c** But if the generate too has partaken of ingenerate participation, and abides endlessly in the nature of the generate, then if, continuing in that nature, it knows itself, it is plainly ignorant of the ingenerate participation; for it is not possible for it to have knowledge about itself of both ingenerate and generate essence; but if ‘ingenerate’ is easily despised because of an aptitude for change, the dignity of the nature is the unchangeable essence of the ingenerate essence, which is confessed to be superior to every cause.

**76,49,2** Refutation. God abides unquestionably in an ingenerate nature — the Father, who created and fashioned all things from things that are not, having begotten from himself a Son consubstantial with himself and in fitting accord with his eternity, and the Holy Spirit that came forth from him,

**76,49,3** existing fittingly in his consubstantiality; and it is not because the Trinity created from things that are not the things that are, visible and invisible, that what corresponds to the dignity of God — the eternity of the One who is — is done away with on account of the recent name of the creatures.

**76,49,4a** But the essence on high, which surpasses them, is set apart from the created things, not being consubstantial with them, but having called them into being from things that are not.

**76,49,4b** Therefore the begotten Son is contemplated, not from things that are not, but from the One who is, together with him and in fitting accord, the essence being neither extended nor contracted; but the Father, being spirit, truly begot the Son as spirit, and brought forth the Holy Spirit from himself, and is not ignorant of himself, nor does he know his own essence as contracted, or broadened, or undergoing division.

**76,49,5** For to know all these things about God is utterly irrational, so as for the divine itself, which is the Holy Spirit, to be ignorant as well; and it is neither the case that the ingenerate does not share consubstantiality with the offspring, nor that the generate does not share eternity with the Father.

**76,49,6** For the Son is known by the Father, and the Father by the Son, the Trinity ever abiding uncreated without end and existing without end, the Only-begotten having been begotten from him who ever is, who truly is, and in his own perfect nature.

**76,49,7** Therefore he has knowledge of himself, and the Son is not without knowledge of the Father’s ingenerate essence, nor is the Ingenerate without knowledge of the Son’s essence, which is from him; for the only-begotten God the Word is to be trusted, who said, “Nobody knows the Father but the Son, and the Son, nobody but the Father.”

**76,49,8** Therefore let the declaratory command of this noble Aetius be removed, which said, “For it is not possible for him to have knowledge about himself, both of ingenerate essence and of ingeneracy.”

**76,49,9a** For the Only-begotten anticipated him by striking out this judicial pronouncement of his, when he said that he himself knows the Father, and no one else, including at the same time the subsistence of his Holy Spirit, as he also says elsewhere, “The Spirit of the Father will teach you.”

**76,49,9b** And if the Spirit is the Father’s, it too is not ignorant of the Father.

**76,49,10** And his having said, “No one knows the Father except the Son”, was so that he might signify himself and the Father and the Holy Spirit as transcending the others, which did not exist eternally but came to be.

**76,49,11** But if he declared beforehand that he ever knows the Father, Aetius creeps in on us in vain with his empty talk, being plainly evident to all as one who reasons as a man, judging in fleshly fashion and being unspiritual, in regard to him who knows himself and the Father and his Holy Spirit.

**76,49,12** God, then, is exempt from every cause — not only the Father, but also the Son and the Holy Spirit — since the Godhead of Father and Son and Holy Spirit is confessed to be superior to every cause.

**76,50,1a** 33. If the ingenerate is exempt from every cause, and there were many ingenerates, they will have an invariable nature.

**76,50,1b** For it is not without having shared, by the allotment of some nature, in what is common and what is proper, that the one would make and the other come to be.

**76,50,2** Refutation. The ingenerate is admittedly exempt from every cause, because the ingenerate and worshipful is one, the worshipful being distinguished from those who worship.

**76,50,3** And the Trinity is worshipful, being a unity, and a Trinity counted in one name — Father and Son and Holy Spirit — possessing within itself nothing of its own that is alien; but the Father, in fitting accord, begot the Son and did not create him.

**76,50,4** For the one is ever from the begetter himself — wherefore the offspring is from the One who is — and so is the Holy Spirit that came forth from him, the Trinity being in one uncreated unity, while all things were created from things that are not by the Trinity itself;

**76,50,5** hence the one Trinity is one God, Father and Son and Holy Spirit, possessing within itself nothing of its own that is alien, uncreated, ingenerate, unfashioned, a Trinity not made but making, having no creature’s name within itself but creating, being one and not many.

**76,50,6a** But all the things from it are many, yet not counted together with it.

**76,50,6b** Therefore no share in the incomparable essence has been allotted to another nature.

**76,50,7** For this is why the nature in the essence of God is not something created, but creative of all the things that cannot share by consubstantiality in the incomparable and one essence of Father and Son and Holy Spirit, as is clear to the man who has been granted knowledge of the truth, revealing that it alone is worshipped, and not all things, just as it alone baptises into its own name, and not the universe.

**76,51,1a** 34. If every essence is ingenerate, neither will differ from the other in being without a master.

**76,51,1b** How then could anyone say that the one is changed and the other changes it, when they do not allow God to bring things into existence from no underlying essence?

**76,51,2** Refutation. Every one of those who have set themselves against the truth, having gathered to himself some petty arguments in a startling manner, has seemed to some to strike at them with overturning force, and to divert them from the way of life and do them harm; as this Aetius now, in this statement, though saying nothing, seems by nature to astound the simple, saying superfluously what he says, having made use on the present occasion too of a name, as he is accustomed to bring things forward superfluously.

**76,51,3** For not every essence is confessed to be ingenerate by those who have understanding, since then every one would be declared God.

**76,51,4** And since not all essences are declared God, but one beyond them all, which is one Godhead in Trinity, how will it still be left to this noble fellow for his startling argument to make headway against the sons of the truth?

**76,51,5** And the one will indeed differ from the other, because the Trinity creates, while all things have been created by it; and it is without a master, while the things that came to be by it are mastered; and the one is changed, while the other has an unalterable nature, ever changing the things changed by it, and able to bring essences and subsistences into being from things that are not.

**76,51,6** For this befits God: from what did not underlie them, and from things that were not — things brought into being by him and given subsistence — to refashion them in the ordering of the world as he wills.

**76,52,1a** 35. Should every essence be ingenerate, each is invariable.

**76,52,1b** And since essence has invariability, acting and being acted upon must be ascribed to chance.

**76,52,1c** And if there are many ingenerate and invariable things, they will differ from one another in a manner beyond number.

**76,52,1d** For things that stand apart, either wholly or in some respect, could not be numbered, since every separation displays some allotment, while the ingenerate nature is set apart from cause.

**76,52,2a** Refutation. Not every essence is ingenerate; for even to think it is foolish, and this reasoning is of Greek ignorance, and so is the pronouncement, whether it was made by Aetius as an assertion or as a question.

**76,52,2b** But plainly as a question.

**76,52,3a** Let him, then, put this question to the children of the Greeks, and let them agree with him that the question holds good from syllogisms, since they ascribe to God some matter coeval with him.

**76,52,3b** But let him be caught together with them, if he agrees, since the truth holds that what makes is one, in the single essence of a perfect Trinity, numbered not by way of merging.

**76,52,3c** But all the other things are generate and created, and not ingenerate.

**76,52,4** And since the Godhead is uncreated — the Father begetting, the Son begotten, the Holy Spirit sent out from the very Father and taking of what is the Son’s — while all things are created, and since invariability in power abides, fittingly, in the Trinity, all Godhead being referred to the Father because of the reasonableness and steadfastness of the unity and its doing away with polytheism, invariability abides in power, and the reasonable order corresponds fittingly, of the Son toward the Father, and of the Holy Spirit.

**76,52,5a** These things, then, being so, the contrivance of this treacherous question will fall from the outset.

**76,52,5b** For the invariable things are not many; there is only the one Trinity in a unity, and in the Trinity one Godhead.

**76,52,6** But all other things stand apart, neither having their being acted upon or acting by chance, nor is the Holy Trinity able to be acted upon in doing anything, since the whole is impassible and worshipful — I mean Father and Son and Holy Spirit.

**76,52,7a** For God made all things through the Son, but not the Son (for he is not with all things; for he works together with the Father and is worshipped together with him), nor the Holy Spirit.

**76,52,7b** For he is not counted among all things, but makes firm the power of all things and is jointly worshipped.

**76,52,8a** And since all things are ranged under the providence of the One, each is borne along and acts, and is acted upon, and so with whatever else they do.

**76,52,8b** Therefore the one Trinity is invariable with respect to itself, while the other things that are from it are varied.

**76,52,9a** For they are neither coeval nor co-eternal.

**76,52,9b** It alone is eternal and uncreated and ingenerate, the Son having been begotten timelessly and without beginning, and ever being, and never ceasing to be.

**76,52,10** Hence the divine word has securely taught that the Father is the head of the Son, and not his beginning, because of the consubstantiality; the Holy Spirit too exists eternally, and is sent forth from the Father, yet ever exists with the Father, and did not begin from a point in time.

**76,53,1a** 36. If ‘ingenerate’ and ‘God’ indicate the same thing side by side, the ingenerate begot an ingenerate.

**76,53,1b** But if ‘ingenerate’ indicates one thing and ‘God’ another, it is not absurd for God to have begotten God, each having received existence from ingenerate essence.

**76,53,1c** But if what is before God were nothing, as indeed it is not, ‘God’ and ‘ingenerate’ indicate the same thing, since the offspring does not admit ‘ingenerate’.

**76,53,1d** Therefore it does not even bear to be named together with its God and Father.

**76,53,2a** Refutation. From what source does Aetius want us to obtain within ourselves the meaning of the questions of his reasonings that he puts forward?

**76,53,2b** And if he says, from reasonings and syllogisms, then our acquisition of the notion too will fall together with him.

**76,53,3a** For no one could ever reason out God by syllogism, nor will the thing formed say to him who formed it, “Why have you made me thus?”, as it is written.

**76,53,3b** But from pious reasoning and rightful security we must turn back to the teaching of the Holy Spirit through the holy Scriptures.

**76,53,4** And since an inviolable text teaches us about those who served the creature, that they became fools, how could this not be found to apply to taking a creature as God, and worshipping and honouring him, when the faith by its nature sets apart the worshipful from the created and the created from the worshipful?

**76,53,5a** For indeed, if this makes no difference at all, there will be nothing in Christianity to be preferred over those who render reverence to the creature.

**76,53,5b** And such a faith will be idolatry rather than godliness.

**76,53,6a** For they too worship sun and moon and powers, heaven and earth, and the other creatures.

**76,53,6b** And the difference among the creatures does not make for any wonder; nor will a pre-eminence make any difference in itself to their equal honour, because of the common name, even if the one outweighs the other.

**76,53,6c** For one is he who made both and allotted to each a variation, not of name, but of essence.

**76,53,7a** For in all created things the name of the creature is ‘slave’, and not ‘free’.

**76,53,7b** And if in one part the slave is worshipped, the worship will make no difference with respect to the other part, even if it is lower.

**76,53,7c** For it is equal to the highest, being akin to it as creature, having received its lot from the One who is out of things that are not.

**76,53,8a** Hence ‘ingenerate’ befits God, and ‘God’ befits the ingenerate.

**76,53,8b** Therefore we call the offspring not a work nor a thing made, but an offspring begotten essentially and undefiledly from the Father, consubstantial with the Father and worshipped together with him; and the Holy Spirit is from him, and not alien, and therefore also worshipped together with him.

**76,53,9a** But the name ‘God’ is not pronounced together with any other of the created things, because it has been removed from ingeneracy, since it has received its being as its lot from things that are not.

**76,53,9b** But the Trinity has eternal being, and ‘God’ is not one thing and ‘ingenerate’ another.

**76,53,10a** And you agree, Aetius, that the Son has been begotten from the Father — in pretence, and not in truth.

**76,53,10b** For everything begotten is not created, and the created is not begotten.

**76,53,10c** But if the begotten is created, it is created in another manner — as, one may say, human beings beget human beings, yet do not create them; but these have been created from above by God; therefore what they beget has been begotten by them, while it is by God that all things have been created.

**76,53,11a** But since God is uncreated, and begot for himself a Son and did not create him, he does not beget anything other than his own essence.

**76,53,11b** How then will the offspring from him be created, when the Father is uncreated?

**76,53,11c** But if with him the offspring is created, it is no longer called offspring, and there is much to be said against such an absurd supposition.

**76,53,12** And it is unbefitting for God to have been once without a Son, and later to be called Father after the Son, and unbefitting for the Son that time should be before him; for time will be greater than his majesty.

**76,53,13a** But it befits the Father ever to have, in the sameness of his dignities, what is unfailing and eternal.

**76,53,13b** And that there was nothing before God is evident.

**76,53,13c** ‘God’, then, as Aetius said, and ‘ingenerate’ indicate the same thing; and somehow, entangling himself, he accuses himself rather than establishes his case.

**76,53,14** For if ‘God’ is said along with God, as indeed it is, ‘ingenerate’ too admits the begotten Son; for it contains ‘God’ comprehended within it.

**76,53,15** And God the Word is named together with the Father, as ‘God’ and ‘uncreated’, and is honoured with the Father, even if this does not occur to Aetius, since every created thing worships the Son, and “every tongue acknowledges Jesus Christ, unto the glory of God the Father”; to him be the glory — to the Father in the Son, together with the Holy Spirit, for the ages of the ages.

**76,54,1a** Amen.

**76,54,1b** Aetius’ farewell at the end.

**76,54,1c** 37. May the God who is self-generate — who for this reason has also been addressed as the only true God by the one who was sent, Jesus Christ, who truly came into subsistence before the ages and is truly of generate subsistence — keep you, men and women alike, in good health, safe from impiety, in Christ Jesus our Saviour, through whom be all glory to the God and Father, both now and always and for ever and ever.

**76,54,1d** Amen.

**76,54,2** Refutation. Even at the end, writing to his own band — whom he called athletes, men and women — Aetius did not leave off this kind of wickedness in words, but even in his farewell displayed the alien character of his teaching.

**76,54,3a** For he says, “May the God who is self-generate keep you in good health”, not perceiving that in one word he has undone the whole of the question he had sown.

**76,54,3b** For having spoken in the chapters above about an ingenerate God, he did not foresee — even the point that God did not make himself either — and here he brings in for us a self-generate God.

**76,54,3c** But every way of thinking comes to forget itself, so that it may be detected.

**76,54,4a** Then he says, “who for this reason has also been addressed as the only true God”.

**76,54,4b** But by his own argument and thinking he either does away with the Son’s being God, and slanders the name in vain by being called by the name of Christian, or he holds the Son to be God indeed, yet not true God, and so for him there will be one God who is true and one who is not.

**76,54,5** And finding one under another by descent, and ranking the Holy Spirit too in a smaller and inferior rank, either he will again have a smaller God, or, not counting him with the Trinity, this pitiable little man will be utterly alien to Christians, and might at last be proclaimed a most complete Greek, and a Sadducee in number, alien to the Holy Spirit,

**76,54,6a** as indeed he is, and reckoned with the Greeks in their portion, saying that there is one great God and one small, one true and one not true — as the Greeks confess one great God and name the others small — while the divine Scripture plainly refutes him, saying of the Father, “God is true”, and of the Son ‘God’ in the same way, and of the Father, “God is light”, but of the Son, “That was the true light”, and of the Holy Spirit, “the Spirit of truth”.

**76,54,6b** Truly, then, the Trinity is proclaimed to us in wisdom and in the depth of riches.

**76,54,7** Then again, consistently, he says, “and by the one who was sent, Jesus Christ”; and he was not ashamed to deem the Only-begotten unworthy of the name of God, but has used the bare word only, as he confessed in the chapters above, allotting to the Son the honour of the name only so far as a bare appellation.

**76,54,8a** And he says, “who truly came into subsistence before the ages, and is truly of generate subsistence”.

**76,54,8b** “And he will preserve”, he says, “from impiety.”

**76,54,8c** But every worthless woman is accustomed to forestall others with her own ways and to impute them to them.

**76,54,8d** For not seeing in how many things he has been impious, he thinks himself pious, as those possessed of madness think themselves to be in their right mind, and the others to be raving.

**76,54,9** And here, at “in Christ Jesus”, he did not even dare to render “our Lord”, but in pretence said “our Saviour”.

**76,54,10a** And he adds, “through whom all glory be to the Father, both now and always and for ever and ever.

**76,54,10b** Amen.”

**76,54,10c** And his very saying “all glory” was so that he might strip the Son of honour and glory — which none of the pious, who have received from the Holy Spirit the gift of the true faith, would ever tolerate.

**76,54,11** We have gone through all these things said by this Aetius with a certain dialectical art and the syllogistic supposition of human trickery in thirty-seven chapters, which we urge you to read with understanding.

**76,54,12** And at once you will know, children of Christians, you who serve Christ and are sons of the truth, all his earthly empty talk and his teaching alien to the Holy Spirit;

**76,54,13** for he did not dare to mention a divine word in even a single expression, or any saying of the Old or New Testament — not from the Law, not from the Prophets, not from the gospels, not from the Apostles — nor to bring forward the testimony of any of the patriarchs, nor of the Saviour himself, nor ever of the Father, nor a word of the Holy Spirit spoken through apostles or through prophets, so that he is caught in the act altogether by the friends of the truth as being utterly alien to God and to his faith.

**76,54,14** And I think that we have also answered him sufficiently, against his propositions, as far as possible, in plain speech, but with the support of what comes from the divine Scriptures and from pious reasoning itself.

**76,54,15** And since we have discoursed clearly and sufficiently about the faith in the refutations against him, we consider it enough, so that we may not, by adding more, cause some further difficulty in the reading.

**76,54,16** But I will take up again and tell briefly a few of the things in which he, puffed up in mind, after his outlandish faith and his hostility toward Christ and toward his Holy Spirit — whatever his mouth, and that of those discipled by him, dared — dared in his boldness to raise his mind on high and to utter monstrous blasphemies.

**76,54,17** For he, and those who come from him, imagined themselves to be beyond every man — not in knowing God by faith, but by nature, by way of acquaintance — as I also mentioned somewhere above, since they say that they know God not simply in the knowledge of faith, but as one knows anything visible and touched with his hands, as if someone were to take in his hands a stone, or a piece of wood, or a tool of some other material; so too this noble fellow said, “I know God as I know myself, and I do not know myself so well as I know God.”

**76,54,18a** Well, to say and to hear foolish things leads many into deception, but for those with understanding it is a matter for mockery.

**76,54,18b** For which of those who have acquired derangement for themselves and have gone mad cannot drive others mad too, especially those who follow along and obey?

**76,54,19** For if someone has asked him and those who come from him, “Do not describe to me your knowing God, the incomparable and incomprehensible, who is not grasped as to form but is known by faith to his servants; but describe to me the foundations of the earth, the storehouses of the deep, the veins of the sea, the place of Hades, the measures of the air, the form and thicknesses of the heavens, what is the summit of the things above, what is the boundary of the things below, what is on the right, what on the left, the account of the creation of one’s own formation, the number and measures of the countless things on earth” — then you would hear these things,

**76,54,20a** as we have heard them from those deceived by him: turning aside into sophistical pretexts, they then say with feigned modesty, having learned it from him, “All these bodily things both exist and we cannot know them.”

**76,54,20b** “But God, who made them, we know clearly — of what sort he is, how he is, of what nature he is, and who he is.”

**76,54,21a** And who, hearing these things, would not laugh at once?

**76,54,21b** For the whole thing is silly: that he says he knows and has exactly ascertained the Craftsman, the incomparable and indescribable (and would that he said he knows him and has ascertained him by faith, and not by some acquaintance of touch) — he dared, and they dare, to say it — while the things made by the Incomparable, because they can be greatly marvelled at in their form by those who see them, he and his followers claim not to know;

**76,54,22** above all when the divine Scriptures everywhere plainly proclaim about God that he is invisible and incomprehensible and inconceivable, and known in truth by faith alone, that “he exists, and becomes the rewarder of those who love him.”

**76,54,23** But whenever one of those who hold right views about God’s glory, and about faith and love and incomprehensibility, says to them, “We know God incomprehensible, God invisible, indescribable; we know that he truly is, but that he is invisible and incomprehensible”, this man who brings us the new dialectic has dared, mockingly and glibly, as though telling some tale, to say, “To what, then, are you and your faith like?”

**76,54,24** To a virgin who has been defiled, but who is blind and deaf and dumb: that she has been defiled is evident to all who know her, but when asked who the defiler is she does not hear, so as to understand, and she has neither seen the one who defiled her, because she is blind, nor can she tell, because she is dumb; so that it turns back upon himself and his own tale, according to what is written,

**76,54,25** “May his toil turn back upon his head; and he will tumble into the pit that he made”, and the like.

**76,54,26** For he himself is like a man blind from birth, born so, who speaks, and speaks a great deal, and hears, and is acquainted with the name of white and of black, of blue and green and red and the other different names, of light and darkness — whose names sound in his ears, yet he does not know what their appearance is, nor can he describe it at all, because he was born blind from the beginning and is ignorant of the variation of each quality of colours and of their appearance.

**76,54,27** For each of these names has the proof of its proper distinction through the senses of sight, but not through description to one who has not known the appearance from the beginning, nor can it be tested by feeling and touch.

**76,54,28** So whenever those blind from birth, who discourse about these things and know how to set black against white and green against blue, and purple and scarlet and the other colours, are asked by us the quality of the appearance and the colour of each quality, they can neither tell it nor be taught it by us, but only by words persuade their own minds and deceive their hearers, as though they knew perfectly about the distinction, even if they speak of it in words, while possessing ignorance through not apprehending.

**76,54,29** So this man too comes to us speaking about God, and mockingly ascribes the defilement to the dumb and deaf and blind virgin, while he himself, by his blasphemy, is rather the one defiled, and possesses ignorance like blindness from birth,

**76,54,30a** speaking about God but portraying him in words — and then he has also trained those discipled by him into shamelessness; for nothing is beyond their daring.

**76,54,30b** They blaspheme, then, the names of prophets and apostles, whenever, being refuted by some, they are hard pressed, at once running off and leaping away and saying, “The apostle said this as a man”; and at other times, “Why do you bring me the things of the Old Testament?”

**76,54,31a** But it is no wonder, according to the words spoken by the Saviour, “If the householder they called Beelzebul, how much more the people of his house?”

**76,54,31b** If, then, the Lord himself and his true glory are denied by them, how much more his prophets and apostles?

**76,54,32** And those discipled by him have been carried away into still greater madness, and so has their successor, one Eunomius, falsely so named, who is still alive to this day: a great and evil audacity; for he rebaptises those already baptised, not only those who come over to him from the orthodox and from the sects, but even those from the Arians themselves.

**76,54,33** And he rebaptises them in the name of an uncreated God, and in the name of a created Son, and in the name of a sanctifying Spirit created by the created Son.

**76,54,34** And so that their workshop might be seen to be wholly one of dice-playing, of the stage and of the theatre — that what they proclaim is no longer a faith but, one might almost say, a workshop of mimes — some have affirmed that he baptises those being rebaptised head downwards, feet up and head down.

**76,54,35** And so he compels them on oath to swear not to leap away from such a sect, contrived by him.

**76,54,36** And they say that this same Aetius, after the death of Constantius, having been recalled from exile by Julian, who then became emperor, while he was still a deacon of his own sect, was advanced to the office of bishop by a bishop of that same sect.

**76,54,37** These are the things that have reached us concerning Aetius and his disciples, on whom some have bestowed the name Anomoeans, because he held views still more extreme than the sect of Arius,

**76,54,38** and more dreadfully; and having gone through them, as minutely as possible, in God, having trampled them with the foot of the truth like a many-footed centipede and the creeping thing called the millipede, and crushed them by the Only-begotten’s true confession, thanking God as is our custom and calling in his power to help our weakness, let us go on, beloved,

**76,54,39** to the remaining sects that follow, according to our power and our understanding, calling on the Master himself, as I said, to be present with us for the exposure of them and the refutation of them, so that in his power we may be able to fulfil the promise of our smallness and slightness.

## Anacephalaeosis VII

Tome 2. The following are contained in the second tome, too, of the same third book, which is the seventh according to the division of the number of the tomes that we have stated — that is, the seventh tome, and the end of the whole treatise — in which there are four sects.

**Anaceph. VII 77a** 1. Dimoerites, who do not confess the incarnation of Christ as complete; some of whom at one time dared to say that the body is consubstantial with the Godhead, while some at one time denied that he had taken a soul, and some, relying on the saying “The Word became flesh”, denied that he took what is according to the flesh from created flesh, that is, from Mary.

**Anaceph. VII 77b** They contentiously said only that the Word had become flesh; but later — with what in mind I cannot say — they say that he did not take a mind.

**Anaceph. VII 78** 2. Antidicomarians, who say that holy Mary, the ever-virgin, was joined to Joseph after she had borne the Saviour.

**Anaceph. VII 79** 3. Collyridians, who on a certain appointed day of the year offer a kind of cake in the name of the same Mary; to whom we have given the name Collyridians.

**Anaceph. VII 80a** 4. Massalians, which is translated ‘those who pray’.

**Anaceph. VII 80b** And joined to these are the following, of the sects devised from among the Greeks: those called Euphemites, Martyrians and Satanians.

**Anaceph. VII 80c** This is the summary of the seventh tome too, and the end of the three books.

**Anaceph. VII 80d** And the sects together are eighty in all.

**Anaceph. VII 80e** And at the very end of the third book, the seventh tome, there comes last the faith of the catholic church, and a defence on behalf of the truth, and the proclamation of Christ’s gospel, and the stamp of the church catholic and apostolic, which has existed from eternity, but in the succession of times was most plainly revealed in the coming of Christ in the flesh.

### Sect 77: Dimoerites (Apollinarians)

Against the Dimoerites, as they have been called by some, who do not confess the incarnation of Christ as complete, the fifty-seventh, but the seventy-seventh in the series.

**77,1,1** Next after these, again, there has flowed into the world a doctrine alien to the faith, grievous to us in its presumption — from what cause I cannot say, but so that the devil, who ever troubles human nature and, so to speak, makes war on it, might not let us alone, casting his bitter poisons into wonderful foods and, as it were, putting bitterness alongside in honey — so it has come through some who are admired for the height of their life and are always proclaimed with praises for orthodoxy.

**77,1,2** For indeed this is his work — his who envied our father Adam from the beginning and is hostile to all men — as it has also been said by some wise men that envy is ever the adversary of great successes.

**77,1,3** So too, through persons of greater standing, he has cast in certain pretexts, so as not to leave us and the holy church of God free of grief, but ever troubled and warred upon.

**77,1,4** For it seemed good to some — even to some who set out from among us, who are held in great affection, and are always extolled with praises by us and by all the orthodox — to turn their mind aside from the coming of Christ in the flesh, and to say that Christ our Lord, when he came, took flesh and soul, but did not take mind, that is, a complete man;

**77,1,5** what they have contributed to the world by this I do not know how to say, or from which of those before them they learned it, or what profitable gain they have made from it, or what favour they have done to us and to their hearers and to the holy church of God, having worked nothing among us except confusion and division, and grief, and the loss of our sweetness and love toward one another.

**77,1,6** For abandoning the sequence and straightness of the divine Scriptures, and the confession of guilelessness, and the prophetic, evangelical and apostolic faith, they have brought in on us a sophistical and fabulous doctrine, and with it a train of many terrible things, fulfilling in themselves the saying, “Some will fall away from sound teaching, giving heed to myths and empty chatter.”

**77,2,1** The aged and venerable man, ever beloved by us and by the blessed Pope Athanasius and by all the orthodox, Apollinarius of Laodicea — he it was who first conceived this teaching and put it forward.

**77,2,2** At first, when it was sounded in our ears by some of those whom he had made his disciples, we did not believe that a man such as he had brought this teaching into the world, and we still waited patiently in expectation and hope until we should learn the exact truth.

**77,2,3** For we said that the young men who came to us from him, not understanding the deep things spoken by so learned and intelligent a man and teacher, were inventing these things of themselves and had not learned them from him.

**77,2,4a** For there were many points disputed among the very people who came to us.

**77,2,4b** For some of them had the daring to assert that Christ brought down his body from above; and this strange talk, lingering in people’s minds, was advancing toward something worse; others of them denied even that Christ had taken a soul.

**77,2,5** And some dared even to say that the body of Christ was consubstantial with the Godhead, and they threw the upper regions into great turmoil; because of them it became necessary for a synod to be convened and to anathematize such people.

**77,2,6** Minutes were also drawn up, copies of which were sent to the blessed Pope Athanasius; and on account of these minutes the blessed man himself was compelled to write a letter against those who say such things, sending it with threatening words to the most reverend bishop Epictetus, because he had deigned to give those who caused the disturbance even a reply on this matter.

**77,2,7a** And the same blessed man, writing clearly about the faith, in that same letter also denounced those who assert these things and stir up trouble.

**77,2,7b** I have thought it altogether necessary to set out a copy of this letter here.

**77,2,7c** And it is as follows.

**77,2,7d** Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, to Epictetus, bishop of Corinth.

**77,3,1a** For my part I supposed that all the idle talk of every heretic of whatever kind had come to a stop as a result of the synod which met at Nicaea.

**77,3,1b** For the faith which the fathers confessed at that synod, in accordance with the holy Scriptures, suffices both to overturn every impiety and to establish the godly faith in Christ.

**77,3,2** That is why, now too, when various synods have been held, in Gaul and Spain and great Rome, all who assembled, as though moved by one Spirit, unanimously anathematized those who kept themselves hidden while holding with Arius — Auxentius of Milan, I mean, and Ursacius and Valens, Gaius from Pannonia;

**77,3,3** and because such people devise for themselves the names of synods, they wrote everywhere that no synod in the catholic church should be named except only the one held at Nicaea, which is a trophy over every heresy, and above all over the Arian, on whose account chiefly that synod was then assembled.

**77,3,4a** How then, after so much, do some still attempt to dispute or to inquire?

**77,3,4b** Now if they are of the Arians, it is no wonder that they slander what was written against them, just as the Greeks too, when they hear “The idols of the nations are of silver and gold, a work of human hands,” count the teaching about the Holy Spirit foolishness.

**77,3,5** But if those who wish to overturn it by their inquiring are among those who are thought to believe rightly and to love what was declared by the fathers, they are doing nothing other than, as it is written, giving their neighbour a muddy overthrow to drink, and wrangling over words to no useful end but to the ruin of the simple.

**77,4,1a** I write thus after reading the minutes drawn up by your Godliness, which ought never even to have been written, so that no memory of these things might pass to those who come after.

**77,4,1b** For who ever heard such things?

**77,4,1c** Or who is it that taught or learned them?

**77,4,2a** “For the word of the Lord will come forth from Zion, and the law of God from Jerusalem.”

**77,4,2b** But from where did these things come forth?

**77,4,3a** What Hades belched out the saying that the body from Mary is consubstantial with the Godhead of the Word?

**77,4,3b** Or that the Word has been changed into flesh and bones and hair and a whole body, and has been altered from his own nature?

**77,4,4a** And who ever heard at all among Christians that the Son wore a body by convention and not by nature, or who was ever guilty of such impiety as to say and think at once that his Godhead, which is consubstantial with the Father, was itself circumcised and became imperfect instead of perfect?

**77,4,4b** And that it was not the body that was nailed to the tree, but the very essence that fashioned nature?

**77,4,5** And who, on hearing that the Word refashioned for himself a passible body, not out of Mary but out of his own essence, would call the man who says this a Christian?

**77,4,6a** And who devised this unlawful impiety, so as even to let it enter his thoughts and to say that anyone who declares that the Lord’s body comes from Mary holds no longer a Trinity in the Godhead but a Quaternity?

**77,4,6b** So that, on this account, those of such a mind say that the flesh which the Saviour put on out of Mary belongs to the Trinity’s essence.

**77,4,7** And from where again did some belch out an impiety equal to those already mentioned, so as to say that the body is not later than the Godhead of the Word, but has been co-eternal with him for ever, since it was composed of Wisdom?

**77,4,8** And how did those called Christians dare even to doubt whether the Lord who proceeded from Mary is Son of God in essence and in nature, while as regards the flesh he comes of David’s seed and of the flesh of holy Mary?

**77,4,9** Who then have grown so bold as to say that the Christ who suffered in the flesh and was crucified is not Lord and Saviour and God and the Father’s Son —

**77,4,10a** or how can people wish to be named Christians who say that the Word came upon a holy man as upon one of the prophets, and did not himself become man by taking the body from Mary, but that the Christ is one and the Son of God another, he who was the Father’s Son before Mary and before the ages?

**77,4,10b** Or how can they be Christians who say that God is one and the Word of God another?

**77,5,1a** These things were in the minutes, stated in different ways, but having one and the same meaning, which looks toward impiety.

**77,5,1b** Because of them, those who pride themselves on the confession of the fathers made at Nicaea were divided and fought against one another.

**77,5,2** And I marvelled that your Godliness bore with it, and did not stop these people from saying these things and set the godly faith before them, so that either they might hear it and be quiet, or, if they spoke against it, be named heretics.

**77,5,3** For the things stated above are not fit to be spoken or heard among Christians; they are in every respect alien to the apostolic teaching.

**77,5,4** This is why I too have had their words written into the letter bare, just as they were spoken, so that the hearer may see from them alone the shame and impiety in them.

**77,5,5** And although it would be fitting to accuse and expose at greater length the shame of those who have conceived these things, still it is well for the letter to go no further than this and to write nothing more.

**77,5,6a** For things shown so plainly to be base ought not to be handled further and laboured over, lest they be thought open to doubt by the contentious.

**77,5,6b** It is enough to answer such things with this alone and to say that these things are not of the catholic church, nor did the fathers hold them.

**77,5,7a** But lest the inventors of evil procure for themselves a shameless pretext from complete silence, it is well to recall a few things from the divine Scriptures.

**77,5,7b** For perhaps even so they will be put to shame and cease from these filthy notions.

**77,6,1a** What put it into your minds, sirs, to say that the body is consubstantial with the Godhead of the Word?

**77,6,1b** For it is well to begin from this, so that when this is shown to be unsound, all the other such things may be shown to be so as well.

**77,6,2a** Now from the Scriptures it cannot be found; for they say that God came to be in a human body.

**77,6,2b** Indeed, the fathers too who assembled at Nicaea said that not the body but the Son himself is consubstantial with the Father.

**77,6,2c** And it is confessed that he is from the essence of the Father, but the body from Mary, again according to the Scriptures.

**77,6,3** Either, then, deny the synod at Nicaea and bring these things in as heretics, or, if you wish to be children of the fathers, do not think contrary to what they themselves wrote; for from this too we may see the absurdity.

**77,6,4** If the Word is consubstantial with the body, which has its nature from the earth, and the Word is consubstantial with the Father according to the confession of the fathers, then the Father himself too will be consubstantial with the body that came from the earth.

**77,6,5** And why do you still find fault with the Arians when they say the Son is a creature, while you yourselves declare the Father consubstantial with creatures, and pass over into another impiety, asserting that the Word was changed into flesh and bones and hair and sinews and a whole body and was altered from his own nature?

**77,6,6** For it is time for us to say openly that he came into being from the earth; for the nature of bones, and of the body as a whole, comes from the earth.

**77,6,7a** What then is this great madness, that you fight even against yourselves?

**77,6,7b** In saying that the Word is consubstantial with the body you signify one thing in relation to another, while in saying that he was changed into flesh you picture an alteration of the Word himself.

**77,6,8a** And who will bear with you any longer, if you so much as utter these things?

**77,6,8b** For you have turned aside into impiety beyond every heresy.

**77,6,8c** For if the Word is consubstantial with the body, the mention of Mary and the need for her are superfluous, since the body could have existed eternally even before Mary, just as the Word himself also does, if indeed, according to you, he is consubstantial with the body.

**77,6,9a** And what need was there, too, of the Word’s coming, that he should either put on what is consubstantial with himself, or else, altered from his proper nature, become a body?

**77,6,9b** For it is not of itself that the Godhead takes hold, so as to put on what is consubstantial with itself.

**77,6,10** Nor indeed did the Word, who ransoms the sins of others, sin, so that, changed into a body, he should bring himself as an offering on his own behalf and ransom himself.

**77,7,1a** But it is not so — far from it.

**77,7,1b** For it is Abraham’s seed that he takes hold of, as the apostle said; hence he had to be made like his brethren in every respect and to take a body like ours.

**77,7,1c** For this reason Mary is truly set in place, so that he might take this from her and offer it for us as his own.

**77,7,2a** Isaiah pointed to her when he prophesied, saying, “Behold, the virgin shall conceive in the womb and shall bear.”

**77,7,2b** And Gabriel is sent to her — not merely to a virgin, but to a virgin promised in marriage to a man, so that by means of the betrothed he might show Mary to be truly human.

**77,7,3a** And Scripture records her giving birth, and says that she wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and that the breasts which he sucked were called blessed.

**77,7,3b** And a sacrifice was offered, because the child born had opened the womb.

**77,7,3c** And all these were the marks of a virgin giving birth.

**77,7,4** And Gabriel announced the good news to her with care, saying not simply “that which is begotten in you,” lest the body be thought to have been brought into her from outside, but “from you,” so that what was begotten might be believed plainly to be from her by nature — nature itself showing this, that the body of a virgin cannot yield milk unless she has given birth, and that a body cannot be nourished with milk and wrapped in swaddling clothes unless it has first been born by nature.

**77,7,5** This is what was circumcised on the eighth day; this is what Simeon received into his arms; this became a little child and grew, and became ten years old, and reached its thirtieth year.

**77,7,6** For it was not, as some have supposed, the very essence of the Word that was turned and circumcised, since it is unalterable and unchangeable, as the Saviour himself says, “See me, that it is I, and I have not been altered,” while Paul writes, “Jesus Christ is yesterday and today the same, and for ever.”

**77,7,7** But in the body that was circumcised and carried, that ate and grew weary, that was nailed to the tree and suffered, was the impassible and incorporeal Word of God.

**77,7,8** This was what was laid in the tomb, when he himself went to preach even to the spirits in prison, as Peter said.

**77,8,1a** This above all exposes the senselessness of those who claim that the Word was turned into bones and flesh.

**77,8,1b** For if this were so, there would have been no need of a tomb.

**77,8,1c** For the body itself would have gone on its own to the spirits in Hades to preach to them.

**77,8,2a** But as it is, he himself went to preach.

**77,8,2b** And Joseph wrapped the body in a linen cloth and laid it to rest in Golgotha, and it has been made plain to all that the body was the Word’s own body, not the Word itself.

**77,8,3** And when it had risen from the dead, Thomas handled it and saw on it the marks of the nails, which the Word himself endured as he saw them being driven into his own body; and though able to prevent it, he did not prevent it, but rather the incorporeal one made the properties of the body his own, as being his.

**77,8,4a** Indeed, when the body was struck by the servant, he said, as though suffering himself, “Why do you strike me?”

**77,8,4b** And though by nature he could not be touched, he nevertheless said, “I gave my back to scourges, and I did not turn my face away from spittings.”

**77,8,5** For what the humanity of the Word suffered, the Word, being united with it, referred to himself, so that we might be able to share in the Godhead of the Word.

**77,8,6** And it was a paradox that he was the one who suffered and did not suffer: suffering, because the body that suffered was his own and he was present in that very thing which suffered; not suffering, because the Word, being God by nature, is impassible.

**77,8,7** And he, being incorporeal, was present within the body that could suffer, while the body held in itself the Word who could not suffer, doing away with the weaknesses of the body itself.

**77,8,8** And he did this, and it came about so, in order that, receiving what is ours and offering it as a sacrifice, he might abolish it, and then, clothing us with what is his, he might make the apostle say, “This perishable thing must clothe itself with imperishability, and this mortal thing must clothe itself with immortality.”

**77,9,1** Yet these things did not come about by convention — far from it — as some again have supposed; but since the Saviour truly became man, salvation came about for the whole man.

**77,9,2** For if the Word was in the body by convention, as they hold, and what is said to be by convention is an appearance, then the salvation and resurrection of human beings that is spoken of is found to be in seeming, according to the most impious Mani.

**77,9,3** But in fact our salvation did not come about in appearance, nor of the body alone, but salvation came about truly in him for the whole man, soul and body.

**77,9,4a** Therefore the Saviour’s body from Mary was human by nature, according to the divine Scriptures, and real.

**77,9,4b** And it was real because it was the same as ours.

**77,9,4c** For Mary is our sister, since we are all from Adam.

**77,9,5a** And no one who remembers what Luke wrote would doubt this.

**77,9,5b** For after he had risen from the dead, when some supposed that they were not seeing the Lord in the body from Mary but were beholding a spirit instead of it, he said, “Look at my hands and my feet and the marks of the nails, that I am he myself; feel me and see, for a spirit has no flesh and bones, as you observe I have.”

**77,9,5c** “And having said this, he pointed out to them his hands and his feet.”

**77,9,6a** From this, again, those can be refuted who dared to say that the Lord was altered into flesh and bones.

**77,9,6b** For he did not say, “as you see that I am flesh and bones,” but “that I have,” so that the Word himself might not be thought to have been turned into these, but might be believed to have them himself, both before his death and after the resurrection.

**77,10,1** Since the proof of these things stands thus, it is superfluous to touch on the rest any further and to labour any point about them.

**77,10,2** For the body in which the Word was present is not consubstantial with the Godhead but was truly born of Mary; and the Word himself did not turn into bones and flesh but came to be in flesh.

**77,10,3a** For the saying in John, “The Word became flesh,” has this meaning, as can also be found from a like case.

**77,10,3b** For in Paul it is written, “On our behalf Christ has become a curse”; and just as he did not himself become a curse, but is said to have become a curse because he took upon himself the curse on our behalf, so too he became flesh, not by being changed into flesh, but because he took up flesh on our behalf and became man.

**77,10,4** For to say “The Word became flesh” is again equal to saying that he became man, according to what is said in Joel, “I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh”; the promise was not for the irrational creatures, but is for human beings, for whose sake the Lord also became man.

**77,10,5** Since this text has this meaning, those will rightly condemn themselves altogether who supposed that the flesh from Mary existed before Mary, and that before her the Word had a human soul and had always existed in it before his advent.

**77,10,6a** And those too will cease who said that the flesh is not capable of death but is of the immortal nature.

**77,10,6b** For if he did not die, how was Paul handing on to the Corinthians what he had also received, that Christ died on behalf of our sins in accordance with the Scriptures?

**77,10,6c** And how did he rise at all, if he had not first died?

**77,10,7** And those are greatly put to shame who have so much as entertained the thought that a Quaternity could come about instead of the Trinity, if the body were said to be from Mary.

**77,10,8** For if we say that the body is consubstantial with the Word, the Trinity stays a Trinity, since nothing alien is brought into it along with the Word; but if we call the body from Mary human, then of necessity, the body being alien in essence and the Word being in it, a Quaternity arises in place of a Trinity on account of the body’s addition.

**77,11,1a** In saying these things thus, they do not perceive how they fall foul of themselves.

**77,11,1b** For even if they hold that the body does not come from Mary but is consubstantial with the Word, none the less, by their own folly, they will be shown to be saying a Quaternity — the very thing they pretended to shun, lest they be thought to hold it.

**77,11,2** For just as the Son, who by their own account is consubstantial with the Father, is not himself the Father, but is called Son, consubstantial in relation to the Father, so the body consubstantial with the Word is not itself the Word, but something other in relation to the Word.

**77,11,3a** And since it is other, their trinity will by their own account be a quaternity.

**77,11,3b** For it is not the true and truly perfect and indivisible Trinity that admits an addition, but the one devised by these men.

**77,11,3c** And how are they still Christians, when they devise another besides the God who is?

**77,11,4a** For again, in another sophism of theirs too, one may see their senselessness.

**77,11,4b** But if, because the Saviour’s body is from Mary and is human, and the Scriptures say that it is so, they think that a Quaternity is spoken of instead of a Trinity, as though the body were called an addition, they err greatly, making the thing made equal to its maker and imagining that the Godhead is able to take on an addition;

**77,11,5** and they failed to see that the Word became flesh not to make an addition to the Godhead, but so that the flesh might rise, nor did the Word come forth from Mary in order to be improved, but in order to ransom the human race.

**77,11,6a** How then is it possible that the body ransomed and given life through the Word should make an addition to the Godhead of the Word who gave it life?

**77,11,6b** Rather, a great addition has come to the human body itself from the Word’s communion and union with it.

**77,11,7** From mortal it has become immortal, and being natural it has become spiritual, and having come from the earth it has passed through the heavenly gates; the Trinity, however, even when the Word has taken a body from Mary, is a Trinity, admitting neither addition nor subtraction, but is ever perfect, and in the Trinity one Godhead is known, and so in the church one God is proclaimed, the Father of the Word.

**77,12,1** From this, then, those too will henceforth be silent who once said that he who came forth from Mary is not himself the Christ and Lord and God.

**77,12,2a** For if God was not in the body, how was he called Emmanuel the moment he came forth from Mary, which is interpreted “God with us”?

**77,12,2b** And how, if the Word was not in flesh, was Paul writing to the Romans, “From whom is the Christ as regards the flesh, who is God over all, blessed to the ages, amen”?

**77,12,3** Let those, then, who formerly denied that the crucified one is God confess that they have erred, being persuaded by all the divine Scriptures, and above all by Thomas, who, after seeing in him the prints of the nails, cried out, “My Lord and my God.”

**77,12,4** For the Son, being God and Lord of glory, was in the body that was ingloriously nailed and dishonoured; and the body suffered as it was pierced on the tree, and from its side flowed blood and water, but, being in fact the Word’s temple, it was full of the Godhead.

**77,12,5a** For this reason the sun, seeing its own Creator enduring in the body that was being outraged, drew in its rays and darkened the earth.

**77,12,5b** But the body itself, having a mortal nature, rose beyond its own nature because of the Word within it; and it has ceased from the corruption that belongs to its nature, and has become the garment of the Word, and having put on the Word who is above man, it has become incorruptible.

**77,12,6a** As for some who imagine and say that, just as the word came to each of the prophets, so too the Word came upon one particular man from Mary, it is superfluous to labour the point, since their folly carries its condemnation openly.

**77,12,6b** For if he came in this way, why was this one born of a virgin, and not he too of a man and a woman?

**77,12,6c** For it was in this way that each of the saints too was begotten.

**77,12,7a** Or why, if the Word came in this way, is it not the death of each of them that is said to have taken place for us, but this man’s death alone?

**77,12,7b** And why, when the Word sojourned with each of the prophets, is it said of him from Mary alone that he sojourned once for all at the consummation of the ages?

**77,12,8** Or why, if he came in this way, as he came in the saints of former times, do all the rest, having died, still remain unrisen, while he from Mary alone rose on the third day?

**77,12,9a** Or why, if the Word came in like manner as to the others, is he from Mary alone called Emmanuel, as being a body filled with Godhead and born of her?

**77,12,9b** For Emmanuel is interpreted “God with us”.

**77,12,10a** Or why, if he came in this way, when each of the saints ate and drank and laboured and died, is it not likewise said that he ate and laboured and died, but only in the case of him from Mary?

**77,12,10b** For what this body suffered is spoken of as though he himself suffered.

**77,12,10c** And while of all the others it is said only that they were born and begotten, of him from Mary alone it is said, “And the Word became flesh.”

**77,13,1** From this it is shown that to all the others the Word came for the sake of prophesying, but from Mary the Word himself, taking flesh to himself, came forth as man, being by nature and by essence the Word of God, but according to the flesh having become man of the seed of David and of the flesh of Mary, as Paul said;

**77,13,2** him the Father too pointed out at the Jordan and on the mountain, saying, “This is my Son, the beloved, in whom I have taken delight.”

**77,13,3** Him the Arians denied, but we acknowledge and worship him, not dividing the Son from the Word, but knowing the Word himself to be the Son, through whom all things came to be and we were set free.

**77,13,4a** That is why we too marvelled how such contention about these things should ever have arisen among us.

**77,13,4b** But thanks be to God: as much as we were grieved in reading the minutes, so much did we rejoice at their outcome.

**77,13,5a** For they withdrew in agreement and made peace on the confession of the godly and orthodox faith.

**77,13,5b** This, then, after much previous reflection, has made me too write these few words, reckoning that perhaps, through silence, grief instead of joy might come to those who by their agreement gave us occasion to rejoice.

**77,13,5c** I ask, then, first your Reverence and secondly those who hear, to receive these things with a good conscience; and if anything here falls short as regards godliness, to set it right and make it known to me; but if it has been written neither worthily nor completely, as by one unskilled in speech, that all may pardon my weakness in speaking of it.

**77,13,5d** Farewell.

**77,13,5e** [It is ended.]

**77,14,1** Since, then, the letter too has been inserted, not only have we set out to write against what is being said on the basis of what we heard from them or from others, but it has also become plain to all that we have slandered no one.

**77,14,2** In what follows I shall deal with the matter as it concerns them, so that we may not on any side be supposed by anyone to be slandering our brethren — though I pray for them even until now that they may correct what seems to grieve us, so that neither they may lose us nor we them.

**77,14,3** For we have often entreated and exhorted this, and we still persist in exhorting them to put away contention and to follow the divine ordinance of the apostles and evangelists and fathers, and the confession of the faith that is free of curious questioning, steadfast and unmoved, and most just in all things.

**77,14,4a** Others have said in our hearing that the Lord, when he came, did not take this flesh of ours, nor flesh like ours, but other flesh besides ours.

**77,14,4b** And would that they said it by way of doxology and praise!

**77,14,5a** For we ourselves too say that the body is holy and undefiled; for he committed no sin, nor was guile found in his mouth.

**77,14,5b** And this is clear to anyone who speaks and thinks about Christ with piety.

**77,14,6** But when we say that it is the selfsame body — that his undefiled body took to itself this very body of ours — the lowliness and impairment in us who have transgressed are not there because the body is alien and strange, but on account of our sins and trespasses.

**77,14,7** For the Lord did not take one body while we have another, but the very same body, kept safe in him and preserved undefiled.

**77,15,1** Others of them, carried along even to this day by a certain contentiousness and led on by alien notions — not following the teaching of the fathers, nor holding fast the head of the faith, from which the whole body, supplied and knit together through the joints and ligaments, grows with the growth of God, as the apostle says,

**77,15,2** but as though perhaps their hearing had been muddied by certain strangers — these too, coming nearer to Valentinus and Marcion and Mani, supposedly for the honour of Christ, indulge in fancies rather than speak the truth.

**77,15,3** Whenever they hear from us that Christ had our body, they at once turn to the fables that belong to their contentiousness,

**77,15,4** saying that he had nails and flesh and hair and whatever else, yet not such as we have, but that he had other nails and other flesh, and all the rest not such as we have but different from ours — wishing again, forsooth, in sophistical fashion, to gratify Christ with their vain words, after the manner of Valentinus and the heresies mentioned.

**77,15,5** For they say — whenever we confess that all that belongs to Christ is perfect (aptly is it written of such people, “busybodies who do no work”) —

**77,15,6** for, alarming the minds of the simpler, they say at once, “Then he had need of what belongs to the habit of the flesh, whether for evacuation or for the privy, or the rest,” all the things that seem to be clever, but are in fact dreadful and rather silly, as the prophet says, “For who has required these things at your hands?”

**77,15,7a** For concerning which of the saints — though the prophets were human beings and not gods, and so were the evangelists, and the rest who were of soul and flesh, being like us and beyond doubt — has anything been written about such matters?

**77,15,7b** And where has Scripture not rather borne witness to the more dignified things in the saints, let alone in the Lord Christ?

**77,16,1** Let them tell us, these scarers of the sheep and frighteners of the doves and chasers of Christ’s lambs and nurslings, where did Moses provide for himself during the forty days?

**77,16,2** Where did Elijah see to his bodily needs by the torrent of Cherith, at the time when he would eat bread in the morning and meat at evening, conveyed to him by the ravens at the command of God?

**77,16,3a** For it would have been foolish for Scripture to talk about these things, as it is foolish now for these people to investigate them.

**77,16,3b** For what profit is there in such things?

**77,16,3c** Or what is the use of it, except only to lead to unbelief in what was received beforehand, holding out pretexts through frigid talk and vain subversion?

**77,16,4** And again, let them tell us for what reason, when God so willed, he made it so that for forty years the children of Israel neither grew their hair long, nor did their sandals wear out, nor were their garments worn through or soiled.

**77,16,5a** Had these too, then, come from heaven?

**77,16,5b** Were such people gods?

**77,16,5c** And yet they were not held in praise, but in many things provoked God to jealousy; were they not of like passions with us?

**77,16,5d** But it was so that God might show that with him all things are possible, and that it rests with him for things both to happen and not to happen.

**77,16,6** For lest some should again ascribe to them what is above nature, because of the things done for them by God as marvels — namely, that their hair did not lengthen, their clothes did not grow old, and the other things, and that man ate the bread of angels?

**77,16,7** For our sake the divine Scripture, taking precaution, says, “Let each take an iron peg in his belt, so that whenever he squats down in a place, he may dig and cover his own dung, for you are a sanctified people, and the Lord dwells in the midst of the camp.”

**77,16,8** And on this point the children of the Hebrews also bring forward a story, that this provision lasted with them for a certain time, until God willed to show this wonder among them: that although they ate both meat and quails, it came about that they had no need even of this.

**77,17,1** And if among the Hebrews, out of regard for their fathers, this is sung either by way of gracious embellishment or in truth — though they know that those whose cause they plead were men, corruptible and not gods, and of flesh and blood and soul —

**77,17,2a** who will bear to hear from these people the audacious things said about Christ, God the Word who came from above, and about his glorious and true coming in the flesh in all respects?

**77,17,2b** In it he fulfilled what was said, “tempted in all things as a man, without sin.”

**77,17,3** For it was in his power, though he had our flesh in truth, not to do the things that seem mean to us, and to do such things as were dignified and befitting his Godhead in due proportion — he through whom the children of Israel too did not grow their hair long and their garments were not soiled; and these things happened to them according to tradition.

**77,17,4a** That he also had garments made by men is beyond doubt.

**77,17,4b** For they divided his garments among them, and for his clothing they cast lots.

**77,17,5** And if his garment was from men, it is plain that it was of wool and of linen; and things made of linen and of wool were lifeless and without sensation.

**77,17,6** But when he wished to display the might of his Godhead, he was transfigured and made his face appear like the sun and his clothes white like snow.

**77,17,7** For all things are possible to the One who is able: to stir up beyond expectation, and to refashion into glory and brightness even things without sensation and without breath, like the rod of Moses, like the sandals of the children of Israel.

**77,17,8a** For it is agreed by all that the apostles were holy men, corruptible in body like us, but incorruptible because of the glory of God that dwelt in them.

**77,17,8b** And Peter’s shadow healed all who were brought to him with infirmities, and handkerchiefs and aprons from Paul’s garments work mighty deeds.

**77,18,1** And how do these people pry into God, fabricating shameful notions about which there has never been any need for discussion — not for a prophet, not for an evangelist, not for an apostle, not for a writer?

**77,18,2** For whatever such things these people say, even if they wickedly suspect ten thousand things beyond these, they will not overturn our ancestral faith, which proclaims Christ in truth.

**77,18,3a** For Christ was born in the flesh in truth from Mary the ever-virgin through the Holy Spirit, and straightway from his conception he is called Emmanuel, which is “God with us”.

**77,18,3b** He is not born a second time.

**77,18,4a** And the child fled into Egypt with Joseph and Mary, since they were seeking the child’s life, as one who could be killed in the flesh.

**77,18,4b** But he was worshipped by the magi as true God, born in the flesh and not in seeming.

**77,18,5** And when he came up from Egypt, because of Joseph’s fear he did not enter Jerusalem, on account of Archelaus, since the child could be seized and suffer in the flesh before the time what he was to suffer.

**77,18,6a** But he was prevented by John, being recognized as Master by the servant, because he was God made man in truth.

**77,18,6b** Yet he did not accept the honour offered by his own servant on such an occasion, so that he might fulfil all righteousness in the flesh, in a true and perfect incarnation, leaving us the pattern of salvation.

**77,18,7** Moreover he grew weary from the journey in truth, and not merely grew weary but also sat down, because he truly became man; and he cried out, saying, “Come, all who toil and carry heavy loads, and I will give you rest,” so as to show his Godhead to be capable of giving rest to all the multitudes of the world that come to him.

**77,18,8** Moreover he underwent temptation by the devil, and continued forty days without eating or drinking, to show that his Godhead lacks nothing.

**77,18,9** For he did not endure it hungry, as one practising abstinence philosophically like us, straining and forcing himself, but without lacking anything, because of his true Godhead.

**77,18,10** And afterwards, Scripture says, he was hungry, to show the true incarnation of the Godhead, which allowed his coming in the flesh to share in needs that are reasonable and real, so that the true course of things might not cause the true incarnation to vanish.

**77,18,11a** For at the fig tree too he was hungry, and he made real clay.

**77,18,11b** But God spoke a word to the fig tree, and it came to pass.

**77,18,11c** And aboard the vessel he rebuked the wind, and it ceased.

**77,18,12** And through the spittle and the clay — by the word of his Godhead, and by the spittle of his incarnation, and by the clay again, as with Adam — he graciously fashioned for this man too the member that was lacking; for all things were perfect in him, suffering in the flesh but impassible in the Godhead, until he rose from the dead, henceforth not suffering at all, no longer dying at all.

**77,18,13a** And if some, because he did not take his body from the seed of a man, think it to be different, it does not at all follow that for this reason it is not like our body.

**77,18,13b** For once it is confessed to be from Mary, it was ours.

**77,18,13c** For Mary too was not different from our bodies, since Adam too was not from the seed of a man, but was fashioned from the earth.

**77,18,14a** And it does not at all follow that, because he was from the earth and not from the seed of a man, he was different from our bodies.

**77,18,14b** For we have been begotten from him, and we are not different from his body, although we are begotten from the seed of a man and from the womb of a woman.

**77,18,15a** But some, often reasoning sophistically about these things and keeping them in mind, have fallen away from the matter in hand, while some again of those who came to us, piling up superfluous talk about ten thousand other things and more, slandered the man who is renowned with many praises.

**77,18,15b** And in truth, I think, they caused the disturbance by going further than was needful, whether through lack of learning or through failure to follow the argument, or by going out on their own account and making pronouncements.

**77,18,15c** But now let what I have said about the superfluous matters suffice up to this point, since readers will understand that we are consumed neither by envy nor by hatred toward the man.

**77,18,16a** For we pray that he may not be parted from the church of Christ and from the sweetness of all the brotherhood, but rather that he may lay aside his insistence on the contention over this word and turn back, according to what is said, “Return, return, O Shulammite, return, and we will look upon you.”

**77,18,16b** Nevertheless, I shall take up again the course of the subject before us.

**77,19,1** He does not wish to call Christ’s coming in the flesh perfect, but he also repels the salvation of some, instilling fear and saying that one must not say that he himself took up a perfect man, supposedly on the basis of the text which says, “The Lord takes up the meek.”

**77,19,2** But there is nothing remarkable in this, nor can anyone show any difference, in saying that the Lord took up flesh, or that he took on a perfect incarnation — just as among us many expressions are often used with the same name.

**77,19,3a** For it says, “The Lord takes up the meek,” and “He took me up out of the flocks of the sheep,” and “He was taken up”; and two men said, “Why do you stand, men of Galilee?

**77,19,3b** This one who was taken up from you.”

**77,19,4a** And “to take up” carries no difference at all in saying “he took up,” or “he took,” or “he formed for himself his own incarnation”; those who wish to rise up against the simple do not frighten us with this expression.

**77,19,4b** And so one ought to speak; and let no one think that we are slandering, or that we speak the words about this subject in mockery.

**77,19,5a** For I often deliberated about writing on this, so that no one should think that we rise up against him out of enmity.

**77,19,5b** For no one has done us any harm, as I speak in human terms, nor carried off what is ours in the world.

**77,19,6** But while I was deliberating about not writing, I was compelled by the truth itself, so as to pass over none of those who have held anything contrary to the faith, so that afterwards too the godly who read it may recognize that our account was not prompted by worldly rivalry.
