**De Fide 5,5** This is why it is said, “One is my dove, my perfect one,” since all things are brought to completion up to her, even if the age should count itself in times and seasons, in years and spans of generations, whether by kings or consuls or Olympiads or governorships.

**De Fide 5,6** And the eighty concubines are those who stand among the queens and before the kingdom in the flesh — that is, the faith — and before this very bride and virgin, the spotless one and dove, the only one to her mother and to her that bore her.

**De Fide 6,1a** For she is the church, born of one faith and brought forth through the Holy Spirit, the only one to the one and only mother who bore her.

**De Fide 6,1b** And all that came after her and before her are named concubines; they have not become altogether strangers to the covenant and the inheritance, but they have not been dowered by the Word, nor have they received the Holy Spirit to dwell in them, but have had only a union with the Word in conscience.

**De Fide 6,2** For the Hebrew expressed the concubine well, calling her phelegestha: pheleg, which is translated ‘half’, and estha, ‘woman’, as if to say ‘half a woman’.

**De Fide 6,3a** For, so far as it concerned the Lord, he has called all to the light of freedom, saying, “As long as you have the light among you, walk in the light,” and so has the holy apostle, saying, “But you are children of day and children of light.”

**De Fide 6,3b** And again in the divine Scripture: “He who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light.”

**De Fide 6,4a** So too concubines are not brought to their husbands openly, nor with the rite of fulfilment, nor with a dowry; even if they have union with the bodies of the men, they cannot have the honour and title and security and marriage portion and bride-gifts and dowry and legitimacy of the free wife.

**De Fide 6,4b** The concubines, then, are the heresies counted in order, eighty, as I said above.

**De Fide 6,5a** And let no one wonder if each of them is also called by other names in each country.

**De Fide 6,5b** But this too must be observed, that often each heresy in turn has split within itself and been divided into many parts and names; for it is no wonder, for that is how it is.

**De Fide 6,6** We find the number eighty and one: the one because of her who is set apart from them all, allotted to the bridegroom alone and acknowledged by him with such a title as this, “My dove is one,” and again, “my perfect one,” since all the concubines are ignoble and are not measured by guilelessness, nor by purity and gentleness.

**De Fide 6,7** So from the beginning there are those connected with what is called Barbarism and Scythianism, up to the Massalians mentioned before, seventy-five in number; and Hellenism, from which come the Hellenic heresies; and Judaism, from which come the Jewish ones; and Samaritanism, from which come the Samaritan ones — the three being added to the seventy-seventh number and filling it up to the number eighty,

**De Fide 6,8** while one remains over, that is, the holy catholic church and Christianity, truly so named from the beginning, believed in alongside Adam, and prior to Adam, and before all ages together with Christ, according to the will of Father and Son and Holy Spirit, and with all who in each generation were well pleasing to God, plainly revealed at his coming into the world, and now, after all these heresies, the concubines indeed, praised again in hymns by us, as in the sequence of the account.

**De Fide 7,1a** For the Word himself counted thus in the Song, speaking of sixty queens and eighty concubines and young women past numbering.

**De Fide 7,1b** “But my dove,” he says, “my perfect one, is one; she is her mother’s only one, the chosen of her who bore her.”

**De Fide 7,2** And afterwards he shows how she will be found among all, as being more honoured than all and ruling over all and alone chosen by him, whose children are heirs of the king and true children, as children born of the promise, not children of the slave woman, nor of a concubine, nor of the others who are described as without number.

**De Fide 7,3** For even if Abraham had children by Keturah the concubine, the children of Keturah are not fellow heirs with Isaac; but they received gifts, by way of a legacy, so that the figure might remain for the higher sense of the account, so that some might not despair of the calling of Christ.

**De Fide 7,4** For the gifts which he gave to Ishmael and to the sons of Keturah were a figure of the good things that were to come for the conversion of souls to the faith and the truth.

**De Fide 7,5** For to Hagar, who was a slave woman and was cast out by Abraham (like the Jerusalem below, which served as a slave together with her children, concerning which it has been said, “I have flung away your mother,” and again, “I gave a bill of divorce into her hands”) — to this slave woman Hagar, I say, he gives, rather symbolically, for the hope of conversion, a skin of water, to show the power of the washing of regeneration, given as a gift of life to the unbelievers and for the conversion of all the nations to the knowledge of the truth.

**De Fide 7,6** But to the sons of Keturah the gifts were a store of goods — gold and silver and clothing — and the things which Abraham, in a mystery, shut up in the bags, frankincense and myrrh and gold, from what came through the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah, that is, through those with Chedorlaomer and Birsha and the rest who had taken the captives from Sodom and Gomorrah and the other cities, and had plundered the horses and carried off the multitude of the people as captives, and seized the possessions and goods of each and a great quantity of other things;

**De Fide 7,7** all this he himself brought back at that time from the slaughter of the kings, and, not daring to give back what had already been set apart for the Lord God, he gave them as gifts, with the other things, to his sons by Keturah, as we have found in the traditions of the Hebrews.

**De Fide 8,1** At the coming of Christ, since these same children of Abraham by Keturah had been sent away by Abraham, and had gone off and settled in the Arabian parts of the country of Magodia, the magi who came from the succession of those seeds offered gifts and presents to Christ in Bethlehem, for a share in the same hope — those same presents — when they came, having seen the star;

**De Fide 8,2a** and of these presents the prophet sets out the clear demonstration, saying, “Before the child knows how to call father or mother, he will take the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria in the presence of the king of the Assyrians.”

**De Fide 8,2b** For these things had been taken from Damascus in the times of Abraham, as I said before, by the kings who came, and from Samaria.

**De Fide 8,3a** When, then, did he take them before he knew how to call father or mother, if not when the magi came and opened their bags — or their treasures, as some of the copies have it — and offered myrrh and frankincense and gold?

**De Fide 8,3b** And do you see how the expressions and sequences of the truth hold together?

**De Fide 8,4** So too these heresies are concubines, and their offspring have obtained gifts, having received the name only, called only by the name of Christ and having accepted the few words from the divine Scripture, so that through them they may understand the truth,

**De Fide 8,5** if they will; but if they will not, but return to Herod (for they are charged not to return to Herod, but to reach their own country by another way) — if they do not do what has been commanded, the gifts are in vain for them, as the journey would have been for those men had they returned to Herod; because these same heresies likewise counterfeit the teachings of the divine words.

**De Fide 9,1a** These, then, are the eighty concubines, whose number is here set down, and those queens are the souls counted by generations, that is, men and patriarchs.

**De Fide 9,1b** And the maidens without number are among the remaining philosophies throughout the whole world and among the ways of life of each soul, one being praiseworthy, another not.

**De Fide 9,2a** For who could count the diversity of this world?

**De Fide 9,2b** For how many others have not sprung up among the Greeks following the four very conspicuous ones already mentioned, and, further, after those heresies and those that followed them, souls and opinions arising each on its own according to each man’s judgement in a show of youthful vigour?

**De Fide 9,3** As some are called Pyrrhonians, and many others, whose names and opinions I shall set out below in order — many indeed are those that have come to our knowledge, but they are a tiny fraction of those that exist in the world.

**De Fide 9,4** And those from the Greeks are these, of which I would place first, from the beginning, the judgement and opinion of Thales of Miletus.

**De Fide 9,5a** For Thales of Miletus himself, being one of the seven wise men, declared water to be the primal origin of all things.

**De Fide 9,5b** For he says that all things are from water and are resolved again into water.

**De Fide 9,6a** Anaximander, the son of Praxiades, himself also of Miletus, said that the boundless is the beginning of all things.

**De Fide 9,6b** For from it all things come into being, and into it all things are resolved.

**De Fide 9,7** Anaximenes, the son of Eurystratus, himself also of Miletus, says that air is the beginning of the universe and that all things are from it.

**De Fide 9,8** Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, the son of Hegesibulus, said that the homoeomeries are the beginnings of all things.

**De Fide 9,9a** Archelaus, the son of Apollodorus, or according to some of Milto, was an Athenian, a natural philosopher; he says that all things have come into being from earth.

**De Fide 9,9b** For this, as he says, is the beginning of the universe.

**De Fide 9,10** Socrates the moralist, the son of Elmaglus, or of Sophroniscus, and of Phaenarete the midwife, said that a man ought to busy himself only with what concerns himself, and with nothing more.

**De Fide 9,11** Pherecydes, for his part, says that earth came to be prior to all things.

**De Fide 9,12a** Pythagoras the Samian, son of Mnesarchus, declared the monad to be God, and that without it nothing has come to be.

**De Fide 9,12b** He said that the wise ought not to sacrifice animals to the gods, nor indeed to eat anything that has a soul, nor beans, nor to drink wine.

**De Fide 9,12c** He said that all things from the moon downward are passible, but that the things above the moon are impassible.

**De Fide 9,12d** He said too that the soul passes into many animals.

**De Fide 9,12e** He also ordered his disciples to keep silence for a period of five years, and at the last he named himself a god.

**De Fide 9,13a** Xenophanes of Colophon, the son of Orthomenes, said that all things come into being from earth and water.

**De Fide 9,13b** And of all things, as he said, nothing is true.

**De Fide 9,13c** Thus the exact truth is unclear to us, and seeming is wrought over all things, especially over things unseen.

**De Fide 9,14** Parmenides, the son of Pyres, an Eleatic by birth, himself also said that the boundless is the beginning of all things.

**De Fide 9,15a** Zeno of Elea, the eristic, holding the same as the other Zeno, says that the earth is motionless and that no place is empty.

**De Fide 9,15b** And he puts it thus: a thing in motion moves either in the place where it is or in the place where it is not.

**De Fide 9,15c** And it moves neither in the place where it is nor in the place where it is not; hence nothing moves.

**De Fide 9,16** Melissus, the son of Ithagenes, a Samian by birth, said that the universe is one, but that nothing is stable by nature, and that all things are perishable in potency.

**De Fide 9,17** Leucippus of Miletus, or according to some of Elea, he too an eristic, also said that the universe is in the boundless, and that all things come about by appearance and seeming and nothing in truth, but that they appear so, like the oar in the water.

**De Fide 9,18a** Democritus the Abderite, son of Damasippus, declared the world to be boundless and to lie over the void.

**De Fide 9,18b** He said also that there is one end of all things, and that cheerfulness is the best, but griefs are the boundaries of vice; and that what seems just is not just, but that what is contrary to nature is unjust.

**De Fide 9,18c** For he called the laws an evil invention, and said that the wise man must not obey laws, but live as a free man.

**De Fide 9,19** Metrodorus of Chios said that no one knows anything, but that the things which we think we know we do not know accurately, and that one ought not to attend to the senses; for all things are in seeming.

**De Fide 9,20** Protagoras the Abderite, son of Menander, declared that gods do not exist, and that there is no god whatever.

**De Fide 9,21** Diogenes of Smyrna, or according to some of Cyrene, held the same opinions as Protagoras.

**De Fide 9,22** Pyrrho of Elis, having collected all the doctrines of the other wise men, wrote counter-arguments to them, overturning their opinions, and was satisfied with no doctrine.

**De Fide 9,23a** Empedocles of Acragas, the son of Meton, introduced fire and earth and water and air as four primal elements, and said that at first there was enmity among the elements.

**De Fide 9,23b** For formerly, he says, they had been separated, but now they have been united, as he says, having become friends with one another.

**De Fide 9,23c** So according to him there are two principles and powers, enmity and friendship, of which the one unites and the other separates.

**De Fide 9,24** Heraclitus of Ephesus, the son of Bleson, said that all things are from fire and are resolved again into fire.

**De Fide 9,25** One Prodicus calls the four elements gods, and then the sun and the moon; for from these, he said, the life-giving power comes to all.

**De Fide 9,26a** Plato of Athens said that God, matter and form exist, and that the world is generated and perishable; and he says that the soul is ungenerated and immortal and divine.

**De Fide 9,26b** And that it has three parts, the rational, the spirited and the appetitive.

**De Fide 9,26c** He used to say that marriages and wives ought to be held in common by everyone, and that no man should keep a single wedded wife privately, but that men who wish should consort with women who are willing.

**De Fide 9,27** Aristippus of Cyrene: being a glutton and a lover of pleasure, he said that pleasure is the end of the soul, and that whoever enjoys pleasure is happy, while he who has no pleasure at all is thrice wretched and ill-starred, as they say.

**De Fide 9,28a** Theodorus, surnamed the Atheist, said that talk about God is nonsense.

**De Fide 9,28b** For he thought that there is no divinity, and for this reason he urged everyone to steal, to swear falsely, to plunder, and not to die for their country.

**De Fide 9,28c** For he said that the world is a single fatherland, and he called only the prosperous man good, and said that the unfortunate man should be shunned, even if he is wise.

**De Fide 9,28d** And that the fool who is rich and unruly is to be preferred.

**De Fide 9,29a** Hegesias of Cyrene: he said that there are neither friendships nor favours.

**De Fide 9,29b** For he said that they do not exist, but that a man gives a favour because he is in need, or does good because he has received something better.

**De Fide 9,29c** He also said that to live is profitable for the worthless man, but to die for the wise, so that some on this account called him the Death-Persuader.

**De Fide 9,30** Antisthenes, born of a Thracian mother but himself an Athenian, at first a Socratic and then a Cynic, said that one must not envy another for his evils, or for the disgraceful things men do among one another; and that the walls of cities are precarious against the betrayer inside, whereas the soul’s walls are unshaken and cannot be breached.

**De Fide 9,31a** Diogenes the Cynic, from Sinope, the city on the Pontus, followed Antisthenes in everything.

**De Fide 9,31b** He said that the good is within the reach of every wise man, and that all other things are nothing but trifles.

**De Fide 9,32** Crates of Boeotian Thebes, himself also a Cynic, said that to own nothing belongs to freedom.

**De Fide 9,33** Arcesilaus maintained that the truth is attainable by God alone, but not by man.

**De Fide 9,34** Carneades held the same opinions as Arcesilaus.

**De Fide 9,35a** Aristotle, the son of Nicomachus, was by birth a Macedonian from Stagira according to some, but according to others a Thracian.

**De Fide 9,35b** He said that there are two principles, God and matter, and that the things above the moon enjoy divine providence, while the things below the moon are without providence and are carried along by some irrational motion, at random.

**De Fide 9,35c** And he says that there exist two worlds, an upper and a lower, the upper being imperishable and the lower perishable.

**De Fide 9,35d** And he calls the soul the entelechy of the body.

**De Fide 9,36** Theophrastus of Eresus held the same opinions as Aristotle.

**De Fide 9,37a** Strato, who was from Lampsacus, said that the hot substance is the cause of all things.

**De Fide 9,37b** And he declared the parts of the world to be boundless, and said that no living creature is receptive.

**De Fide 9,38** Praxiphanes the Rhodian held the same views as Theophrastus.

**De Fide 9,39** Critolaus of Phaselis held the same opinions as Aristotle.

**De Fide 9,40a** Zeno of Citium, the Stoic, said that one ought not to build temples to the gods, but to have the divine in the mind alone, or rather to hold that the mind is God; for it is deathless.

**De Fide 9,40b** And he said that the dead should be thrown to animals, or to fire.

**De Fide 9,40c** And that one may make use of favourite boys without restraint.

**De Fide 9,40d** He said that the divine governs all things.

**De Fide 9,40e** And that the causes of events are in one respect in our power and in another not in our power; that is, some events are in our power and others are not in our power.

**De Fide 9,40f** He also spoke of the soul following its severance from the body, and he named it a long-lived spirit; yet he did not say that it is altogether imperishable, for it is consumed by the length of time into the invisible, as he says.

**De Fide 9,41** Cleanthes says that the good and the noble are pleasures, and he called the soul alone the man, and said that the gods are mystic figures and sacred names, and he maintained that the sun is the torch-bearer and the world the initiates, and he called those possessed by things divine ‘rites’.

**De Fide 9,42** Persaeus taught the same doctrines as Zeno.

**De Fide 9,43a** Chrysippus of Soli wrote unlawful laws.

**De Fide 9,43b** For he said that sons ought to unite with their mothers, and fathers with their daughters.

**De Fide 9,43c** In other matters he agreed with Zeno of Citium.

**De Fide 9,43d** Besides this he said also that men may eat human flesh.

**De Fide 9,44a** And he said that the end of all things is luxurious enjoyment.

**De Fide 9,44b** Diogenes of Babylon said that all things are constituted from pleasure.

**De Fide 9,45a** Panaetius of Rhodes said that the world is immortal and ageless, and paid no heed whatever to divination, and did away with what is said about the gods.

**De Fide 9,45b** For he said that talk about God is idle chatter.

**De Fide 9,46** Posidonius of Apamea said that the greatest good among men is wealth and health.

**De Fide 9,47** Athenodorus the Tarsian shared the opinions of Chrysippus and taught the same as Zeno.

**De Fide 9,48a** Epicurus, son of Neocles, brought up at Athens, followed a pleasure-loving life and did not blush to consort publicly with licentious women, besides what we said about him earlier.

**De Fide 9,48b** Again, he said that there are no gods, but that chance alone governs all things, and that nothing in life is voluntary, neither learning nor want of education nor any other thing, but that everything comes about for everyone against their will.

**De Fide 9,48c** And one ought not, as he says, to blame anyone or to praise anyone; for they do not undergo these things willingly.

**De Fide 9,48d** He said that one ought not to fear death.

**De Fide 9,48e** And he affirmed, as I have already said, that the universe has its constitution from atoms and that the world is in the boundless.

**De Fide 10,1a** These, then, are the ones from the Greeks who have come to our knowledge.

**De Fide 10,1b** But as for the others, as many as there are throughout the barbarian, Greek and Roman lands and the other regions of the inhabited world:

**De Fide 10,2** seventy-two distasteful philosophies are recorded in the brotherhood of the Indians — of the Gymnosophists, of the Brahmans (these alone are praiseworthy), of the Pseudo-Brahmans, of the corpse-eaters, of the doers of shameful things, of the callous; to speak of these one by one, and of the abominable things done among them, we have thought superfluous and not even fitting, because of the great corruption among men, both of vice and of its practice.

**De Fide 10,3** For in Media, again, six different heresies are said to exist; and in Ethiopia how many, and among the Persians, or in Parthia, or in the Elamite country, or the Caspian, or the country of the Germans, or Sarmatia, or how many among the Daunians, or among the Zicchi and the Amazons, the Lazi and the Iberians and the Bosporans, or the Geli, or the Seres, or the other nations — differences of laws, and of philosophies, and of heresies, and a measureless multitude of differences!

**De Fide 10,4a** So among the Seres the men braid their hair, sitting at home, perfuming themselves and making themselves womanish, preparing themselves for the women, while the women, on the contrary, crop the hair of their heads, gird themselves with a man’s girdle, and carry out all the work of the fields.

**De Fide 10,4b** But with the Geli, by contrast, the doers of base deeds win praise from their very laws.

**De Fide 10,5a** And among the Greeks, how many mysteries and rites are there?

**De Fide 10,5b** As the women who keep the Megara and the women who keep the Thesmophoria differ from one another, and so many other things: the mysteries at Eleusis, of Deo and Pherrephatta, and the shameful deeds of the shrines there, the stripping of women — to put it more decently — drums and flat cakes, bull-roarer and basket, wool worked up, and the cymbal, and the kykeon prepared in a cup; and so many others: the mysteries of Archemorus at Pytho,

**De Fide 10,6** and others at the Isthmus, of Athamas and of Melicertes the offspring of Ino; and those who carry the phallus about, and the women who perform the phallic exercises of shamelessness; and the men who serve Rhea, who have cut off the male child and go on living without the form of their parts, no longer able to be men and not become women; and others,

**De Fide 10,7a** the Dionysians, who initiate into the Curetes and the distribution of flesh, wreathed with snakes, crying in their revels “oua, oua”, still calling upon that Eve who was deceived through the serpent, or, with the rough breathing, calling upon the serpent, taking the word from the Hebrew to serve their own error.

**De Fide 10,7b** For the children of the Hebrews call the woman Eua when it is pronounced with the smooth breathing, but the serpent Heuia when it is pronounced with the rough breathing.

**De Fide 11,1a** And what shall I say?

**De Fide 11,1b** For time will fail me as I tell of the things that are unspeakable in number among the differences of men with respect to virtue and wickedness:

**De Fide 11,2a** how many there are in the land of the Egyptians, some initiated to Cronus, shutting themselves up in iron collars, with hair grown very long and with filthy and contemptible clothing, as they pierce their own nostrils with rings each day for Cronus in the place called Astu (this is a small town, a chief village in the so-called Prosopite nome), at the accursed rites of the public gathering of those led astray, and of those who beat out a din and celebrate orgies, putting on a show, so they claim, of frenzied sacred revelations.

**De Fide 11,2b** These men are utterly accursed.

**De Fide 11,3** And among how many others: as those near the Butic nome, or in the little town of Buto itself, who nurse Harpocrates, who are already old men in age, who at the sacred festival are compelled by the demon to perform the fantastic frenzies of Horus.

**De Fide 11,4** Each of the citizens, even one who is already exceedingly old, together with young men of like ways and others of every age from youth upward, priests, so they claim, of this same Horus and of Harpocrates, shaven on the head — or rather, each shamelessly bears the mark, at once servile and accursed and childish, bearing it — given over to playthings besides the clever things that come from the demon, frenzied and senseless, rush about laughing without restraint;

**De Fide 11,5** and first anointing their faces with gruel and fine flour and other vulgar contrivances, putting their faces into a boiling cauldron, and deceitfully goading the crowds into frenzy with a supposed wonder from the face, they wipe it off the face with the hand and share it with each of those who ask, for a partaking of health and as a cure for pains.

**De Fide 12,1** If I were to describe the women of Memphis and Heliopolis who celebrate orgies, who take the enchantment into themselves with drum and pipe, the dancing women and the women of the triennial festivals, and the women at Batheia and at Menouthis who have abandoned modesty and womanly bearing — with how many swellings of tongue, or with how great a breadth of composition, giving myself up to it, shall I be able to devote myself to the unspeakable number mentioned before?

**De Fide 12,2** For even if I were to take upon myself an exceeding labour, I should leave the comprehension of these things incomplete, since it has been said, “maidens without number.”

**De Fide 12,3** The things at Sais, at Pelusium, at Bubastis, at Abydos, the precincts of Antinous and the mysteries there, those at Pharbaethus, those concerning the goat of Mendes, so many at Busiris, how many at Sebennytus, how many at Diospolis — as in some places they perform rites to the ass in the name of Seth, that is, of Typhon, while others perform them to Tithrambo, which is interpreted Hecate, others are initiated to Senephthys, others to Thermouthis, and others to Isis.

**De Fide 12,4a** And how many such things there are to tell, to speak of which one by one would consume much time!

**De Fide 12,4b** Therefore the saying, fulfilled, will embrace them on every side, through the words “maidens without number.”

**De Fide 12,5** And again, of many other mysteries, and of heresiarchs and makers of schisms, the leaders among the Persians are the Magusaeans, and among the Egyptians those called prophets, the leaders of the shrines and temples [and of the magi]; among the Babylonians those called Gazarenes, wise men and enchanters; among the Indians those called Euilaeans and the Brahmans; and among the Greeks the hierophants and the leaders of the temple-wardens, of the multitude of Cynics and of other unspeakable philosophers.

**De Fide 13,1a** So, as I said before, among the Persians there are those called Magusaeans, who abhor idols but worship idols — fire and moon and sun.

**De Fide 13,1b** And others again in Greece, called Mysians, the Abii, who live on mares’ milk and dwell in an altogether wild country.

**De Fide 13,2** And how many of these things, so many and so great, that are named, even among the praiseworthy ones, will the mind of men be able to gather — how many differences there are of the maidens without number: some for praise and others not praised; some gathering for themselves from their own mind the things that pertain to the practice of a way of life and a rule, and going about openly with long hair; other holy brethren sitting at home in sackcloth and ashes; and still others fully assured in their ways of life and exceeding fasts and toil towards God, in youthful vigour, with a perfect conscience towards the bridegroom; and others,

**De Fide 13,3a** as I said before, not rightly, but acting the bold youth tyrannically against the truth according to some preconception of the mind — as Zacchaeus, who died a short while ago in the hill country around Jerusalem, continued praying with no one at all, but also, on the same principle, boldly undertook to touch the holy mysteries and, though a layman, to perform the sacred rite without scruple.

**De Fide 13,3b** And another, whoever that man was, one of those reputed to have lived at the very summit of the way of life, who dwelt in a monastery in the desert parts towards Egypt,

**De Fide 13,4** and another near Sinai, acted the bold youth, receiving the laying on of hands for the episcopate as if from dreams, and they themselves undertook to sit and to perform the functions of bishops.

**De Fide 13,5** And others, and not a few, have dared to make themselves eunuchs contrary to what has been commanded, for the sake, so they claim, of youthful zeal.

**De Fide 13,6** And others, who suppose that they are showing youthful zeal, are so bold — setting out from among the orthodox, in opposition to those who are already there, and drawing a gathering to themselves — as even to rebaptise, without the judgement of an ecumenical council, those who come to them, supposedly, from the Arians,

**De Fide 13,7** though the matter has not yet, as I said, been decided by the judgement of a council, because the peoples are still mixed until now, and many are orthodox but joined in outward pretence to those who hold the priesthood, until an excommunication of this blasphemous heresy takes place, and then what concerns it will be defined.

**De Fide 13,8a** Of those who rebaptise in this way on their own authority, one has come to our hearing, a presbyter in the country of the Lycians.

**De Fide 13,8b** And there are also others, each of whom prays by himself and not with anyone at all, and others who go about in collars, contrary to the rule of the church.

**De Fide 13,9** Therefore at the end of the whole work I spoke of maidens having no number, those which, according to their own notion, act the bold youth for themselves, not, however, towards the good that perfects the forms of wisdom, of prudence and courage and temperance and justice; and from these others, acting the bold youth towards greater tyranny, turn themselves away from the truth too, so that they cannot be numbered.

**De Fide 14,1** But this one dove and holy virgin confesses God, Father and Son and Holy Spirit — a perfect Father, a perfect Son, a perfect Holy Spirit; the Trinity consubstantial, the Trinity not a fusion, but the Son truly begotten of the Father, and the Holy Spirit no stranger to the Father and the Son;

**De Fide 14,2** the Trinity always existing and never in need of addition, having nothing in itself that is lower, but referred to one unity and one source, that of the God and Father; and that from this Trinity, Father and Son and Holy Spirit, all things have been created, things which once were not, which did not coexist with God nor pre-exist, but came into being out of nothing from the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.

**De Fide 14,3** And that this Father and Son and Holy Spirit deigned from of old to show himself to his saints in visions, so far as each could contain it, according to his gift through the Godhead, which he bestowed on each of those who were deemed worthy — in some cases to behold the Father, as each was able to hear his voice, as far as he could receive it;

**De Fide 14,4a** as he said by the mouth of Isaiah, “Behold, my beloved servant will understand” — this is the Father’s voice; and as Daniel beheld the Ancient of Days — this is the Father seen in a vision.

**De Fide 14,4b** And as again in the prophet, “I multiplied visions, and by the hands of the prophets I was represented” — this is the voice of the Son.

**De Fide 14,4c** And as in Ezekiel, “And God’s Spirit took hold of me and cast me out into the plain” — this concerns the Holy Spirit.

**De Fide 14,5** And there are many such things to tell, of which, recalling a few in part and in passing, we have set down these two sayings to show the character of the church, though there are ten thousand and more like them recorded in the divine Scriptures of the Old and New Testament.

**De Fide 14,6** And that the Lord himself fashioned the body for Adam and breathed into him the breath of life, creating for him a living soul; and that God himself gave the law to Moses — Father and Son and Holy Spirit, the one Godhead; and that it was by this same Godhead that the prophets were dispatched; and that he himself is our God, being God of both Jews and Christians, having called to justification the Jews who do not deny the coming of our Lord Jesus, and saving all who live in accordance with his true faith and who do not deny the truth of the preaching of his true gospel teaching.

**De Fide 14,7** For he came, the Only-begotten came; and so holds our mother the church, the calm harbour of peace, the gladness that breathes the fragrance of the vine in blossom, bearing for us the cluster of blessing, and granting us each day the drink that frees from toil, the blood of Christ, unmixed and true.

**De Fide 15,1** That Christ was born in truth of Mary the ever-virgin through the Holy Spirit, not from the seed of a man, but took the body from the holy virgin herself in truth and not in appearance — flesh truly, a body truly, with bones and sinews and all that is ours, differing from us in nothing except only in the gloriousness of his holiness and Godhead and of a vessel of holiness and righteousness, and having all things perfectly and without sin, and having had a human soul in truth, a human mind in truth — not that we affirm the mind to be a hypostasis, as others say.

**De Fide 15,2** All of them undefiled by sin: a mouth that told no lie, lips that did not speak deceit, a heart that did not turn aside to provocation, a mind not diverted to what it ought not, flesh that did not work the pleasures of the flesh; perfect God from above, who did not come to dwell in a man, but himself wholly became man, not changed in nature, but having embraced his own becoming man together with the Godhead;

**De Fide 15,3** who came to be in the womb of a virgin in truth, was carried in the womb for the due time, was born through the passages of birth without shame, undefiled, unpolluted; who was nursed and taken up in the arms by Simeon and Anna, was carried by Mary, walked, journeyed, became a child, grew up in stature, having all things in himself in perfection; who was reckoned in a number of years, in a number of months, was carried in the womb,

**De Fide 15,4** born of a woman, born under the law; who came to the Jordan and was baptised by John, not needing washings, but, in keeping with his becoming man under the law, not disturbing what is right, so that, as he himself said, all righteousness might be fulfilled; to show that he had put on true flesh, a true becoming man, going down into the waters, giving rather than receiving, providing rather than needing, enlightening them, empowering them as a figure of those who were to be perfected in him, so that those who have believed in him in truth and hold the faith of the truth may learn that he truly became man and was truly baptised,

**De Fide 15,5** and so, through his condescension, they themselves too, coming, may obtain the power of his descent and be enlightened by his illumination, while the saying in the prophet is fulfilled, “for a change of power, for the provision of salvation, of the power of bread taken from Jerusalem, and of the might of water.”

**De Fide 16,1** Here, in Christ, the bread’s power and the water’s strength are made mighty, so that bread may not become power for us, but the power of bread; and while the bread is food, the power within it serves for giving life; and not that the water should only cleanse us, but that in the strength of the water, through faith and working and hope, and through the completion of the mysteries and the naming of sanctification, it may become for us the perfecting of salvation.

**De Fide 16,2** Coming up from the Jordan, he heard the voice of the Father, within earshot of the disciples who were there, to make plain who it was that was borne witness to; and the Holy Spirit came down in the form of a dove — as we have said in many of the heresies — so that the Trinity might not be thought a fusion, the Spirit taking a form in his own hypostasis, and alighting and coming upon him, so that he who was borne witness to might be seen, so that the holy flesh, being dear and well-pleasing to the Father and the Spirit, might be borne witness to, so that the Father might be proclaimed as well pleased with the Son’s coming in the flesh, so that the Son might be seen to be true and might fulfil what was said, “And after this he was seen on earth and lived among men” —

**De Fide 16,3** having come up from the Jordan, and having been tempted by the devil in the desert, clearly and in truth, and having afterwards been hungry, because of the sequence and truth of his coming in the flesh.

**De Fide 16,4** And he chose disciples and proclaimed the truth and healed sufferings; he slept, hungered, journeyed, worked divine signs, raised up the dead, granted the blind their sight, made the lame and the paralysed strong; as he preached the good news, the truth, the kingdom of the heavens, his love for mankind and that of the Father and of the Holy Spirit.

**De Fide 17,1** He who endured the passion for us in truth, in the flesh and in the perfect becoming man, suffered in truth on the cross, the Godhead being with him, yet not changed so as to suffer, but being impassible and unchangeable — the two sequences being clearly understood: Christ suffering for us in the flesh, but remaining impassible in the Godhead;

**De Fide 17,2** not the man being apart by himself and the Godhead apart by itself, but the Godhead being with him, yet not suffering, on account of the purity and incomparable character of its essence, while he suffered in the flesh and was slain in the flesh, yet lives for ever in the Godhead and raises the dead;

**De Fide 17,3** the body being buried in truth and remaining without soul for the three days, without breath and without motion, wrapped in the linen cloth, placed in the sepulchre, enclosed by the stone and by the seal of those who set them there; the Godhead not shut in, the Godhead not buried,

**De Fide 17,4** but going down with the holy soul into the regions under the earth, carrying off from there the captive host of souls, breaking the sting of death, shattering the bars and the adamantine bolts, and loosing the pangs of Hades by its own authority, coming up with the soul, the soul not having been left in Hades nor the flesh having seen corruption,

**De Fide 17,5** the Godhead raising it up, or the Lord himself, God the Word and Son of God, rising with soul and body and the whole vessel, the vessel being thenceforth united into spirit, the very body having become spiritual — the body that once was subject to touch and was handed over to scourges by the voluntary will of the Godhead, and was permitted to be tempted by Satan, and to come near to hunger and sleep and weariness, grief and distress.

**De Fide 17,6a** The holy body itself was thenceforth united with the Godhead, the Godhead being united without omission to the holy body that had suffered such things.

**De Fide 17,6b** For he rose and united it into himself, into one spirit, into one unity, into one glorification, into his own one Godhead.

**De Fide 17,7a** For he appeared in truth, and was touched by Thomas, and ate and drank with the apostles, and stayed with them forty days and forty nights.

**De Fide 17,7b** But he came in when the doors were shut, and after coming in he displayed sinews and bones, the print of the nails and the print of the spear, to show that it was the true body itself.

**De Fide 17,8a** And that it was joined into one unity and one Godhead, no longer expected to suffer, no longer dying, as the holy apostle declares, “Christ has risen; he dies no longer; death is no longer lord over him.”

**De Fide 17,8b** What was passible ever remaining impassible, the divine with body and soul and the whole becoming man,

**De Fide 17,9** being God himself, he ascended into the heavens and took his seat in glory at the Father’s right hand, not having laid aside the body, but having united it into the spiritual, in the perfection of one Godhead; as our bodies too, “which are now sown natural, are to be raised spiritual; which are now sown in corruption, to be raised in incorruption; which are now sown in death, to be raised in immortality.”

**De Fide 17,10a** If, then, ours are thus, how much more that holy, ineffable, incomparable and pure body united with God, which is thenceforth one and of a single form?

**De Fide 17,10b** As the apostle too bears witness in this, saying, “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, we know him so no longer.”

**De Fide 17,11** Not that he separated the flesh from the Godhead, but that it exists and is united with God, yet is no longer according to the flesh but according to the spirit, as he says, “according to the spirit of holiness, from the resurrection of the dead” of our Lord Jesus Christ; and she holds him as God at once, impassible and having suffered, buried and risen, and ascended in glory, coming to judge the living and the dead, as I have said, in truth, “of whose kingdom there will be no end.”

**De Fide 18,1** For this holy church, our mother, believes — as it has been truly proclaimed to her and truly enjoined on her — that we shall fall asleep and rise again with this body, with this soul, with the whole of our vessel, so that each may receive according to what he has done.

**De Fide 18,2** For that there is a raising of the dead, and eternal judgement, and a kingdom of heaven, and rest for the righteous, and an inheritance of the faithful, and a choir with the angels for those who have kept the faith and purity and hope and the commandments of the Lord — these things are true, and it has been proclaimed and made sure and believed that “these will rise to eternal life,” according to what is written in the gospels.

**De Fide 18,3** For all that the apostle and all the holy Scriptures say is true, even if it is taken otherwise by those who have disbelieved and understood amiss.

**De Fide 18,4** But for us this is the faith, and this the honour, and this our mother the church, saving through faith and strengthened through hope and perfected by the love of Christ, in the confession and in the mysteries and in the cleansing power of the washing —

**De Fide 18,5** since “Go and baptise into the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit” — and into the name of a divine Trinity, the naming having no difference; but that one God has been proclaimed and announced to us in the law and in the prophets and in the gospels and in the apostles, in the Old and New Testament, Father and Son and Holy Spirit,

**De Fide 18,6a** the Godhead not being any fusion, but being a Trinity truly perfect: a perfect Father, a perfect Son, a perfect Holy Spirit, one Godhead, one God; to him be the glory, honour and might for ever and ever.

**De Fide 18,6b** Amen.

**De Fide 19,1** This is the faith, the business of our life; this the foundation of the truth; this the virgin of Christ and the guileless dove; this is the life and the hope and the assurance of incorruption.

**De Fide 19,2** But I beg all of you who read this to pardon my lowliness and the weakness of my very small mind, which has grown numb from the great venom of the heresies and is sickened, like one who spits and is nauseated, in the places where, being carried along, it was led into harsh words against some, or called some wretches, or charlatans, or men led astray, or deceivers.

**De Fide 19,3** For because of the great pain of the venom, although we are not in the habit of lashing at anyone readily, we have been compelled to treat them with such words, so as to turn away the minds of some, lest they should in some way suppose that, because we had not openly exposed and published what is said or done among them, we have a share in a mind that assents to the false belief of each of the heresies.

**De Fide 19,4a** I have also composed a short proem for the opening of the treatise, securing myself in advance about these very things and asking pardon, so that no one may hurl any displeasure at us, supposing us worsted and rushing to mockery.

**De Fide 19,4b** And in the proem we also showed which heresies we were going to speak of, and into how many books we divided the whole work, and how many and which we have spoken of in each book, as here too, recalling it again, I likewise point it out, for the benefit of those who read, from every side.

**De Fide 20,1a** There are three books, seven tomes.

**De Fide 20,1b** And in the first book there are forty-six heresies, set out according to the number of the names, and set out in order from the first and the second book to the one that happens to be last: the first book contains forty-six heresies in three tomes, the second book twenty-three heresies in two tomes, and the third book eleven heresies in two tomes.

**De Fide 20,2a** All of you, then, who share in our labour and patiently persevere in reading our work, and who go through it, be exhorted and be deemed worthy to gain the benefit, and to turn the distasteful things of the heresies away from your mind.

**De Fide 20,2b** For we have not exposed them to do harm, but for benefit and for watchfulness, so that none may fall into the allurement of the things mentioned before.

**De Fide 20,3** And when you have gone through the whole labour, or even parts of it, pray for us and entreat that God may grant us a share in the holy, sole, catholic and apostolic church, true and life-giving and saving, and may deliver us from every heresy; and if in anything —

**De Fide 20,4** as men unable to reach out to the limit of the incomprehensible and indescribable Godhead, but as men hard pressed in making a defence, compelled to speak on God’s behalf in human fashion — we were carried away by boldness, as God pardons, do you yourselves pardon too.

**De Fide 20,5a** And again, pray for us that the Lord may grant us the portion we have asked in his holy faith, the only one free from all contrariety, and may grant pardon for our own sins, many as they are, in our Lord Christ Jesus; through him and with him be glory to the Father together with the Holy Spirit for ever.

**De Fide 20,5b** Amen.

**De Fide 21,1** What this only catholic church and guileless dove holds concerning faith — she who is one for her husband, as he says, “One is my dove” — and likewise concerning the unspeakable maidens without number, we have stated briefly: concerning the consubstantiality of Father and Son and Holy Spirit, and concerning the coming of Christ in the flesh, his perfect coming, and other parts of the faith.

**De Fide 21,2** But concerning her ordinances, I must again set out briefly, in part, the form of these ordinances, as many as have by nature been kept in her and are kept, some by command, others by the acceptance of free choice, God rejoicing in the virtue of his teaching.

**De Fide 21,3a** First, the foundation and, so to speak, the first step in her is virginity, practised and kept by many and held in honour.

**De Fide 21,3b** Following on this virginity is the solitary life, among very many monks and nuns.

**De Fide 21,4a** After this, continence, founded on the same course.

**De Fide 21,4b** Then widowhood, with all watchfulness and undefiled conduct.

**De Fide 21,5** Following these orders is honourable marriage, held in great honour, above all marriage to one spouse and with the keeping of the commandments.

**De Fide 21,6** And if anyone, on his wife’s death, or any man’s wife, on her husband’s death, desires to be joined to a second wife or a second husband, following the death of the first husband or of the first wife.

**De Fide 21,7a** The crown of all these, or, so to speak, their mother and begetter, is the holy priesthood, drawn for the most part from virgins, and if not from virgins, from monks.

**De Fide 21,7b** And if there are not monks enough for the ministry, it is drawn from men who abstain from their own wives, or who have been widowed after a single marriage.

**De Fide 21,8** But it is not permitted in her to receive a man twice married into the priesthood, even if he is abstaining or a widower, beginning from the order of bishop, and of presbyter and deacon and subdeacon.

**De Fide 21,9a** After this priesthood comes next the order of readers, drawn from all the orders, that is, from virgins and monks and the continent and the widowed, and from those still in honourable marriage; and if there is need, also from those who after the death of their first wife have been joined to a second.

**De Fide 21,9b** For the reader is not a priest, but is as it were a scribe of the word.

**De Fide 21,10** Deaconesses too are appointed, for the service of women only, for the sake of modesty, should need arise, for the washing or for the examining of bodies.

**De Fide 21,11a** And these too are women married once who have practised continence, or who have been widowed after a single marriage, or who are perpetual virgins.

**De Fide 21,11b** Then next after these come exorcists, and interpreters from one language into another, whether in the readings or in the sermons.

**De Fide 21,11c** Then also the gravediggers, who lay out the bodies of those who have fallen asleep, and the doorkeepers, and all the good order.

**De Fide 22,1a** Assemblies have been appointed by the apostles to be held on the fourth day of the week, on the day before the sabbath, and on the Lord’s day.

**De Fide 22,1b** On the fourth day and on the day before the sabbath they are held in fasting until the ninth hour, because the Lord was arrested as the fourth day was dawning and was crucified on the day before the sabbath;

**De Fide 22,2** and the apostles handed down that fasts should be kept on these days, the saying being fulfilled, “When the bridegroom is taken away from them, then they will fast in those days”;

**De Fide 22,3** and the fast has been enjoined on us not that we may do a favour to him who suffered for us, but that we may confess, for our salvation, the passion of the Lord, which he himself took on for us, and that our fasts for our sins may be acceptable to God on our behalf.

**De Fide 22,4** And throughout the whole year the fast is kept in this same holy catholic church — I mean on the fourth day and on the day before the sabbath until the ninth hour —

**De Fide 22,5a** except only for the whole of Pentecost, the fifty days, during which there is no kneeling and no fast is enjoined.

**De Fide 22,5b** Instead of the assemblies at the ninth hour on the fourth days and the days before the sabbath, the assemblies are held in the morning, as on the Lord’s day; and further,

**De Fide 22,6** in the fifty days of Pentecost of which I spoke before there is no fast, nor is fasting allowed on the Epiphany day, on which the Lord was born in flesh, even if it happens to fall on a fourth day or a day before the sabbath.

**De Fide 22,7** But by good free choice her ascetics fast at all times, except on the Lord’s day and in Pentecost, and keep vigils at all times.

**De Fide 22,8** Every Lord’s day this holy catholic church counts a day of delight, and holds assemblies from dawn, and does not fast; for it is inconsistent to fast on the Lord’s day.

**De Fide 22,9** The same church is accustomed likewise to observe the Forty Days that precede the seven days of the holy Passover, continuing in fasts, but not on the Lord’s days at all, not even in the forty days themselves.

**De Fide 22,10** The six days of the Passover all the people pass in dry eating — I mean that at that time they take bread and salt and water, towards evening.

**De Fide 22,11a** But the zealous also extend their fasts to two and three and four days together, and some the whole week until cockcrow, as the Lord’s day dawns; and they continue in vigils through the six days.

**De Fide 22,11b** Again, they hold assemblies on these same six days, and through the whole forty days from the ninth hour until evening;

**De Fide 22,12** and in some places they keep vigil only on the night after the fifth day, as it dawns into the day before the sabbath, and on the night before the Lord’s day.

**De Fide 22,13a** In some places the service of the dispensation takes place on the fifth day at the ninth hour.

**De Fide 22,13b** And so the dismissal is given, while they remain in the same dry eating.

**De Fide 22,14a** In other places the service of the dispensation is not held except only as the Lord’s day dawns, when the dismissal is given around the crowing of the cocks, on the resurrection day, and at the great festival on the day of the Passover, as has been enjoined.

**De Fide 22,14b** The other mysteries, concerning the washing and the inner mysteries, are performed as the tradition of the gospel and of the apostles has it.

**De Fide 23,1a** For the dead they make commemorations by name, offering prayers and services and dispensations.

**De Fide 23,1b** In this same holy church there are continual morning hymns and morning prayers, and lamp-lighting psalms and prayers together.

**De Fide 23,2** Some of her monks live in the cities, while others dwell in monasteries and withdraw far away.

**De Fide 23,3a** Some have also chosen to wear their hair long, supposedly for the sake of their way of life, from their own mind, though the gospel did not command it and the apostles did not accept it.

**De Fide 23,3b** For the holy apostle Paul cut off this fashion.

**De Fide 23,4** There are other select ways of life kept in this same catholic church — I mean abstaining from all meats, of four-footed animals and of birds and of fish, and from egg and cheese — and other different ways of life, since each will receive his reward according to his own labour.

**De Fide 23,5a** And some abstain from all these, others from four-footed animals only, but take birds and the things that follow.

**De Fide 23,5b** Others abstain from birds too, but take eggs and fish.

**De Fide 23,5c** Others do not take even eggs.

**De Fide 23,5d** Others take fish only.

**De Fide 23,5e** Others abstain from fish too, but take cheese.

**De Fide 23,5f** Others do not take even cheese.

**De Fide 23,5g** And others again abstain even from bread, and others from tree fruits and cooked food as well.

**De Fide 23,6a** Many also make their beds on the ground, while others do not so much as put on shoes.

**De Fide 23,6b** Others wear sackcloth hidden — those who wear it rightly, for virtue and repentance.

**De Fide 23,6c** For it is unseemly to go out in sackcloth that is in plain view, as some do, and unseemly too, as we have said, to go out in collars, as some have thought fit.

**De Fide 23,6d** Most abstain from the bath.

**De Fide 23,7** And some have renounced worldly life, devising for themselves light and untroubled crafts, so that they may not pass an idle life nor eat their bread as a burden.

**De Fide 23,8** Most of them train themselves in psalmody and continual prayers, in readings of the holy Scriptures and in recitation by heart.

**De Fide 24,1** As for hospitality and kindness, and almsgiving to all, the fruit of this holy catholic and apostolic church has been proclaimed to all.

**De Fide 24,2a** She has the washing in Christ in place of the circumcision that has grown old.

**De Fide 24,2b** She rests in the great sabbath instead of the little sabbath.

**De Fide 24,3a** She abstains from communion with all heresies.

**De Fide 24,3b** She renounces fornication and adultery and licentiousness and idolatry and murder and all lawlessness, and magic and sorcery, astrology, omen-taking, the observing of twitchings, incantations, amulets, the so-called phylacteries.

**De Fide 24,4** She renounces theatres and horse races and hunting shows, and musicians, and all evil-speaking and slander, and all strife and blasphemy, injustice and greed and usury.

**De Fide 24,5a** She does not approve of traders, but regards them as the lowest of all.

**De Fide 24,5b** She accepts offerings from those who do no wrong and do not break the law, but live justly.

**De Fide 24,6** She enjoins that prayers be sent up to God continually, with all frequency and earnestness and kneeling, on the appointed days, by night and by day.

**De Fide 24,7a** In some places they also hold assemblies on the sabbaths; not everywhere, however, but among the topmost branches, is the rule kept of not swearing at all, nor reviling, nor cursing, by the command of the Saviour himself, nor indeed lying, so far as possible.

**De Fide 24,7b** Most sell their possessions and give to the poor.

**De Fide 25,1a** This is the character of this holy church, with the faith set out before, and these are the ordinances recorded in her.

**De Fide 25,1b** For such is the church’s character, drawn together from the law and the prophets and from apostles and evangelists, like a sound antidote prepared from many myriads of things for the salvation of those who use it, through the will of Father and Son and Holy Spirit.

**De Fide 25,2a** These are the features of this august bride of Christ.

**De Fide 25,2b** This is the dowry and the testament of inheritance, and the will of her bridegroom, the heavenly Jesus Christ, our Lord; through him and with him be to the Father glory, honour, might, together with the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever.

**De Fide 25,2c** Amen.

**De Fide 25,3** All the brethren with us greet your honour, especially Anatolius, who was deemed worthy, with much labour and the noblest purpose, to write down and correct, in shorthand signs and on drafts, the work against these heresies — the eighty, I mean —

**De Fide 25,4** and with him Hypatius, our most honoured fellow deacon, who made the fair copy from the drafts in quires; for them too be pleased to pray, most honoured and most dear brethren, in all truth.

**De Fide 25,5a** The peace of Jesus Christ our Lord, and the grace, and the truth according to his command, be with you all, most excellent and beloved brethren.

**De Fide 25,5b** Amen.
